News.title: Jewel thieves steal £3m royal necklace decorated with 673 diamonds in daring smash-&-grab heist as CCTV unmasks suspects
News.content:
GEM RAID Jewel thieves steal £3m royal necklace decorated with 673 diamonds in daring smash-&-grab heist as CCTV unmasks suspects

DARING thieves who allegedly swiped a 600-diamond necklace worth an eyewatering £3million are the subject of a major international manhunt.

Two unmasked men were captured on CCTV during the spectacular smash-and-grab heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) in Vienna.



They are accused of shattering a glass display case with a hammer in broad daylight before making off with a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds.

Originally designed for Egyptian royalty, the high-end bling was on loan to the museum as part of an exhibition on the jewellers Van Cleef & Arpels.



Police released photos of their two suspects, who they say made a dash toward Vienna Stadtpark, just south of the museum, after the heist.

One of the perpetrators was believed to be carrying a real firearm, they added in an appeal for witnesses.

Lilli Hollein, MAK general director, said: “The theft of a highly valuable piece of jewellery has hit us hard.”

She added that special security measures had been taken for the glitzy exhibition and that they had been taken “very seriously”.

Hollein said that staff acted as trained during the “armed incident” and that no one had been injured.

Security measures have been ramped up in recent years, “particularly in light of the incidents at major museums,” she added.



Europe has been plagued by a string of similar high-profile heists lately.

Only this Thursday, a trove of prehistoric jewellery and artefacts was pilfered from a Spanish museum.

It came after four “priceless” Renaissance paintings were stolen from a museum in Sicily only a fortnight ago.



Days earlier, Italy’s specialist art-crime unit recovered three masterpieces by Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse.

The paintings, worth a combined €9million (£7.8million), were snatched from a museum near Parma in March during a lightning raid lasting just minutes.

Last October, a gang brazenly stormed the Louvre in Paris and made off with historic jewellery worth a staggering €88million (£75m).

Europol has said that museum heists were becoming “increasingly aggressive, with a shift towards violent and forceful methods”.

The agency added that this change in modus operandi could indicate that “new criminal networks” are getting into the game.



The necklace stolen on Friday was described as a “triumph of white jewellery”.

It was work by Egyptian Queen Nazli in 1939 at the the marriage of her daughter Fawzia to the future Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.

When it was auctioned a decade ago, it had an estimated value of between £3-4million.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Police dog units have since been deployed in Vienna and the surrounding area as forensic experts analyse evidence and CCTV footage.

The exhibition has since been reopened.

News.title: Reform council hires private security guards over asylum seeker fears in worrying first
News.content:
PRIVATE security guards will be hired by a council over asylum seeker worries for the first time.

Leaders at Reform-run Essex blasted Home Office plans to increase the number of migrants living at a former RAF base from around 800 to as many as 1,245.



Minibuses take residents of the Wethersfield centre into Braintree, Colchester and Chelmsford each day.

Council leader Peter Harris spoke of safety fears “particularly among women and girls” and said security officers will patrol the areas.



He said: :“This is a positive and proportionate response to the concerns residents have been raising for many months now.

“It regards the daily bussing of asylum seekers from Wethersfield to Braintree, Colchester and Chelmsford.

“Concerns for community safety are clearly there.

“Particularly among women and girls, because of the daily gatherings of asylum seekers – gatherings which will increase in number and size as the facility expands.

“I have voiced these concerns directly to the Home Office, which now runs a fleet of 17 minibuses to the three nearest towns and cities on a daily basis.”

Mr Harris said “Operation Vanguard” will see security officers patrol the three areas.



He said that two private security officers will now be deployed in each centre to provide a visible presence, reassure residents and deter anti-social behaviour.

Meanwhile, Reform says it will use its conference next week to unveil how it would start fixing “broken Britain” in a first 100 days of government.

News.title: Meet Lindsay Clancy prosecutors Jennifer Sprague & Shanan Buckingham who wore hair bow tributes at trial for Cora, 5
News.content:
A HAIR bow has put an unexpected spotlight on the two veteran prosecutors trying to prove Lindsay Clancy was criminally responsible for killing her three children.

Assistant District Attorneys Jennifer Sprague and Shanan Buckingham have spent five weeks presenting the Commonwealth’s case against the 36-year-old mom.



At Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts, the pair have questioned dozens of witnesses, handled disturbing evidence and challenged Clancy’s claim that postpartum psychosis robbed her of the ability to know right from wrong.

But Buckingham has also attracted attention for something far removed from the legal argument, the large bow she has repeatedly worn in her hair.



The accessory immediately stood out after Buckingham used her opening statement to describe five-year-old Cora Clancy’s personality.

“Cora had just turned five. She was sweet, silly smart. She loved sparkly dresses and wearing bows in her hair,” Buckingham told jurors.

She was later seen questioning witnesses with different bows in her own hair, including a black one and a large white one.

The choice was was quickly interpreted by some court watchers as a quiet tribute to Cora.

But Buckingham has never publicly said the bows were intended to honor Cora, and another lawyer says the prosecutor wore similar accessories long before Clancy’s trial.

Massachusetts public defender Craig Tavares, who has previously faced Buckingham in court, told CT Insider, “My recollection always in a bow or scrunchy.”



He said her appearance during the blockbuster trial was consistent with how he remembered her dressing in other cases.

Still, the coincidence has generated debate because Buckingham specifically drew jurors’ attention to Cora’s love of bows before appearing in them throughout the proceedings.

Some people online have accused the prosecutors of trying to create an emotional visual reminder of the child.

University of Connecticut law professor Todd Fernow told CT Insider

even an unintended choice could raise questions if jurors viewed it as carrying meaning, although he did not believe the accessory alone was likely to become a major legal issue.

The bow debate has placed additional attention on Buckingham, who has spent more than a decade prosecuting cases in Plymouth County.



She joined Plymouth County District Attorney’s Office in 2011 and is chief of its Family Protection Unit, according to her professional profile.



Buckingham graduated from Stonehill College with a political science degree in 2003 before earning her law degree from Northeastern University School of Law in 2011.

She was admitted to the Massachusetts bar that November.

Her work has extended beyond individual criminal prosecutions.

A Massachusetts child-fatality review report listed Buckingham as the team leader for Plymouth County, alongside District Attorney Timothy Cruz.

Sprague, meanwhile, brings more than two decades of experience to the Clancy prosecution.



She has worked for Plymouth County DA’s office since December 2003 and says she has tried 28 homicide cases.

Her experience also includes more than 40 Superior Court trials involving sexual assault, guns, drugs and domestic violence, along with hundreds of district court cases.

Sprague graduated from Bridgewater State University with a political science degree in 1999.

She received her law degree from New England Law Boston in 2003 and was admitted to the Massachusetts bar that December.

Sprague has also been tapped for work involving sexual and domestic violence outside the Plymouth County courthouse.



In 2023, she was among the members sworn into Massachusetts’ Governor’s Council to Address Sexual Assault, Domestic Violence and Human Trafficking.

And the Clancy case is far from the first major prosecution Sprague and Buckingham have handled together.

Just months before Clancy’s trial, the pair prosecuted Michael Hand in the notorious 1986 murder of 15-year-old Tracy Gilpin.

Gilpin disappeared from Kingston, Massachusetts, before her body was found in Myles Standish State Forest.

Hand was arrested more than three decades later after investigators reopened the cold case.



He was sentenced to life in prison in March 2026, with the Plymouth County DA’s office crediting Sprague and Buckingham as the prosecutors on the case.

They also have previously worked together on other serious prosecutions, including a Brockton manslaughter case stemming from the 2017 death of a 64-year-old man.

Their roles in the Clancy trial have again put them at the center of one of Massachusetts’ most closely watched criminal cases.

Buckingham delivered the prosecution’s opening statement on July 27, painting Clancy’s actions as deliberate rather than the product of a psychotic break.

Sprague took the lead for the Commonwealth’s closing argument a month later.



She told jurors that Clancy’s documented mental-health struggles were not themselves enough to make her legally not responsible for the killings.

“This case is not about our mental health system or how it treats women,” Sprague said in her closing argument Thursday.

She argued Clancy deliberately sent her then-husband Patrick away to pick up medication and takeout before taking five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson and eight-month old Callan into the basement.

Clancy had admitted strangling the children with exercise bands on January 24, 2023, before cutting herself and jumping from a second-floor window.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Her attorneys say she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and should be found not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility.



Prosecutors acknowledge Clancy was mentally ill but argue she still understood that killing her children was wrong and deliberately carried it out.

News.title: Moment drug dealer is woken up in bed & arrested by cops after falling asleep next to bricks of cocaine worth £240,000
News.content:
THIS is the moment a drug dealer is woken up while in bed and arrested by armed cops after falling asleep next to several bricks of cocaine worth £240,000.

Rennie Ash, 47, was taken into custody on March 12 after Kent Police stormed into his home in Westover Gardens, Broadstairs.



The dozing drug dealer was found with £240,000 worth of cocaine wrapped in plastic beside his bed.

Bodycam footage captures the raid where cops barged into Rennie’s cluttered bedroom and woke him up.



They shout at him to put his hands in the air and the dazed crook, still wearing his eye mask, followed the orders.

The police snapped handcuffs onto his wrists and asked if there were any controlled drugs in the property, to which Rennie said “no”.

But minutes later, the cops discovered three 1kg bags of cocaine stuffed into a chest of drawers next to his bed.

Tightly wrapped in silver tape and cling film, the illegal haul was worth nearly a quarter of a million pounds.



Officers also seized £3,500 in cash and a mobile phone.

Rennie is then bundled into the back of a police van, wearing a black waterproof coat.

He was arrested and charged with possession of cocaine with intent to supply and possession of criminal property.



In Canterbury Crown Court, Rennie pleaded guilty to both offences.

It was heard that he was already on licence for previous drug dealing offences.

Rennie was sentenced on Thursday 27 August to four years in prison.

Detective Inspector Rob Hemsley said: “The value of the drugs held by Rennie Ash was very high.

“To have £240,000 worth of cocaine flooding a community could have had a real detrimental impact on others.



“His actions displayed a selfish greed which gave no consideration to little else.

“Our officers work relentlessly to deter and disrupt drug dealers like Ash, to ensure their criminality is stopped from harming others.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Financial investigators will now work to ensure that any money Ash made from drug dealing is confiscated.”

News.title: Dolly Parton fans flock to her beloved theme park to celebrate her life with pink tributes, tears & her favourite cakes
News.content:
DOLLY Parton fans are celebrating her life in style at her beloved theme park.

The Sun visited Dollywood three days after the country music icon died from cancer at 80 — and found thrill seekers embracing her belief in “having a lot of fun”.



We joined them on the junior roller-coaster Whistle Punk Chaser, which travels at a sedate 16mph.

The speed suited Dolly because she did not want her wigs to fall off.



She once said: “I got so much to lose, like my wig or my shoes. I don’t like to get messed up.

“I’m gonna have some handsome man mess it up.



“I don’t want some ride doing it.”

Dollywood, which has attracted millions of visitors annually since it opened in 1986, is lined with pink posters of the music legend with the slogan: “I will always love you.”



Visibly emotional fan Sarah Markis, 32, said: “There’s a sense of joy at being able to feel close to Dolly at one of the places she loved the most.

“She wanted her fans to have fun here.”

Members of staff have been told to wear pink as a tribute to the singer.



And a touching memorial has been set up at the front gates where guests can pin flowers, letters and teddies.

Some fans have even brought candles to light, along with letters expressing their love for the star.

One message read: “Heaven is sweeter because of you. Thank you for my childhood.”



A pair of Velour-brand false eyelashes were tucked behind a jar of sunflowers, with the message: “Cried these off from Texas!”

There was also a poster-making station allowing kids to create their own personal notes to Dolly.

Presley Wolan, four, made a touching poster that read: “Live, Love, Dolly.”

Mum Alicia, 35, from Michigan, told The Sun: “She is a massive fan. She bawled her eyes out when she learned of Dolly’s death.

“Her favourite song is 1989 hit Why’d You Come in Here Lookin’ Like That. She can sing the entire thing.”



The Sun has been told the park is “planning something special” for Dolly and her fans. It is currently “top secret” but will be announced next week.

The park’s president Eugene Naughton said: “She taught us how to dream big, so we have very ambitious plans that I know she’ll be proud of.”

In every corner of the park — nestled in the Great Smoky Mountains of Pigeon Forge, Tennessee — Dolly’s life is remembered.

There is a replica of her childhood home, designed by her family, and her music blares from speakers.

Guests can also head to the Dolly Experience, which houses her costumes from events and movies.



And there is a chapel where fans can take a break from the rides and reflect.

Before we left, we tried the park’s famous funnel cakes — deep-fried batter — which were Dolly’s favourite sweet treat.

Dolly was known to say: “I can’t leave the park without funnel cakes.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

One worker said: “She couldn’t get enough of ’em.”

News.title: How is it John Healey’s once unyielding demand for 3% of GDP on defence can suddenly wait now he’s Chancellor?
News.content:
Chancer-lor?

JOHN Healey was hailed as a man of principle when he quit as Defence Secretary over the failure to boost funding for Britain’s hollowed-out Armed Forces.

His bombshell resignation dealt a mortal blow to Sir Keir Starmer just a week before the crucial by-election that put Andy Burnham in pole position to steal his crown.



In a farewell blast, he accused the lame-duck PM of making the country less safe amid “rising threats” and lambasted the Treasury for being “unwilling” to stump up the cash.

But three months on he’s changed his tune.



The threats facing Britain haven’t disappeared.

Nor has the need for stronger defences. The only thing that has changed is Mr Healey’s job.

Now he is Chancellor, responsible for making the Treasury sums add up, his principles have gone out of the window.

His once unyielding demand that Britain must spend three per cent of GDP on defence by 2030 can suddenly wait.

And when it comes to tackling the ballooning £334billion welfare bill, that has been put on hold until next year.

You can hear the clatter of political cans being kicked down the road.



Baffled defence chiefs will rightly ask whether harsh economic reality has finally dawned on Mr Healey now he occupies the Treasury hot seat.

Or if his much-hailed resignation was little more than a cynical and shameless act of theatre?

Pump action

BRITAIN’S motorists are feeling more pain at the pumps, with the cost of petrol at a four-year high.

For hard-working families, every fill-up is another blow to the household budget.

With energy bills and food costs soaring, the prospect of losing the 5p-a-litre fuel duty cut in January spells more misery for many Britons.



Millions rely on their cars to get to work, shop and care for loved ones. They need help — not another tax grab.

The PM promised to give us all some “breathing space” from rising living costs. He should remind the Chancellor of this — and The Sun’s fuel duty campaign — ahead of his Budget in October.

And tell him to KEEP IT DOWN.

Off the rails

NOBODY should face profane or abusive behaviour while doing their job.

That message is often heard over the public address system at major railway stations.



Yet staff are being assaulted in growing numbers, while the chance of offenders facing justice is shrinking.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Court backlogs may explain the collapse but they do not excuse it.

Railworkers are entitled to protection and victims deserve justice.

News.title: Making work pay and properly tackling crime are the only way to save us from a nation of Middlesbroughs
News.content:
IF Broken Britain needs a capital, nowhere fits the bill better than Middlesbrough.

The Teesside town has had the highest crime rate in England for some time, yet still the crime wave of the past week has come as a shock.



Since a car travelling the wrong way down the A66 dual carriageway crashed into a police car early last Saturday morning, killing five youths and two police officers, the town has descended into what many suspect to be an orgy of gang-related violence.

A seven-year-old girl and her aunt were killed in an arson attack on their home, a couple of houses were rammed by cars and a man was stabbed in his own home.



But it is not just the acts of violence themselves that have been so remarkable, as the lawless vigils held by families and friends of the youths who died last weekend.

On Thursday night, five — presumably stolen — cars were set alight in an act of memorial for one of those killed.

Criminality is being brazenly celebrated in a way not seen in Britain since the funerals of the Kray twins three decades ago.

Middlesbrough is becoming like Belfast in the 1970s, albeit without the religion and sectarian divides.



It is descending into a dystopian hellhole straight out of TV show Line Of Duty, where gangs acting according to criminal codes of behaviour are overwhelming the official forces of law and order.

The local police force has had to be reinforced with officers from outside the town in an attempt to regain order.

None of this is to say, of course, that the vast majority of residents of Middlesbrough are not decent, neighbourly people who just want to get on with their lives. But the events of the past week have shown how easy it is for a malign minority to usurp control of a town.



The veneer of civilised values that normally hides the less savoury elements of society has never seemed so thin.

It is so sad to see this happening to a town that once brimmed with pride. The Quaker industrialists who founded the place would have been appalled.

Middlesbrough was once “Ironopolis”, one of the biggest producers of pig iron in the world, as well as a centre of shipbuilding.



Its shipyards turned out trawlers by the dozen, as well as many of the warships that helped keep the transatlantic food convoys moving during the Second World War. They also built the first container ships in the 1960s, before closing in the 1980s.

It is not hard to see the underlying cause of problems in Middlesbrough and elsewhere. Figures released this week by the Office for National Statistics show that 981,000 under-25s in the UK — one in eight of the total — were “NEETs”, which means they were “not in employment, education or training”.

That is shocking enough in itself, yet doesn’t do justice to the full scale of worklessness in former industrial towns like Middlesbrough.

Since heavy industry went into decline in the 1980s we have had a couple of generations grow up in some families without ever knowing paid employment.

If you are aspirational and growing up on a sink estate the obvious opportunities to “better” yourself may well seem to lie in the world of crime.



If we are to avoid more Middlesboroughs, it is absolutely vital that the Government reforms the welfare system so that work pays, and that living a life of idleness on benefits no longer becomes an option.

School and college leavers need to be incentivised to search for work, and rewarded when they find it. If they do not get their careers off to a good start it may rapidly become too late to save them from being sucked into a life of crime.

On the other side of the equation, it needs to be made absolutely clear to people that crime will not pay.

It is sickening to think four of the five who died in the vehicle that crashed into the police car had 37 convictions between them — in spite of the eldest being just 23 and a couple being only 17.

Their crimes included drugs offences, theft, stealing vehicles and assaulting a police officer.



The police and criminal justice system were doing their job in bringing prosecutions against these thugs, yet they were still free to roam the streets.

We could do with a policy of “three strikes and you’re out”, which brought order to US cities in the 1990s, where a third conviction — even for a relatively minor offence — takes you off the streets for a very long time.

Andy Burnham has staked his reputation on reviving the industrial North, and bringing “growth to every postcode”.

Middlesbrough, rather than plush Manchester, should be where he starts.

But he will have to do better than Home Office minister Anna Turley, who last week said she had laid flowers “to pay my respects” to the youths who died.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Their deaths might be a tragedy for their families, but no, they do not deserve our respect. They were thugs who have helped to reduce a once-proud industrial town to a nightmare of criminality.

Removing such people from the streets is going to have to be a large part of winning Middlesbrough back for the decent and law-abiding majority.

News.title: 97-year-old woman rescued after Nepali floods looked like 'a warrior'
News.content:
A 97-year-old woman pulled from flood debris in Nepal is recovering in hospital, according to her doctors.

Guna Maya Bohara's great-nephew, Dipak Bohara, has told BBC Nepali she looked like "a warrior" who had returned victorious from battle.

The operation to pull Bohara out of the rubble of her care home took four hours.

Bohara travelled from Kathmandu to help rescue his great-aunt.

Hundreds of people have been confirmed dead after Wednesday's flash floods, which scientists believe were triggered by a glacier collapsing in the Himalayan border region with Tibet.

Video produced by Mansi Kapur and Kamal Pariyar. Video edited by Suneth Perera, Jasmin Dyer and Andrew Webb.

More on this story here.

News.title: What we know about the 33 British nationals missing in Nepal
News.content:
Families are flying out to Nepal to help the ongoing search for 33 British nationals still missing after deadly floods hit the country.

The brother of Neetu Goyal Tiwari, one of the missing Brits who has not been seen since Wednesday, has appealed to officials to locate his sister.

"Please help us find her", Naresh Goyal told the BBC as he struggled to hold back his emotions.

On Friday, Nepalese authorities named 573 tourists who are still missing in the country and despite fears of a second wave of flooding, search efforts have continued.

To help, the UK is deploying a rapid deployment team to Nepal to support British nationals affected in the region.

The specially-trained crisis response team is expected to arrive in Kathmandu on Saturday, a move that follows Prime Minister Andy Burnham's pledge of Â£5m worth of humanitarian support for relief and recovery efforts.

And as rescue efforts continue in the aftermath of the disaster which killed at least 538 people, details of the missing are slowly emerging.

News.title: Man dies and at least six injured after sign falls at Christian festival
News.content:
A 41-year-old man has died and at least six other people have been injured after reports a large sign had fallen at a Christian festival in West Sussex, police said.

Sussex Police said it was called to the Big Church Festival at Wiston Park, near Steyning, at about 15:38 BST on Friday.

At least six people were taken to hospital for treatment, and a 41-year-old man, from Eastbourne, died at the scene, the force said.

Organisers said following the incident the festival would be brought to a close.

Det Ch Supt Richard McDonagh said he recognised the "immense distress this will have caused people at the festival" and the police were working to establish what happened at the site in Washington Road.

"We know there were thousands of people at the festival and we're urging anyone with any information, or any relevant video footage, to please come forward. You can report it online or call 101, quoting Operation Igloo."

The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) and local authority have been informed, the force added.

Festival organisers said their thoughts were with those affected, and their immediate priority is the wellbeing of those involved and helping people leave the festival site safely.

News.title: 'It's destroying our town': Residents tell of concern after violent incidents near Middlesbrough
News.content:
Residents near Middlesbrough have told the BBC of their concern after a spate of violent incidents in their area, including a crash that killed seven people including two police officers and a house fire that killed a woman and a seven-year-old girl.

Police have said the two incidents are not connected. They have made a series of arrests in relation to the crash and two arrests in relation to the house fire.

On Friday Redcar MP Anna Turley said disorder at a balloon release for one of the young men who died in the crash was "unacceptable".

News.title: Norway's 'grandfather': King Harald remembered as son Haakon takes the throne
News.content:
People across Norway paid tribute to the nation's late King Harald who died in the early hours of Friday morning at the age of 89 after 35 years on the throne.

Mourners gathered outside of the Royal Palace to lay flowers and remember him while his son, King Haakon VIII, officially succeeded him and met with his government.

Harald had been treated at the national hospital in Oslo for a rare blood condition.

On Friday evening, hospital staff and crowds gathered on the streets as the late king's coffin was moved from the hospital to the Royal Palace.

Tributes have been shared within the country and internationally - including by UK King Charles III who sent his "most heartfelt condolences".

News.title: BBC tracks one week of Israeli settler violence in occupied West Bank
News.content:
Violence by Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank is set to reach record levels this year, as human rights groups warn that they are increasingly spreading into new areas of the territory.

Attacks on Palestinians have risen under Israel's current government, alongside a rapid increase in Israeli settlements, illegal under international law.

Many of these attacks are not widely reported on.

The BBC's Lucy Williamson has been tracking settler attacks on Palestinians, which have been observed over the last week alone.

News.title: Wife of man who died after turbulence sues Singapore Airlines
News.content:
Kitchen and her husband, described as her "soul mate", were starting a six-week holiday to Singapore, Indonesia and Australia when the incident happened in May 2024.

The turbulence hit over Myanmar, with the flight then diverted to Bangkok, in Thailand, for an emergency landing.

"There had been some turbulence over Europe, and it had been shaky over the water, but it was around 10 hours into the flight when we encountered the main turbulence," Kitchen said.

"It was so severe; it felt like the aircraft was dropping. I noticed my Kindle and Geoff's phone had fallen to the floor, and I thought the plane was going down."

As the aircraft plummeted, Kitchen said her husband fell on top of her, squashing her into the armrest. Eventually, others helped to move him and a doctor on board began CPR.

Kitchen was taken to hospital while her husband was still on the plane. It was two days before she was told he had died.

It is understood that Geoff suffered a heart attack after the plane suddenly dropped at high altitude.

News.title: Sarfaraz denies knowing about Pakistan threat to end tour
News.content:
Head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed said he and his players did not know about a Pakistan Cricket Board threat to the England and Wales Cricket Board over a Sky interview with the sons of Imran Khan.

During lunch on day one of the second Test, Sky Sports aired an interview with Suleiman and Kasim Khan, the sons of former Pakistan captain and prime minister Imran, who has been in prison for the past three years.

It is understood the PCB raised the prospect of cancelling the Test at Lord's and the remainder of the three-match tour if the interview aired.

A version of the interview was broadcast, and the players returned to the field after the interval to continue the match.

"I don't know anything. I'm just focusing on the match," said Sarfaraz at the end of the second day's play.

"You're talking about the interview? We don't know about the interview."

Asked if there was ever a possibility his players would return for the afternoon session on day one, the former Pakistan wicketkeeper said: "All are OK. We were having lunch at that time."

Legendary all-rounder Imran Khan, 73, had a 21-year international career for Pakistan and famously led his team to World Cup glory in 1992.

He served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022. Since 2023, Khan has been in jail on corruption charges which he denies.

News.title: Four plead guilty to arson attack on Jewish community ambulances
News.content:
Four men have pleaded guilty to destroying four Jewish community ambulances in an arson attack causing Â£1m of damage in north-west London.

Hamza Iqbal, 20, Rehan Khan, 19, Judex Atshatshi, and Saif Ali, both aged 18, pleaded guilty at the Old Bailey to a charge of destroying or damaging property being reckless whether life would be endangered.

The attack, which took place in the early hours of 23 March, saw four vehicles operated by the charity Hatzola set alight in Golders Green.

Prosecutors had said they believed the incident was a targeted attack against the Jewish community.

The court heard three of the men set fire to the fully stocked ambulances, while a fourth had waited in a nearby car.

After the ambulances were set alight, gas canisters exploded inside the vehicles.

As well as destroying each of the Â£250,000 vehicles, the fire damaged four electrical charging stations and cables costing approximately Â£5,000 each.

Leo Seelig, prosecuting, told the court that the Crown Prosecution Service would be arguing that the four men should be sentenced on the basis that the arson attack was related to terrorism.

Mrs Justice Cheema Grubb said she would not rule on the question of terrorism at this stage - with defence counsel arguing that there was no evidence for such a connection.

The judge said that the four would be sentenced following the outcome a trial of a fifth man, Subhan Ahmed, who has denied assisting an offender.

Iqbal and Khan, of Leyton, Atshatshi, of Dagenham, and Ali, of Walthamstow, were remanded into custody.

Run by volunteers, Hatzola has served the north London community of Golders Green, which has a large Jewish population, since 1979.

Hatzola, the Hebrew word for save or rescue, is a large non-profit, Jewish-led organisation that provides a free emergency medical response and transportation to hospitals regardless of faith by volunteer medics.

Community Security Trust, a charity working to protect British Jews from terrorism and antisemitism, welcomed the pleas and said the four's actions "caused immense shock and distress across the Jewish community".

"This was an appalling antisemitic act against a volunteer ambulance service providing emergency medical assistance to people of all backgrounds across north London, simply because those ambulances belonged to a Jewish charity," a spokesperson added.

News.title: Disorder at balloon release unacceptable, says MP
News.content:
Serious disorder at a balloon release for one of the young men who died in the A66 car crash is "unacceptable", an MP has said.

Durham Police said a large crowd gathered on a privately owned field near Haswell, County Durham, on Thursday evening where five vehicles were set on fire and balloons, flares, and fireworks were released.

Redcar MP Anna Turley said it put lives at risk, while Assistant Chief Constable Jon McAdam said the force condemned "anyone who would use that tragedy as an excuse for disorder".

In an update on Friday afternoon, Cleveland Police ACC Dave Sutherland said the force was not currently linking the A66 crash to a house fire which killed a woman and a seven-year-old girl.

It had previously said it could not rule out a link to organised crime in relation to the house fire and the crash.

Earlier this week 17 people were arrested in connection with the investigation into the crash which killed PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38,

Seven more men have also been arrested, bringing the total number of arrests to 24.

Turley said the police force had been "at pains to say we shouldn't think that these are all connected, and we shouldn't be jumping to conclusions".

The BBC understands the King has written to the families of two officers killed in the crash to express his deepest sympathies for their loss.

Meanwhile Middlesbrough FC said it would ask supporters to pay their respects to the officers before Saturday's fixture against West Bromwich Albion.

"We are also showing our appreciation for the dedication and hard work of both men, and to Cleveland police force in protecting and supporting our local community," the club said in a statement.

Seven people, including PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough, died in the crash near Middlesbrough on Saturday. Two people were arrested on suspicion of murder following the house fire in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, on Wednesday.

With regards to Thursday night's disorder, Labour Home Office minister Turley said it "put lives at risk" and left residents "frightened and angry in their own communities".

She added: "People have a right to grieve and to pay their respects - but people also have a right to feel safe in their own homes and neighbourhoods."

News.title: Stadium closures for Old Firm over fan disorder
News.content:
Celtic and Rangers have both been ordered to play their next home Scottish Cup matches behind closed doors after last season's quarter-final was marred by fan disorder.

Both clubs will also have to pay Â£100,000 to the team they are drawn against in that fixture.

The two clubs could also face a second home match without fans if there is a further incident of either side's supporters engaging in "unacceptable conduct" in a Scottish Cup fixture.

Celtic progressed to last season's semi-finals by beating Rangers on penalties at Ibrox, after which fans of both teams spilled on to the pitch.

The sanctions are likely to come into force when both sides enter this season's Scottish Cup in January.

Meanwhile, Rangers say they will provide Celtic with 300 tickets for next month's Scottish League Cup quarter-final at Ibrox.

Celtic had been given 8,000 tickets for the 8 March Scottish Cup tie.

News.title: UK soldiers could get paragliders to drop behind enemy lines
News.content:
British soldiers could soon be given powered paragliders to enable them to fly up to 200 miles behind enemy lines.

The backpack-sized gliders mean Royal Marine and Parachute Regiment troops could fly into hostile areas during the night without the need to drop from aircraft.

Manufacturer Blakcro, which is based in Wiltshire, say the machines can be assembled in eight minutes and launched on foot.

The Ministry of Defence is spending Â£6m on the system, with trials set to begin "in the coming months".

Defence Minister Luke Pollard said the government was building a "more resilient, homegrown defence supply chain and ensuring our armed forces receive the pioneering equipment that can give them the edge on the battlefield".

The paragliders, which have a range of up to 200 miles, can carry body armour, night vision equipment and weapon mounts.

The manufacturers say the titanium-framed machines can be used to enter hostile territory covertly as they are more difficult to detect by radar or sound than traditional aircraft.

The gliders will be powered by a fan but pilots will be expected to launch them on foot.

The technology is currently being used by other Nato member countries.

Blakcro, which employs 11 people, was founded in 2023 and has received government support for two other projects.

The company also works with the US Department of Defense.

The government has said it wants to spend more on UK-made defence equipment and bring smaller companies into the supply chain.

Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to increase defence spending after he resigned from Sir Keir Starmer's government in protest at its investment plans.

As defence secretary, he accused Starmer's government of having no clear timetable to reach the target of spending 3% of the UK's national income on defence.

He is expected to increase spending further - but will not be setting out any plans in his first Budget in October.

Instead, a revised defence plan will be set out as part of a wider government spending review in the spring.

A government spokesperson said: "The first duty of government is to keep its citizens safe.

"The prime minister and chancellor are committed to fully funding the defence investment plan.

"At the spending review we will set out a pathway to meet our NATO commitment of 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 and will set a target date to hit 3% on that path."

News.title: Burnham says he will not vote on assisted dying unlike Starmer
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has revealed he will not vote on the assisted dying bill for England and Wales unlike his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

MPs are likely to get the chance to debate and vote on the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill in two weeks' time.

The bill is identical to the one put to Parliament last year, where it passed in the House of Commons but stalled in the Lords after an unprecedented number of amendments meant it ran out of time.

Burnham said he has his "own personal views on the issue" but it was "a matter for Parliament to decide". Starmer voted in favour of the previous bill when he was PM but did not campaign in favour of it, remaining officially neutral.

Writing to Labour MPs on Friday, Burnham said: "My role, as the prime minister, will be to lead a government that implements the will of Parliament in this area â whether that is to change the law or not.

"I also do not want to unduly influence the debate as prime minister and for every colleague to know it is a genuinely free vote.

"For these reasons, I have taken the decision that it is most appropriate for me not to vote at Second Reading."

He added that "there is no single right position" and it was an "incredibly important and personal debate".

"It is vital that those different views are treated with dignity and respect," he wrote.

While his abstension is a departure from Starmer's support, Burnham stressed that the government as an entity would officially remain neutral on the bill.

When he was Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham indicated he was in favour of assisted dying in principle.

But in June he suggested it would be challenging to implement before social and palliative care were improved.

The assisted dying law would allow adults over the age of 18 who are expected to die within six months to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

News.title: Paul Heaton scores first number one album as Dolly Parton's 9 to 5 finally reaches top 40
News.content:
English singer-songwriter Paul Heaton has scored his first solo UK number one album, his sixth overall.

Heaton's latest chart-topping LP - titled Jenius - follows his three with the Beautiful South and two more alongside former bandmate Jacqui Abbott.

The former Housemartins musician reached the top on Friday, in part, by shifting more vinyl copies than any other album over the past seven days.

Dolly Parton, who died earlier this week, aged 80, has three singles in the top 40, including 9 to 5, which landed at number 12 in this week's UK chart, having previously peaked at 47 in 1981.

Elsewhere on Friday, Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's Rein Me In extended its record as the longest-running number one single in UK chart history.

News.title: Hundreds of migrants enter UK after 10-day lull
News.content:
Tap the questions below

How many people cross the English Channel in small boats?

Between 1 January and 27 August 2026, a total of 16,391 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 43% on the same period the previous year.

These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.

Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered.

Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026.

Boats that arrived in the UK from 28 August 2025 to 27 August 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021.

Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN).

When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

The government has pledged to âsmash the gangsâ behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers.

News.title: Serial rapist police officer passed vetting despite warnings, BBC reveals
News.content:
A police officer - who was later exposed as a violent serial rapist - passed vetting checks to join the force despite having two reports of criminal behaviour against women on his record, BBC Disclosure can reveal.

Alan Greer was investigated by police in 2002 and 2005 for making inappropriate phone calls to women, with one case resulting in a formal police caution.

He was accepted into Strathclyde Police in 2009, despite vetting staff being aware of his previous offending.

The revelation comes a month after Police Scotland told the BBC there had been no "missed opportunities over the years" to identify Greer's offending sooner.

In response to further questions from the BBC, Police Scotland moved to clarify its earlier comments.

It said it had "provided answers to questions relating to Alan Greer's offending during the course of his police career" and did not believe it had been answering questions about his police vetting record.

President Donald Trump on Friday said the U.S. has entered an agreement with Venezuela to take control of 65 billion barrels of the South American country’s oil reserves.

Trump in a social media post announced the agreement he said was negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez.

“The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!” Trump wrote.

The announcement of the deal comes nearly nine months after the U.S. military at Trump’s direction carried out an operation to capture Venezuela’s president Nicolás Maduro and spirit him to the United States to face federal narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges.

Trump faces mounting pressure to address high gas prices as the war in Iran reaches a six-month milestone with no conclusion in sight. The U.S. has tapped its strategic petroleum reserves, which in early August fell below 300 million barrels, down by more than 100 million barrels since the start of 2026.

In the days following Maduro’s ouster in January, Trump floated the idea of U.S. oil companies returning to Venezuela to tap its oil reserves. Trump has argued that Venezuela stole U.S. oil when former Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez’s moved decades ago to nationalize hundreds of foreign-owned assets, including those owned by American oil companies.

Venezuela has one of the largest oil reserves in the world, with an estimated 303 billion barrels of crude oil in the ground. That’s about 17% of the world’s supply, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Unlike other parts of the world, where geologists have to search for untapped oil, the reserves under Venezuela’s soil are largely mapped and known, experts say. But because of dilapidated infrastructure, the country only produces about 1% of the world’s oil.

Thousands of women across the UK develop undiagnosed post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) each year after giving birth, new research has found.

According to a report, the condition is being missed in at least 15,000 women as many GPs mistake PTSD for postnatal depression, which means they do not urgently receive specialist help.

The warning comes after two damning reports into maternity and neonatal services in England from Baroness Amos and Donna Ockenden, which found that mothers and babies were being failed by the NHS.

The report, conducted by University of East Anglia and published in the British Journal of General Practice, has urged the health service to better equip GPs to ensure more women don’t fall through the gaps.

According to recent figures, suicide remained the leading cause of death among women between six weeks and one year after pregnancy in the UK during 2021-2023.

open image in gallery A new report found that many GPs mistake PTSD for postnatal depression

These deaths have been described as the "tip of the iceberg", arguing that many more women are living with serious mental health difficulties but are unable to access the support they need.

Lead researcher and GP Dr Megan Foreman, from UEA’s Norwich Medical School, said: “Research shows that around one in 20 postnatal women develop PTSD, which is equivalent to tens of thousands of mothers across the UK.

“It usually happens after a traumatic pregnancy or delivery, but it can also happen after a medically uncomplicated birth.

“The consequences of untreated birth trauma for women and families can be far-reaching.

“Some women become so anxious that they repeatedly seek reassurance from healthcare professionals for themselves or their baby. Others avoid healthcare services altogether, including during future pregnancies.

“They may also request elective Caesarean sections in later pregnancies to regain a sense of control. Or others may reject recommended medical care or opt for home births, even in high-risk pregnancies, to avoid interventions associated with their previous experience.”

open image in gallery The report found that women may request an elective Caesarean in later pregnancies to regain control ( PA Wire )

While birth trauma is mentioned in national guidance from NICE and NHS England, the report shows that GPs are not given practical advice on how to measure the severity or assess the risks posed.

As a result, Dr Foreman said doctors are effectively “diagnosing in the dark” without the right information to make proper assessments.

Misdiagnosis can be detrimental to women with PTSD because they are then prescribed antidepressants, which are not as effective for treating the condition as psychological therapy.

Dr Foreman said: “Many new mothers attend appointments with their newborns, often combining their own health check with baby examinations or vaccinations. Some may not yet feel able to discuss a traumatic birth experience.

“Asking the wrong questions at the wrong time could leave women feeling unsupported or retraumatised.”

The report warned that any future guidance should be accompanied by better GP training, improved awareness and clear referral pathways into specialist services.

“GPs are uniquely placed to spot warning signs,” said Dr Foreman. “But without better evidence and practical tools, many mothers with childbirth-related PTSD risk being left to cope alone, without the support they need.”

Professor Victoria Tzortziou-Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs, said: “This paper highlights an important gap in how we identify and support women experiencing PTSD following childbirth. Giving birth can be traumatic for some women, and it is vital that those experiencing significant psychological distress are recognised and able to access the right support.

“The six-to-eight-week postnatal check is an important opportunity for GPs to discuss a woman’s physical and mental wellbeing, as well as the health of her baby. But childbirth-related PTSD can be complex to identify. Symptoms may overlap with depression, anxiety and other postnatal mental health problems, and may not become apparent until months after the birth.

“Recognition therefore cannot depend on a single consultation. Women need joined-up support throughout the postnatal period, across maternity services, health visiting, general practice and specialist mental health services.

“We would welcome better evidence, guidance and appropriate tools to support GPs and other healthcare professionals in recognising childbirth-related PTSD. But this must be accompanied by sufficient time to have these important conversations and, crucially, timely access to specialist perinatal mental health services when women need them.”

The recent announcement of Pennsylvania’s first measles-related deaths in decades has ignited a public feud among politicians and health officials who disagree over the role of the contagious disease in the fatalities.

Independent experts say the conflict is a symptom of a social and political debate over how to frame a national surge in measles cases, the worst seen in more than three decades.

Pennsylvania officials this week reported that two unvaccinated residents died after being infected with measles, with Gov. Josh Shapiro stressing that vaccinations could have averted the deaths.

But the announcement quickly came under fire, as a clash erupted between Shapiro, a vaccine-promoting Democrat, and U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a Trump administration appointee with a history of raising alarms about established vaccines. Kennedy said in a social post the deaths “may even have been altogether fabricated.”

Kennedy’s attack echoed statements he made last year, when three measles-related deaths were recorded. Kennedy questioned whether one of the children who died was killed by measles.

Medical experts say the brouhaha has diverted focus from an exploding public health threat.

“Now it's turned political,” said Dr. Amesh Adalja, an infectious disease doctor in the Pittsburgh area and a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. “It's no longer about getting answers and figuring this out.”

The challenges of tallying measles deaths

The U.S. eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status.

Complicating the situation in Pennsylvania are questions about what counts as a measles death, which is rare in the United States. The World Health Organization counts a death when a person has tested positive for measles and when the death occurs within a month from when a rash appears and the death is not obviously due to another cause such as trauma.

State health officials are the ones who report measles cases and measles-associated deaths. The question of defining a measles death hasn't come up much in recent decades because vaccination rates were high and measles illnesses and deaths had become rare.

Recent trends are driving conversations among health officials about how to better track the consequences of a surging problem.

“As measles infections increase, we also need to prepare for more of the tragic complications we have largely avoided in this country for decades," including not only deaths but also hospitalizations and brain injuries, said Janet Hamilton, executive director of the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists, in a statement.

What's known and not known about the measles deaths

In Pennsylvania, what's not disputed is that both people who died had been infected with measles and they were unvaccinated. The unresolved question is whether measles was the main cause, or a contributing cause, of their deaths.

In one of the deaths, an official has reached a conclusion. The Lancaster County Coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, said he is aware of only one death with evidence of measles infection. It was a newborn baby boy who died August 14 — someone too young to get a recommended measles vaccination.

Because one of the boy's family members had measles, investigators tested the boy's lung tissue and found evidence of measles infection, Diamantoni said.

But investigators did not see signs of a swollen spleen or other ravages from a measles infection that would have contributed to the death. The cause is being attributed to a tear in the spleen, but the coroner's office says the virus did not play a role.

The baby “did not die as a result of measles,” Diamantoni said.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health initially refused to disclose any details about the two people who died. But on Wednesday night, state health officials posted on social media that one of the deaths is under investigation by the coroner's office. No information has been released about the second death.

The department said it stands by its announcement, adding that it relies on two questions to determine if a death was measles-related: Did the person have measles and did they die?

As of Friday, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has not updated the latest national tally of measles cases and deaths. The agency said on its website that the scheduled update was delayed, but did not disclose why.

Dr. Paul Offit said he’s worried that two measles-related deaths are an unusually high number in a county that reportedly has about 400 cases. The expected death rate for measles is 1 in 1,000 cases.

That suggests there are a large number of other unreported infections in the Lancaster County area, said Offit, a Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia vaccine researcher.

That’s worrisome, given that this is the time of year when kids go back to school, which could increase the spread of an extremely transmissible disease. Vaccination efforts need to be stepped up “to prevent what I think is a coming disaster,” Offit said.

Adalja faulted Pennsylvania officials for how they announced the deaths earlier this week. It should have only been health and medical officials, stating what is known and not yet known.

“They should learn to keep the politicians out of it,” he said.

The leader of the Seneca Nation in upstate New York is criticizing President Donald Trump's decision to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America,” saying it violates a more than 225-year-old treaty and shows a “blatant disrespect” for the Indigenous people who gave it its name in the first place.

Seneca Nation President J. Conrad Seneca on Friday called for Trump's order to be rescinded and for the Lake Ontario name to remain as a reflection of the Indigenous people in the U.S. and Canada who lived in territory around and along the lake long before the creation of either nation.

“The President cannot assert ownership over our culture or erase it through irresponsible political action," he said in a statement.

Trump this week signed an order directing the Interior Department to update the lake’s name in the U.S. geographic naming service, part of his escalating trade war with Canada. The order showed the change is supposed to be made in 30 days.

Seneca said the renaming violated the 1794 Treaty of Canandaigua, which was signed by President George Washington and the Haudenosaunee confederacy promising perpetual peace and friendship. The Seneca are one of the six nations of the confederacy, also known as the Iroquois Confederacy.

The name Lake Ontario comes from the Huron Indigenous people’s word “oniatarí:io,” which means “lake of shining waters.” The Canadian province of Ontario, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.

In the traditional Seneca language, the lake's name is “sga:nyodai:yoh," meaning “beautiful lake," Seneca said.

Trump floated the name change in recent days as the U.S. announced it was imposing new tariffs on Canadian goods after talks broke down between the countries. Canada responded with its own retaliatory tariffs on American goods, while the country's leaders slammed the idea of changing the lake's name.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the move, noting the lake’s Indigenous roots and that the name predates both the Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence. Trump can't force Canada to follow along with the renaming.

Trump has argued that Canada has been ripping off the U.S. on trade and military issues and suggested Canada should be absorbed as the 51st state.

Most employees on zero-hours or variable contracts stay in insecure roles for at least two years, research suggests.

The Trades Union Congress (TUC) said its analysis disproves assertions that zero-hours positions are primarily sought by students.

The union body condemned "baseless scaremongering" regarding proposed bans on exploitative contracts and rights to guaranteed working hours.

Its study revealed more than half of zero-hours or variable-hour workers report staying with their employer for at least two years, while one in six have stayed for a decade or more.

TUC general secretary Paul Nowak described attempts to weaken new employment protections as "blatant scaremongering", adding: "We are talking about low-paid precarious workers who don’t know how much they’ll be earning from week to week or the hours they’ll be working.”

"This analysis shatters the cynical claim that these are just students with a side hustle who can afford to lose shifts at the drop of a hat. The reality is most of these workers are reliant on their jobs as the main source of their income.”

open image in gallery ( Getty Images )

"That’s why it’s so important that the new Prime Minister ends the scourge of insecure work in Britain and delivers these new rights to guaranteed hours in full.”

"Good employers have nothing to fear from these new rights. This will level the playing field for them and stop the cowboys."

Joanne Thomas, general secretary of the shopworkers’ union Usdaw, said: "Many of our members are regularly working hours that aren’t guaranteed in their contract, which has a massive impact on their lives.

"The right to a guaranteed-hours contract has the potential to provide much greater security for millions of low-paid workers.

"The Government must deliver this right in full to give people the baseline of security that they were promised in the manifesto."

A man has died and at least six others have been injured after a sign fell on visitors at a Christian festival in West Sussex.

The tragic incident took place at Big Church Festival, near Steyning on Friday afternoon.

Sussex Police said officers were called to the site on Washington Road at about 3.38pm to reports that a large sign had fallen and injured a number of people.

On Friday evening, police confirmed a 41-year-old man from Eastbourne died at the scene. His next of kin have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.

Detective Chief Superintendent Richard McDonagh said: “This is a tragic incident and our thoughts go out to the man’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time.

“At least six other people were also injured during this incident and have been taken to hospital for treatment.

“I recognise the immense distress this will have caused people at the festival, and we are working with a number of partners as we seek to establish exactly what happened.

“We know there were thousands of people at the festival and we’re urging anyone with any information, or any relevant video footage, to please come forward. You can report it online or call 101, quoting Operation Igloo.”

open image in gallery Police, ambulance crews, critical care paramedics and specialist response teams were at the scene in West Sussex ( PA Archive )

In an Instagram update posted shortly after 5.30pm, event organisers informed attendees that Friday’s entertainment had been cancelled, adding that all day visitors "must leave the site now".

South East Coast Ambulance Service (Secamb) said its crews were called to reports that “multiple people” needed medical attention.

“Ambulance crews, critical care paramedics and specialist response teams are currently on scene with six patients confirmed so far,” a Secamb spokesperson said.

“We have no further information to share at this time but will provide updates as soon as possible.”

The festival began on Friday and had been set to run until Sunday, but has been cancelled following the tragic incident.

A statement from Big Church Festival said: “We are devastated by the serious incident that took place at Big Church Festival 2026 today, in which a sign fell, injuring at least seven people, one of whom tragically lost their life.

“First and foremost, all of our thoughts are with those who have been affected, their families and friends, and everyone who witnessed what happened. Following today’s incident, we have made the decision to bring Big Church Festival 2026 to a close.”

“If you are camping with us, please return to your campsite and await further updates.

“Campers may leave the site if they wish to do so.

“Thank you for your patience and understanding. We will share further updates as soon as we can.”

According to its website, Big Church Festival was founded in 2009 and is the UK’s biggest Christian festival.

Lauren Daigle, CeCe Winans, Bethel Music and Elevation Rhythm are among the act scheduled to perform.

The Met Office had urged festivalgoers to prepare for windy conditions over the bank holiday weekend.

According to its UK weather map, wind speeds of up to 27mph were recorded in Shoreham, West Sussex, on Friday afternoon.

News.content:

Taking a bit out of Apple’s streaming platform is going to cost a little more now.

The tech giant raised its monthly price of Apple TV to $14.99 per month and $119 per year on Friday - up from 12.99 and $99. Apple One, the company’s bundled service package that includes Apple TV, increased to $21.95 from $19.95.

It’s the company’s fourth streaming service price hike since launching in 2019 for $4.99. It went up to $6.99 in 2022, $9.99 in 2023, and $12.99 in 2025, according to MacRumors.com.

Social media users were not happy with the decision.

“If the price goes any higher than this I will have to give it a re-think,” user VeryClearlyDefined wrote in response to a Reddit post about the price changes. “Apple is not a streaming company, they can afford to keep the price of their service reasonable.”

open image in gallery Hannah Waddingham attends the premiere for Apple TV's Ted Lasso season four at BAM Harvey Theater on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, in New York. Apple TV customers will now pay $2 more per month for access to the show and other content on the streaming platform. ( AP )

Apple isn’t the only company raising subscription costs. In 2026 alone, Peacock, YouTube Premium, Netflix and Amazon Prime Video have increased their monthly fees on at least one of their streaming tiers, according to digital news site Nerdist.

Not only do the services cost consumers more, but the average American isn’t using around half of the streaming services they pay for, an August study from financial services firm Self Financial found.

The company’s new subscription prices come during a year in which Apple has raised prices on several types of hardware.

iPads, Macs and home devices went up 18 percent to 33 percent in June, reported tech site CNET. Apple’s Chromebook competitor, the MacBook Neo, saw a $100 price increase from $599 to $699 in June.

While the company did not offer an explanation about its Apple TV rate increases, CEO Tim Cook said the hardware hikes have to do with a global memory shortage known as “chipflation.”

“On the pricing front, we reluctantly raised prices, I would say,” he said during an Apple earnings call in June. “We did it because we're in what I would characterize as a 100-year flood on the memory pricing, with exponential increases in memory prices.”

open image in gallery The price of an Apple MacBook Neo went up $100 earlier this year due to limited supply and high demand for memory chips ( David Phelan/The Independent )

Memory chips are an essential part of AI data centers. Manufacturers have recognized this and dealt consumers a double blow.

They’ve raised memory prices and have prioritized AI data centers over retail stores and consumers, said Asif Alam, an electrical engineer and president of Florida International University’s Engineering Research Society.

“The companies that make chips earn far more money selling to AI data centers than to the firms that build your television, so they have shifted their factories to serve AI first,” Alam told The Independent in an email.

The Tampa Bay Rays got county approval Friday on a financing plan that will allow them to build a new stadium, a day after city officials approved their part for the $2.3 billion ballpark project that will replace the domed Tropicana Field.

The Hillsborough County Commission voted 5-2 on Friday to approve its $796 million share of the mixed-use entertainment district that includes a new 31,000-seat stadium that will be near Raymond James Stadium, home of the NFL's Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The Rays' new stadium is expected to open in 2029. The Tampa City Council city voted 4-3 on Thursday to approve $80 million.

Rays CEO Ken Babby said the team’s partnership with the county and city on the project secures the long-term future of Major League Baseball in Tampa Bay.

“We now look forward to celebrating before breaking ground with Hillsborough County and the City of Tampa on a future that has long been doubted, but will indeed happen,” Babby said. “By making the Forever Home a reality, the Rays are now home forever in Tampa Bay.”

The Rays have committed to contributing at least $1.3 billion, plus any cost overruns. Another $30 million will come from federal disaster recovery funds.

The Rays ownership reached an agreement earlier this year with Hillsborough College to build the stadium and entertainment district on the campus and to renovate some of the school’s buildings. The property is located next to the New York Yankees’ spring training facility and across a highway from the NFL stadium.

Since the team's inception in 1998, the Rays have played at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, except for moving home games to the Yankees’ George M. Steinbrenner Field in 2025 following hurricane damage at the Trop. The Rays’ lease runs through at least the 2028 season. The team returned to the Trop last month for the start of this season.

A proposed $1.3 billion redevelopment deal for a new ballpark adjacent to the Trop fell through last year, raising new questions about the future of the team, which was bought last September by Patrick Zalupski’s ownership group.

“This has been a long and challenging process, and we know that transformational projects rarely come easily,” Zalupski said Friday. “Today’s vote represents an extraordinary milestone, not simply for the Rays or for a ballpark, but for the future of Tampa and the entire Tampa Bay region.”

News.title: Cherki magic helping Maresca to step out of Guardiola shadow
News.content:
Rumours of Manchester City’s supposed demise without Pep Guardiola appear to be much exaggerated.

They swept past Crystal Palace at Selhurst Park with a style of play under new manager Enzo Maresca that was just as swashbuckling as under his predecessor, with Rayan Cherki playing the role of chief architect. The Frenchman’s two goals included a captivating mazy dribble, which will long be remembered by those who had the fortune to see it.

City created enough space for themselves through clever movement. With Cherki zigging one way and Phil Foden zagging the other, they created even more by dribbling past a mesmerised Palace back three that became a back five at times and still could not cope.

Erling Haaland also scored twice. Even with the creative and unpredictable talents of those behind in a four-man attacking City midfield, Haaland remains irreplaceable with his ability to convert chances.

However, this night belonged to Cherki. Guardiola chided him publicly after he set up a City goal with a “rabona” cross last season. The thrust of Guardiola’s comments were that Cherki was not Lionel Messi. Of course not, but he possesses a genius all of his own, which Maresca would surely be foolish to rein in.

The jaw-dropping splendour of Cherki’s first goal drew a collective intake of breath at Selhurst Park.

Collecting a Foden pass, he attacked the Palace area on a diagonal path, slaloming between Jaydee Canvot, Takehiro Tomiyasu and Chris Richards, before having the spatial awareness and technique to flick his left foot at the ball to send it rolling on a perpendicular trajectory past Dean Henderson.

News.title: England light years ahead of lamentable Pakistan
News.content:
Who needs Ben Stokes? Actually, it is hard to think of any side that would need him against this Pakistan team.

After just five days of cricket, and despite their own limitations with the bat, England are on the cusp of a series victory at Lord’s with a 261-run lead and power to add thanks to the prowess of a seam attack that has emerged quickly from the shadow of its former captain.

It will take longer to feel the full effects of Stokes’s absence. When England need a spinner in the side, they will miss the seam-bowling all-rounder to balance the XI. There will be times when they are up against it on a flat deck on a boiling day and be desperate for Stokes’s sheer will to win. It is still hard to think he will not play some part in the Ashes next summer.

For the final two years of his career it was Stokes’s bowling that was top class, his batting having become ordinary. But with bowlers of the quality of Ollie Robinson, Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson gelling, England are more than making up for Stokes’s retirement. This bowling attack against Pakistan’s batting was a complete mismatch.

Joe Root has stepped into Stokes’s shoes confidently, laying down the law off the field and tactically he has been spot on, although Pakistan have hardly stretched him. The only stir they have made since arriving was the stink they kicked up over Sky Sports’ interview with Imran Khan’s sons.

Conclusions are impossible to draw with any confidence against such poor opponents. Sri Lanka and West Indies two years ago put up a stronger fight in the first two Tests of their series. Tamim Iqbal scored two hundreds as Bangladesh at least landed some blows in 2010. Pakistan have managed one fifty in three innings and were bowled out for 171 and 135 at Headingley and a lamentable 110 here.

They were a batsman down at Lord’s because of a calf injury to opener Imam-ul-Haq, but only reached three figures because England dropped top scorer Azan Awais on eight; he went on to score 46.

England’s batting is hardly firing, but with a 180 first-innings lead, they could afford to be 13 for two without panic spreading. Losing Root for 24 kept Pakistan interested, but Emilio Gay toughed it out in the gloom to reach stumps unbeaten on 30; England 81 for three, light years ahead in the game.

Robinson’s astonishing figures of 13-6-11-4 set him on the way for a probable third man-of-the-match award in a row and continued his unexpected resurgence. Rarely did his pace go above 78mph, he just landed the ball time and again on a length and let movement off the seam do the rest.

News.title: I’ve lived in Norfolk for more than 30 years. Here’s how to explore England’s windswept east
News.content:
Norfolk’s vast sandy beaches are its chief draw for visitors: even on the busiest summer day there is always space for games, kite-flying or a family picnic in the dunes. Boating, crabbing, digging for cockles and wading in creeks provides hours of entertainment for all.

But there’s much more to Norfolk’s coast than its beaches. It’s also a landscape of dense pine forest and large expanses of salt marsh, which flush purple with sea-lavender in August. Birdlife is astonishingly rich, and wildflowers include yellow-horned poppies and lilac-flowering sea pea.

Inland, the undulating countryside and sleepy flint-built villages are perfect for gentle cycling, walking or touring by car. Grand stately homes make enjoyable days out, and almost every village has a sublimely beautiful medieval church at its centre.

Lively Georgian towns such as Burnham Market and Holt offer quirky shopping – and, wherever you are, you’re never far from an atmospheric pamment-floored pub serving local ales, or an excellent delicatessen selling the region’s specialities. Look out for pungent cheeses, smoked fish and salt-marsh flavoured honey.
