World.title: Zambia, Brazil seek enhanced trade ties
World.content:
Government says it is implementing reforms aimed at reducing the cost of doing business and making the country a more attractive investment destination for Brazilian businesses and other investors.

Ministry of Commerce, Trade and Industry Permanent Secretary for Investment and Industrialisation, Crusivia Hichikumba says Zambia seeks to deepen trade and investment cooperation with Brazil, particularly in agriculture, manufacturing, tourism, mineral value addition, healthcare, infrastructure and renewable energy.

Speaking in Lusaka today when he officiated at the Zambia-Brazil Business Forum, which is being held under the theme: Cooperation, Trade and Investments, Mr Hichikumba said the forum provides an opportunity for Brazilian and Zambian businesses to explore joint ventures, share knowledge and identify new trading opportunities.

“This Business Forum represents a milestone in strengthening commercial and investment ties between the Republic of Zambia and Brazil,” he said.

Mr Hichikumba says the government is undertaking reforms to simplify business registration processes and strengthen the regulatory framework as part of efforts to improve the business environment.

“The government of the Republic of Zambia has undertaken and continues to embark on significant reforms to improve the cost of doing business through simplifying registration processes and enhancing the regulatory framework,” he said.

Mr Hichikumba has further encouraged Brazilian entrepreneurs to explore opportunities in agricultural processing, manufacturing, mineral value addition, healthcare and infrastructure.

He pointed out that there is also strong potential for cooperation in agro-processing, plastic products, light engineering, renewable energy and information and communication technology.

However, Mr Hichikumba noted that despite the potential for increased economic cooperation, bilateral trade between Zambia and Brazil has not yet reached significant levels.

He further said the forum is therefore expected to help address this gap by creating opportunities for business matchmaking and stronger private-sector partnerships.

Mr Hichikumba has since urged Brazilian businesses to use the forum to connect with Zambian enterprises, while establishing lasting partnerships, adding that stronger engagements between the two countries has the potential to increase trade and investment while contributing to economic growth and shared prosperity.

Speaking at the same event, Zambia Development Agency (ZDA) Director General Albert Halwampa, highlighted Zambia’s stable economic policies, peaceful political environment and ongoing business reforms as key factors that make the country an attractive investment destination for Brazilian companies.

Mr Halwampa said the country has undertaken significant reforms to reduce red tape and create a more predictable environment for investors and exporters.

He explained that Zambia’s leadership has placed private-sector development at the centre of economic reforms, including through the Public-Private Dialogue Forum, which provides a platform for businesses to identify regulatory bottlenecks and work with the government to resolve them.

“We want to reassure you, investors from Brazil, when you come to Zambia, we believe in moving towards zero red tape, zero challenges, as far as providing an environment for you to invest,” he added.

Mr Halwampa charged that the establishment of the Presidential Delivery Unit has further strengthened the implementation of reforms by assigning timelines for resolving identified bottlenecks.

He also mentioned that predictable and stable government policies are also critical for investors because businesses need certainty when planning long-term investments.

Mr Halwampa encouraged Brazilian companies to consider Zambia not only as an investment destination but also as a base for exporting goods and services to other African markets.

And Brazilian Ambassador to Zambia Arthur Nogueira has urged Brazilian businesses to increase investment and trade with Zambia, saying Zambia has overcome various economic challenges and is ready for business.

Mr Nogueira said measures to address these problems had improved the country’s economic outlook and increased confidence in its business environment.

He highlighted Brazil’s expertise in tropical agriculture, livestock and disease control and pest management, while noting that similar environmental conditions could support cooperation in agriculture, energy, manufacturing and trade.

Also at the event, Ambassador Alex Giacomelli from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Brazil said Brazil is seeking to deepen trade and investment relations with Zambia as part of its renewed drive to strengthen economic partnerships with Africa.

Mr Giacomelli acknowledged that although bilateral trade has been growing, it remains at a modest level, creating significant scope to diversify trade and investment between the two countries.

He said the two countries need to build long-term solutions based on patience and resilience in response to growing global uncertainty and changes in globalisation.

Meanwhile, President of ApexBrazil, a Brazilian Trade and Investment Promotion Agency, Laudemir Muller said Brazil is ready to support Zambia’s economic transformation through technology transfer, investment and stronger business to business linkages.

Mr Muller said Brazil sees significant opportunities to partner with Zambia in modernising agriculture by providing agricultural machinery, bio-inputs, animal genetics and technologies developed for tropical conditions.

He also said Brazilian companies are also ready to provide specialised machinery and technical expertise to help Zambia process its raw materials locally, increase domestic supply and promote value addition.

He further identified renewable energy, biomass and biofuels as areas where Brazil can support Zambia in diversifying its energy mix and meeting the energy needs of industries and rural communities.

ApexBrasil and the Zambia Development Agency have signed a Memorandum of Understanding aimed at bringing Brazilian and Zambian companies closer together and creating new opportunities for trade and investment.

World.title: AVAP explains high voter turnout in Solwezi
World.content:
Solwezi District Anti Voter Apathy Project, (AVAP) Coordinator, Jack Lumima, says the high voter turnout recorded in the 2026 general elections is attributed to the mass voter education conducted in the district.

Mr Lumima says the voter turnout in the district, is an achievement for AVAP as it worked tirelessly to sensitise members of the public on the importance of upholding their civic duties.

He said more than 50 percent of registered voters in Solwezi North and Central constituencies cast their votes.

“AVAP conducted massive sensitisation and we worked closely with various stakeholders such as persons with disabilities, women, youths and church leaders at different levels,” he said.

Meanwhile, Mr Lumima said although some parts of the country recorded good voter turnout, some recorded low turnout calling for more sensitisation on voter education.

He has called for serious introspection on the voter turnout by ensuring that people are sensitised on the importance of their civic duties.

Mr Lumima stated that voter education should be a continuous process and not only conducted during an election year.

He said AVAP will engage partners for support to enable continuous voter education across the country.

Mr Lumima has thanked the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ), for working with stakeholders such as AVAP in sensitising members of the public on the importance of participating in civic duties like voting.

World.title: NCZ targets to produce 50,000 metric tonnes of compound D fertiliser
World.content:
The Nitrogen Chemicals of Zambia (NCZ) has set a target of producing 50,000 metric tonnes of compound D fertiliser and 5,000 metric tonnes of blended fertiliser in 2026, as the firm moves to meet national demand ahead of the rainy season.

NCZ Chief Executive Officer, Chanda Mongo, says the company has so far produced about 20,000 metric tonnes of compound D fertiliser, with part of the stock stored at the central warehouse and part of it distributed across various depots in the country.

In an interview with ZANIS, Mr Mongo revealed that NCZ has already started distributing the inputs for the next agricultural season through its 48 outlets spread across all 10 provinces.

He said the company also has about 7,000 metric tonnes of Urea fertiliser in stock.

Mr Mongo said NCZ’s primary focus remained on supporting the agriculture sector, adding that the company is currently manufacturing and blending D-Compound basal dressing fertilizer.

“NCZ’s production is directly tied to national food security. By manufacturing high-quality fertiliser locally, NCZ is ensuring that Zambian farmers receive this essential input on time and at competitive prices,” he said.

Mr Mongo said local production would help reduce the country’s reliance on imported fertiliser, protect farmers from global price shocks and support the Government’s agenda of making agriculture a major driver of economic growth.

He said continuous improvement remains part of NCZ’s corporate governance and operational strategy.

“We are currently evaluating the possibility of revamping the ammonium nitrate plant so that we can start producing top-dressing fertiliser,” said Mr Mongo.

He added that, apart from compound D fertiliser and specific blends, NCZ is also producing soil-specific fertiliser blends designed to respond to the varying needs of farmers and soils across the country.

He reaffirmed NCZ’s commitment to supporting farmers and ensuring that quality fertiliser was available on time for the coming planting season.

Meanwhile, Kafue District Commissioner, Maurice Hikapulwe said NCZ continues to play an important role in supporting agriculture and the local economy.

Mr Hikapulwe noted NCZ’s operations in Kafue are significant to the district, particularly through its contribution to the agriculture sector and the livelihoods of local communities.

World.title: FRA urged to secure Maize from damage
World.content:
Muchinga Province Permanent Secretary, Tuesday Bwalya has instructed the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) in the region to secure all the maize that it is buying from farmers during the current crop marketing season.

‎‎Dr Bwalya said the agency should ensure that all the maize it is procuring is protected from either sunlight, rains or any damage.

‎‎He said he does not want to see any wastage of maize which the FRA is buying using taxpayers money.

“As government we want to ensure that each bag that has been purchased is protected either from the sun or the rains. And as PS for Muchinga Province I am not going to allow a situation where maize is soaked. I’m in touch with FRA to procure enough trampoline so that we protect the maize “he said

He urged the FRA at both the provincial and in districts to procure enough trampolines to ensure that the maize is secure.

The Permanent Secretary said this when he visited Kampemba Satellite Depot in Chinsali district to check on the progress of the crop buying exercise.

He also advised FRA to start transporting excess maize from satellite depots into main storage sheds to create enough space for procuring more maize.

Dr Bwalya said the government wants to buy all the maize that farmers have brought at the satellite depots but noted that some satellites are experiencing storage challenges of storage.

“I’m informed that we have procured more than 20,000 bags of maize and this goes to show that our farmers produced enough maize and we expect to buy more maize as you can see the place is all littered with maize, “he said

He further urged the extension officers to work with the depot clerk and supervise the construction of a temporal slab to put the maize which would be purchased from farmers.

Meanwhile, the Permanent secretary has disclosed that the government is constructing six storage sheds, to help store more maize in the Province.

He said three sheds are being constructed in Mpika district and another three in Chinsali district.

“We are making six extra sheds, big-big sheds, three in Mpika and three in Chinsali so that we can mop all the maize that we are buying this year and that which we bought last year, we are going to secure it,’’ he said.

Kampemba Satellite Depot Clerk, Hastings Banda, stated that the team has temporarily suspended the buying exercise as they have nowhere to put the new grains.

Mr Banda disclosed that FRA working with the community have since started constructing a temporal slab to store more maize and clear the farmers.

He said the agency has so far procured about 20,000 by 50 kg bags of maize while more maize is still awaiting to be purchased.

Meanwhile, Ireen Bwalya, a farmer from the area, thanked the government for the initiative to pay the farmers through mobile money and bank accounts.

Ms Bwalya said the initiative is serving farmers of their precious time to do other things instead of waiting at the bank.

World.title: Kenya ready to purchase maize in Zambia
World.content:
A Kenyan grain Trading Company, Baita Trading Limited, says it is ready to immediately purchase 10.8 million bags of maize from Zambia to help meet Kenya’s urgent grain deficit.

Baita Trading Limited Director, Martin Kinoti says the company is responding to an immediate need in Kenya, where the country is expected to record a below-normal maize harvest this year.

Mr Kinoti said Kenya has declared a national requirement of about 25 million bags of maize, equivalent to approximately 2.2 million metric tonnes when calculated using 90-kilogramme bags.

He was speaking today during a meeting with Deputy Secretary to the Cabinet for Finance and Economic Development, Siazongo Siakalenge at Cabinet Office, where discussions with regard to the export of maize from Zambia to Kenya were held.

Mr Kinoti explained that the Kenyan government has tasked the private sector to facilitate maize imports, with the government maintaining a regulatory and facilitative role.

Mr Kinoti emphasised that Baita Trading is ready to off-take the available maize in Zambia, starting with an immediate shipment of 10.8 million bags, with a further 3 million bags expected to be required thereafter.

Speaking at the same event, Deputy Secretary to the Cabinet for Finance and Economic Development, Siazongo Siakalenge said Zambia has sufficient maize stock to meet Kenya’s demand.

Dr Siakalenge expressed Zambia’s readiness to facilitate exports to the East African country once the two sides conclude discussions on the terms of trade.

He said Zambia currently has about 5.1 million metric tonnes of maize, in addition to the more than 1.6 million metric tonnes carried over from last year.

Dr Siakalenge said this demonstrates that Zambia has adequate stock to support the regional market, including Kenya, which is seeking to import large quantities of maize.

World.title: ECZ orders fresh parley election in Mandevu
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) has resolved to conduct a fresh Parliamentary election in Mandevu Constituency of Lusaka District.

According to a statement made available to ZANIS today, by ECZ Chief Electoral Officer Brown Kasaro, the decision follows a security incident that disrupted the aggregation of results from the August 13, 2026 general election.

Mr Kasaro stated that following a report submitted by the Lusaka District Electoral Officer on August 18, indicating that unknown individuals attacked the results-totalling centre in Mandevu Constituency, destroyed result transmission kits and fled with election documentation.

He said the incident rendered the Returning Officer unable to declare the results of the Mandevu National Assembly election.

Mr Kasaro has since advised that a date for the fresh election will be communicated in due course.

World.title: Ghana: Ghana's Kente Protection Opens New Economic Possibilities
World.content:
Ghana’s geographical indication for kente could help weavers protect the celebrated cloth from imitation, reach new markets and earn more from generations of skill. Turning legal recognition into livelihoods will require collective standards, business support and the revival of local raw-material production.

It is early morning in Ziope, in Ghana’s Agotime-Kpetoe District, 22 kilometres east of the Volta regional capital, Ho. After sweeping his work area, Emmanuel Kofi Atsisey says a prayer, arranges his threads by colour and organises his tools. He then settles onto a self-made folding stool attached to his loom and begins using both hands and feet to create a design.

Income from the craft he began learning 21 years ago helps Atsisey support his family and pay the bills. He is now considering taking his skills to neighbouring Burkina Faso in the hope of earning more.

“The same kente we sell here in Ghana for about GH¢2,500 (US225) can go for more than GH¢4,000 (US360) when converted from CFA francs. I even thought of relocating there if the opportunity is real,” he says, recalling a conversation with a contact there.

Kente weaving is often passed down within families, but Atsisey took a different route. He entered a formal apprenticeship with a master weaver before becoming an independent artisan.

Kente embodies generations of knowledge passed down through skilled artisans. Its patterns tell stories of power, dignity, wealth and community identity, and the cloth is often worn on significant occasions.

Coming from one of Ghana’s major kente-producing areas, Atsisey has spent years combining tradition with innovation. Although he says earnings do not reflect the labour involved, the fabric’s global standing gives him pride.

“Even if you push yourself, you may produce only one or two pieces. More complex designs take four to six weeks to complete a set,” he explains.

Alongside established patterns, Atsisey creates original designs that reflect both cultural continuity and personal creativity.

“The block in Fatia kente is called Sukluikpe — sugar cubes. I designed it differently and named it ‘Life is sweet’. I have created many designs myself,” he says. Known fully as "Fatia Fata Nkrumah" kente cloth, it translates from the Akan language to "Fatia befits Nkrumah." Fatia was the wife of Ghana's first President, Dr. Kwame Nkrumah from Egypt.

Kente’s growing presence in contemporary fashion at national and international events is encouraging artisans and entrepreneurs to see the cloth as both cultural heritage and an economic asset.

According to the Annual Non-Traditional Export Statistics Report by the Ghana Export Promotion Authority (GEPA), the country’s industrial arts and crafts subsector recorded 23% export growth in 2024. GEPA said the export value of Kente products rose to US $38,901.83 in 2024, compared to US $6,256.00 in 2023, representing growth of 522% and an indication of rising international demand for Ghanaian textiles.

As demand grows, artisans in production centres are also working to protect the historic fabric’s authenticity.

At 27, traditional textile artisan Richmond Quarshie, from Agbozume in southeastern Ghana’s Volta Region, is part of his family’s weaving business. The income helped support him through secondary school.

“I started around 19,” he says. “All my brothers are involved. It is the work we inherited.”

Quarshie learnt the craft from his two older brothers and specialised in the Bonwire style of kente for customers in the Ashanti Region. After completing school, weaving became his main livelihood.

“For now, I’m working for someone,” he says. “I don’t have the capital to start on my own. That’s my biggest challenge.”

Quarshie believes the government could help by creating structured employment and production systems. He also points to the cost of imported thread as a barrier, underscoring the need for local production support as Ghana seeks to strengthen its manufacturing sector.

“The government can set up a place, like a factory, and bring weavers together to work,” he suggests.

His experience reflects a broader reality: young artisans are eager to grow but remain constrained by limited capital, weak support structures and fragmented markets.

Kente became Ghana’s first protected geographical indication (GI) in August 2025. The Registrar-General’s Department (RGD) and its partners formally launched the designation in Accra a month later.

This followed the inscription of kente weaving in Ghana on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in December 2024.

The RGD described the GI as a symbol or logo used on products that have a specific geographical origin, with verifiable qualities or characteristics.

For years, industry participants had raised concerns about labour-intensive, handwoven kente designs being copied and reproduced commercially on other fabrics in Ghana and abroad, without adequate benefits reaching the original artisans.

Godson Sena Adjavor, a textile consultant and engineer who specialises in reviving dormant factories, says institutions such as the RGD must now ensure that GI protection creates economic value for weavers.

“This is an opportunity for us to leverage the protection and earn intellectual-property income from anyone who wants to use kente designs,” Adjavor says.

Richard Akakpo, bird story agency Dr. Courage Besah-Adanu, Head of Geographical Indication,working on his laptop at the Ghana Industrial Property Office on August 19, 2026.

He argues that long-term protection will require the RGD to register artisans in different weaving communities and recognise community-based intellectual property in the production hubs.

An experienced trainer and consultant in the development sector, Adjavor calls for investment in textile science, finishing, branding and business development. This, he says, would expose artisans to market trends and design principles that could improve their products.

He also believes the industry must move beyond ceremonial wear. Using authentic kente in furniture, fashion accessories, footwear and everyday clothing could expand the sector and raise weavers’ incomes.

“Everything that fabric is used for, kente can be used for,” says Adjavor.

But legal protection and product diversification will not resolve all the industry’s constraints. Adjavor says Ghana’s dependence on imported yarn raises production costs, while the decline of local cotton cultivation and limited spinning capacity restrict access to locally produced thread.

“Once we grow the cotton and process locally, the weavers can afford the yarns to produce softer fabrics, but the country doesn't have the spinning capacity. The imported cotton yarns are expensive,” he says.

Ghana has five major kente production hubs across two regions. Bonwire and Adanwomase are in Ashanti, while Agotime-Kpetoe, Agbozume and Tafi Atome are in Volta. Smaller weaving areas surround these centres.

Dr Courage Besah-Adanu, head of geographical indications at the RGD’s industrial property office, says kente’s GI status goes beyond national recognition. It strengthens an identity that resonates across Africa and commands value globally. Work towards the designation began in 2016 with repeated community engagements and the development of multiple documents.

He describes it as an opportunity to unite weaving communities in the two regions and modernise the industry. The RGD has already begun engaging artisans in the main production centres.

“We needed to engage each community and train them in collective branding, management and marketing, what intellectual property means and how they fit into it. We have been doing this community by community,” he says.

He further says a national association has already been formed, though it is yet to be officially launched, and draft regulations are also in place. The next step is to move from the national level towards international registration, “as it is the practice in GI registration, and also more training for the producers across the country so they can fully utilise the protection for economic gains".

“For geographical indications, you need what is known as a book of specifications, or a common code of practice,” Besah-Adanu says.

According to him, the system is designed to deliver three outcomes: better remuneration for weavers, stronger national branding and consistent quality for consumers.

Consumers in Ghana and across the international markets are assured of authentic labelling with a verification system. The GI also translates into structured membership for weavers, training, and inspections.

"The weavers have the right to use the approved GI tag only when standards are met; these are the next steps we are working on after registering the national association.”

Together, these could improve market access and help artisans earn more from skills preserved over generations.

“For geographical indications, the product must have certain characteristics associated with it over a long period and recognised by consumers,” he explains.

“For consumers to keep experiencing those consistent characteristics, the people involved must have acquired particular skills and developed at least some form of grassroots organisation.”

Naomi Panin has a fabric shop at Menaba Plaza in Accra’s central business district for 10 years, with kente accounting for a significant share of her stock. She manages the business with her brother, who works directly with weavers in the Volta and Ashanti regions. Sourcing from verified producers has helped them earn customers’ trust in the authenticity of their fabrics.

Although sales occasionally dip, Panin says the business has proved resilient. Her customers come from across Ghana and from countries including Nigeria, Tanzania, the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada.

Beyond its commercial value, she regards kente as a powerful symbol of national identity and pride.

“If I see someone in Canada wearing kente, I know it is from Ghana. I feel happy because it shows our culture. It tells you where the person is connected to,” she says.

Victoria Azah, who operates a fashion centre in Accra, says kente has become increasingly popular among customers dressing for graduations, weddings and other special occasions.

“I often make outfits using kente. Demand has gone up,” she says.

Azah also values its versatility. A single piece can become several types of garment, while offcuts can be repurposed so that little goes to waste.

For weavers such as Atsisey and Quarshie, however, the measure’s success will ultimately be judged by whether legal recognition translates into stronger markets, sustainable businesses and better incomes.

“The whole world got to know for the first time that Ghana and Africa is taking hold of what belongs to her,” said Besah-Adanu.

World.title: Benin: How Benin Is Turning Its Cotton Wealth Into An Industrial Economy
World.content:
Benin is using its position as West Africa’s largest cotton producer to pursue a bigger economic prize: processing more of what it grows at home. At the Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone (GDIZ), cotton is being turned into fabrics and garments, creating jobs and retaining value that previously left the country with the trade of raw fibres. Its progress offers an emerging model for industrialisation for the continent.

At the Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone, about 45 kilometres north of Cotonou, young workers such as team leader Inès Alowakinnou are gaining experience in an industry that barely existed at this scale a few years ago. Their work lies at the centre of Benin’s ambitious attempt to turn its cotton wealth into factories, formal employment and a more diversified economy.

“Working conditions are good, I’m gaining experience, and I wouldn’t hesitate to encourage any young person to follow my example,” says Alowakinnou, who works in the industrial engineering department.

According to the IMF 2024 Country Report, Benin's exports have been mainly concentrated in commodities such as cotton and cashews, accounting for more than one third of total export between 2016 and 2021 (before adjusting for informal trade flows).

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

For Benin Textile Corporation maintenance supervisor, Manfaz Lamidi, the satisfaction comes from maintaining production and solving technical breakdowns and defects. Their experiences reflect the larger ambition behind GDIZ: to transform Benin from an exporter of raw agricultural commodities into a manufacturer and seller of higher-value products.

Benin harvested 533,590 tonnes of seed cotton during the 2025/26 season, regaining its position as the leading producer in the CFA franc zone. But producing large volumes of cotton does not automatically deliver the full economic value of the crop. That value increases as fibre moves through ginning, spinning, weaving, knitting, dyeing, garment production, branding and retail.

GDIZ is attempting to bring more of those stages inside Benin.

“For many decades, most African countries have always exported raw commodities without any value addition. But in Benin, we have decided to take matters into our own hands to change that paradigm so that we can create more wealth and jobs out of our natural resources,” says GDIZ CEO Létondji Beheton.

The foundations of the GDIZ model's success

GDIZ is a public-private partnership between Benin and industrial infrastructure developer Arise Integrated Industrial Platforms (ARISE IIP) covers a planned 1,640 hectares, with 400 hectares allocated to its first phase. Construction started in 2021.

Although cotton and textiles are central to its operations, the zone is also intended to process locally produced cashew nuts, soybeans, maize and other agricultural commodities, and mineral resources such as clay, kaolin, granite, etc.

“We do not copy and paste in Benin,” Beheton says. “What we do, we look at other models and we create our own model, and this is what we have done here.”

For decades — since the first free zones emerged in the 1960s and 70s — the success of a Special Economic Zone was measured by its tax incentives. Today, industrial investors weigh reliable power, ready-built factory space, port access, and workforce training as much as tax breaks. The GDIZ has built its pitch around exactly these — a 1,640-hectare site with turnkey infrastructure, on-site logistics to the Port of Cotonou, and worker-training programs like Azôli, which has already placed more than 5,000 young people into factory jobs.

“In this zone, we have a single window counter where you have more than 17 public entities,” Beheton says, citing immigration, tax, customs and other government services. These are intended to give investors one point of contact in terms of all the paperwork that is needed for them to develop their business .

Companies located in the GDIZ benefit from major exemptions, including a total and permanent exemption from corporate income tax, business tax and VAT on inputs, as well as full customs duty exemption on imported equipment.

The GDIZ has transformed Benin's cotton sector by mobilizing over €1.3 billion in investments, creating 16,000 direct jobs in the textile industry, and reaching a capacity of 40,000 tons of fiber processing and 24 million garments annually, making it Africa's top industrial zone.

“This model works because of the quality achieved through initial investments that have positioned the company among the most modern,” explains independent consultant and agricultural economist Sourou Prisciron Zinsou.

"All Beninese people benefit. Directly, there are the employees and their families, but there are also the infrastructure projects financed by taxes collection, including those collected from the GDIZ," Zinsou says.

“It brings agricultural production closer to industrialization (….). The primary beneficiaries are evidently the cotton producers,” says economics and local development expert Rouhaïmatou Bio Sanna .

Employment is one of GDIZ’s biggest drawcards. The zone reports that more than 25,000 jobs have been created across textiles, garment manufacturing and agribusiness, with women and young people making up a substantial share of its workforce. “The zone's overall objective is to reach 300,000 direct jobs and approximately 600,000 indirect jobs by 2030,” says Beheton.

Achieving that target would make GDIZ a significant source of formal industrial employment. It would also open new career paths for young people in a country where many livelihoods remain concentrated in agriculture and informal commerce.

Capturing more value from every harvest

GDIZ’s three integrated textile units have the capacity to process 40,000 tonnes of fibre annually which Beheton says is equivalent to 12.7% of Benin’s annual fibre output.

“Within the next five to seven years, we’ll process the entire output,” he says.

According to the World Bank, investment and the expansion of the GDIZ are important drivers of Benin’s economic growth. The company benefits from a local consumption market made of several brands including but not limited to Susu and Obalè which is a premium brand.

"The goal is to guarantee high-level marketing, both for export and domestically, because our primary market is ourselves. We must set an example,” says former Minister of Trade Alimatou Shadiya Assouman.

According to Beheton, the GDIZ show companies have worked with international clothing businesses and brands, including The Children’s Place, H&M, KIABI, GEMO, C&A and US Polo Assn. It also reports exports to European markets, including France, Germany and Spain.

Another opportunity has emerged through the WTO's C4+1 partnership initiatives — including a 2022 agreement with FIFA to source more cotton for the federation's sportswear and merchandising from Benin, Burkina Faso, Chad and Mali, and a $12 billion investment push launched with UNIDO in 2024 to help these countries, along with Côte d'Ivoire, process more of their fibre into finished textiles and clothing.

The FIFA-related programme includes ‘Football for Schools’, and Beheton says Benin is the only participating country to supply products under this initiative.

“We have supplied over 170,000 pieces already,” he says.

Building skills alongside factories

Benin’s textile industry still depends heavily on imported machinery, advanced technology and foreign technical expertise but GDIZ’s leadership has a longer-term objective to grow local skills.

Close 

“We are developing skills here in Benin, so we are able in the long run to manufacture our own equipment,” Beheton says, pointing to innovation hubs such as Sèmè City. The goal, he adds, is to build “an industry that is sustainable and not so much dependent upon foreign vendors”.

Sèmè City is a flagship smart eco-city project launched in 2017 by the Beninese government and aims to become a regional hub for higher education, scientific research, and tech entrepreneurship in West Africa.

Competing beyond incentives

Benin has a competitive advantage which is crucial in economic growth. Unlike countries such as China and Bangladesh which import cotton fibre, the West African country has a local source of supply of good quality fiber at a reasonable cost.

“Fibre is available, it is processed. So, we have the advantage of going directly from the fibre to the market,” says GDIZ director Létondji Beheton.

But heavy industry requires power and rising fuel costs are a risk, along with a limited grid capacity. This is something the government is working hard at addressing.

“So far, we are producing more than 200 megawatts,” Beheton says. “We are adding every year more megawatts through the solar plant, as well as other projects that are ongoing.”

Economics and local development expert Rouhaïmatou Bio Sanna warns that GDIZ companies must build true, long-term competitiveness and cannot rely on the fact that their cotton resources are grown locally. But Beheton is confident about the outlook.

“Benin will fully transform its own agricultural commodities [and] mining resources locally, and create a lot of jobs and wealth for its people, that is the way forward.”

World.title: Africa: Africa Brought Deals to Washington - The Test is Whether the Money Moves
World.content:
The Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, the Asantehene or king of the Ashanti Kingdom in Ghana, with other dignitaries at the opening of the African Business and Investment Forum, convened under his patronage by the Millennium Excellence Foundation.

Washington, DC — The inaugural Africa Business Investment Summit saw a target of $500m of structured commitments, a royal keynote and an unusually candid accounting of why capital still hesitates.

Otumfuo Osei Tutu II had been speaking for barely five minutes when he put the question the rest of the day would attempt to answer. The Asantehene looked out at the ballroom and asked why, given everything that had just been claimed for the continent, Africa is still not developed.

It was a striking thing to ask at a summit built to answer it. The Africa Business Investment Summit, convened for the first time by the Millennium Excellence Foundation under his patronage, gathered more than 500 delegates at MGM National Harbor in Oxon Hill, Maryland, on 27 and 28 August. It was designed, in the words of Ghana's Deputy Minister for Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, Sampson Ahi, as a deal-making arena, one in which discussion must lead to capital, capital to enterprise, and enterprise to jobs.

The organisers arrived with roughly $4 billion of opportunities and set themselves a smaller test: at least $500m in structured commitments, signed as memoranda of understanding and letters of intent before the delegates go home.

Speaking for President John Dramani Mahama, Ahi set the scene for the day's discussions with an update on Ghana's progress. He reported inflation down from 23.8% in December 2024 to 5.4% a year later, and 4.6% by July 2026. GDP grew 6% in 2025, the fastest since 2019, with non-oil growth at 7.6%, the highest in fourteen years. Foreign direct investment reached $2.62bn.

That last number is the registration figure. The balance of payments tells a subtler story. Net foreign direct investment on that measure was $1.91bn, and 95.4% of it came from reinvested earnings, leaving something in the order of $88m of genuinely new money arriving from abroad. Investors already in Ghana are staying and expanding. Persuading new ones through the door is the harder problem.

It is also the problem almost every session that followed was arguing about.

Reta Jo Lewis, the former president and chair of the Export-Import Bank of the United States, gave the most practical account. During her three years leading the agency, she said, its Africa portfolio went from $109m in 2022 to a record $3.6bn in authorisations across 2023 and 2024. The constraint was rarely capital. It was readiness.

She has little patience for the language investors use. "The minute somebody tells me, do you have a bankable project, I already know they're about to tell me they're not going to do my deal."

The financing conversation has to be part of a project's design, not a question asked after it. "Let's get to yes, not get to no."

Critical minerals

One area that is expected to drive Africa's development forward in the decades to come is exploitation of the continent's enormous critical minerals reserves.

Africa's mineral endowment is not in dispute and neither, said Ben Kincaid, chief executive of ReElement Technologies Africa, is the political will. Governments have written policies restricting the export of unprocessed material. What is missing is the midstream. Without regional refining capacity, a rule against exporting concentrate is unenforceable, because there is nowhere else for the concentrate to go.

Ayo Sopitan, chief executive of Metalex Commodities, which is building copper and cobalt production in Zambia, put the scale in perspective. By his count roughly 750 million tonnes of copper have been produced in all of human history, and the world will need about as much again within twenty-five years. The US Geological Survey's own estimate of cumulative production is nearer 700 million tonnes.

African Business and Investment Forum Dr. Alex Apau Dadey, Founder and Executive Chairman of the wholly Ghananian-owned KGL Group, receiving an award during the African Business and Investment Forum in Washington, DC.

Meanwhile, China is already securing vast supplies of critical minerals from Africa and restricting its own exports. It restricted antimony exports in 2024 and extended controls to refining technologies themselves in October 2025, covering smelting, separation and magnet manufacturing.

Those October measures were suspended for a year after the Busan meeting between the American and Chinese presidents, though the earlier controls remain.

For the West to compete, said the panel, capital cannot be the only answer. The US and other countries must boost processing capacity as well as extraction of the ore if they are to play a meaningful role in Africa's critical minerals space.

Remittances are another area of huge potential. They are now Africa's largest single source of external finance, at over $124bn in 2025 against roughly $70bn of foreign direct investment, while bilateral aid from OECD donors to sub-Saharan Africa fell by more than a quarter last year. In Ghana, central bank governor Johnson Asiama put 2025 inflows at nearly $7.8bn, about 6% of GDP, and said they now exceed foreign direct investment.

Rebecca Enonchong, founder of AppsTech, added the uncomfortable corollary. Sending money to sub-Saharan Africa costs about 8.5% on the World Bank's measure once currency conversion is counted, even where the visible fee is two dollars. Governments have not always helped. A mobile money tax penalises the digital transfer while leaving cash untouched, she noted; Ghana repealed its own e-levy last year. Her broader warning was about dependency. When a government comes to assume the diaspora will cover healthcare, remittances have stopped being a private transfer and become a substitute for the state.

Energy – utilities must step up

Energy closed the day. Rachel Moré-Oshodi of ARM-Harith Infrastructure Investments argued that infrastructure is among the lowest-risk asset classes globally and that Africa's loss rates, at around 1.7%, are the lowest anywhere. Her own firm, even so, has not closed a large-scale generation project in roughly seven years, because bankability depends on offtakers, and the utilities that sign those contracts are frequently not creditworthy.

Chantelle Abdul, whose MOJEC International Holdings describes itself as sub-Saharan Africa's largest manufacturer of smart electricity meters, recalled arriving in Nigeria to find utilities issuing estimated bills to customers who had been away for months. Almost half of sub-Saharan Africa still has no electricity at all. Nigeria's self-generation capacity, she said, is around ten times what the national grid actually delivers.

Mission 300, the World Bank and African Development Bank programme, aims to connect 300 million Africans by 2030. More than $50bn has been pledged, the two banks accounting for $48bn of it, and just over 50 million people have been connected so far.

Time for action

But Kwabena Osei-Sarpong of RIFE International named the gap the whole summit had been circling. There are capital commitments, and there is capital deployment, and the distance between them is where most announcements go to die.

Which is the fair test of this summit.

Day Two ends with a signing ceremony for memoranda of understanding, letters of intent and an investment communiqué – but follow-through will prove more significant than mere announcements.

The Africa Business and Investment Summit was organized by the Millenium Excellence Foundation. African Business was a media partner and producer of the Summit.

World.title: South Africa: Thabo Bester Trial Postponed Again, This Time to 2027
World.content:
While in prison in Mangaung, Thabo Bester ran a business and even appeared by video link at an event.

The plea and trial of Thabo Bester and Nandipha Magudumana has been postponed to 19 April 2027.

Bester's legal team has raised concerns about prison conditions and his access to a laptop to prepare his defence.

The plea and trial in the Thabo Bester prison escape case has been postponed yet again, this time until next year.

The matter returned to the Free State High Court in Bloemfontein on Friday, where judges were due to hear whether outstanding legal issues had been resolved and the case was ready to proceed.

Bester and his former girlfriend, Nandipha Magudumana, appeared virtually, while their co-accused appeared in person. Once again, the matter was postponed.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"The matter is then so postponed for plea and trial to 19 April 2027, up until 18 June 2027, again here in Bloemfontein in the Free State division of the High Court," Judge Mareena Opperman said.

Proceedings were last delayed in June, after Bester's legal team asked for more time to consult, keeping the case in limbo despite its high public profile.

Bester, a convicted murderer and rapist, Magudumana and their co-accused face charges linked to his escape from Mangaung Correctional Centre in May 2022. Prosecutors allege he faked his death in a cell fire before orchestrating the breakout, sparking a nationwide manhunt. Bester and Magudumana were eventually arrested in April 2023, roughly 10km outside Arusha, Tanzania, after fleeing the hotel where they had been staying.

Among the co-accused are Magudumana's father, Zolile Cornelius Sekeleni, and former G4S employees Senohe Matsoara, Teboho Lipholo, Buti Masukela, Tieho Frans Makhotsa, Zanda Moyo and Joel Makhetha. They face charges including fraud, corruption, money laundering, assisting an inmate to escape, violation of a corpse, arson and defeating the ends of justice.

The case has been repeatedly complicated. Sekeleni has said he has no lawyer after Legal Aid rejected his application, a decision now under appeal. One accused suffered breathing difficulties during an earlier hearing, disrupting proceedings, and charges against one former G4S employee have since been withdrawn.

Magudumana has separately taken her arrest and extradition to the Constitutional Court, arguing her detention and transfer from Tanzania were unlawful; prosecutors maintain they followed due process.

Judge Opperman has warned of further delays given the sheer volume of evidence still to be reviewed. Bester's lawyer has also raised concerns about prison conditions and his access to a laptop to prepare his defence.

World.title: Kenya: Police Deployed As Nairobi Traders Protest Increased Taxes On Imports
World.content:
Nairobi — Police have been deployed around the Archives, Luthuli Avenue and Railways Roundabout in Nairobi's central business district as traders prepare to march to the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) offices in protest against a revised customs valuation benchmark.

The heightened security comes as a section of businesses in the CBD remained closed on Friday, with traders joining a boycott over the increase in the minimum yield for consolidated cargo from Sh2.5 million to Sh3.2 million.

Police officers were stationed at key entry points and along major roads as traders gathered ahead of the planned march to present their grievances to the taxman.

The demonstrations have disrupted business activity along parts of the CBD.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

A spot check by Capital FM revealed closed shops along Moi Avenue, Kenyatta Avenue and Tom Mboya Street.

A trader said the group intends to deliver its grievances directly to the KRA leadership.

"We are hoping to present a memorandum to the KRA commissioner on our grievances. We will continue with these protests until we are heard," the trader said.

The protests follow a decision by KRA to raise the minimum yield used under its simplified clearance arrangement for consolidated cargo.

The benchmark increased by Sh700,000, representing a 28 percent rise from Sh2.5 million, a move that has unsettled small-scale importers who commonly pool their merchandise in shared containers, particularly from China.

Traders in Kamukunji, Gikomba and Nyamakima had earlier threatened to shut their businesses nationwide on Friday in opposition to the review.

They argue that the higher benchmark could increase the cost of importing goods and put further pressure on already narrow profit margins, potentially forcing businesses to raise retail prices or scale down operations.

KRA has, however, rejected the interpretation that the Sh3.2 million figure amounts to a fixed tax on every consolidated container.

The authority says the minimum yield is a risk-management benchmark rather than the actual tax liability, and is used to determine whether shipments qualify for simplified clearance.

According to KRA, the actual customs liability depends on the nature, value and classification of goods in a shipment, alongside other factors such as freight and insurance.

The authority says traders can also request verification of their cargo outside the simplified arrangement or de-consolidate shipments so that individual importers make separate declarations and pay applicable taxes.

Close 

KRA has attributed the review to changes in exchange rates, freight costs and national and East African Community tax laws, as well as efforts to address undervaluation, under-declaration and misclassification of imports.

The revised benchmark took effect on August 21, after the authority granted traders a grace period to prepare for implementation.

World.title: Michelle Obama shrugs off missing active motherhood after daughters leave, says, 'I'm good'
World.content:

Former first lady Michelle Obama faced criticism Friday after telling Jon Stewart on Wednesday's "IMO" podcast that she did not miss having her adult daughters at home, with California Republican Party Delegate and mother, Elizabeth Barcohana, telling Fox News Digital that the remarks conveyed resentment amid a national debate over motherhood.

Obama offered a terse response after Stewart explained that the daily job of parenting had given meaning and structure to his life and asked whether she missed it.

"I’m good," Obama said.

MICHELLE OBAMA’S ‘ME’ ANSWER ABOUT NEXT CHAPTER DRAWS SOCIAL MEDIA BACKLASH

Barcohana said Obama appeared relieved that the active years of raising daughters Malia and Sasha had ended.

"There is a difference between a mother expressing exhaustion from the demands of motherhood — which is real and relatable — and expressing resentment," Barcohana said. "Resentment is what appears to come through in Michelle Obama’s remarks, and it is especially painful to hear amid the national conversation surrounding the Lindsay Clancy trial."

"She seems happy that her daughters’ childhoods are over. That is not a relatable feeling for most mothers at all," she added.

Obama said she did not miss having her daughters at home but immediately stressed that she loved them and planned to see them for dinner that night.

OBAMA ADMITS 'GENUINE TENSION' IN MARRIAGE OVER PRESSURE TO STAY IN POLITICS

"I don’t miss them. I don't. I love them. I’m going to see them tonight for dinner. I love them," she said. "But Barack cried when they went to college. I was like, ‘Bye, little— goodbye.’ Now I— now Friday nights aren’t wrecked with terror and fear about, ‘Where are you? Where are you?’"

Conservative commentator Matt Walsh accused Obama of appearing eager for her children to leave despite the assistance he claimed the family's wealth afforded her.

"And yet she still couldn’t wait for the kids to leave because the minor demands they made on her time and energy were still too much for her. Just a total raging narcissist," Walsh said.

BARACK AND MICHELLE OBAMA'S FILM PRODUCTION COMPANY REPORTEDLY LEAVING NETFLIX TO GO INDEPENDENT

Political commentator Link Lauren criticized Obama for what he characterized as repeated complaints about her family and lifestyle.

"This podcast is just her sitting around her mansion in Martha’s Vineyard complaining about how hard her life of luxury is, and how much she despises her husband and children," Lauren said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Obama further explained her empty-nest reaction by saying she welcomed her daughters' independence and had already spent substantial time actively raising them.

"I love my schedule. I have a great schedule and it’s all mine," Obama said. "I mean, I’ve had so much quality time with my children. So much. Yeah, yeah. I know them inside and out."

Obama also praised Barack Obama’s parenting last year, explaining that both parents deliberately prioritized their daughters throughout his presidency.

"It was important for both of us, for me and Barack, to carve out that time in those eight years when our girls were in their formative years, you know," Obama said.

World.title: Tennessee moves to rename Nashville airport for Dolly Parton days after beloved icon's death
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee and Nashville International Airport announced Friday that they intend to name the airport in honor of Dolly Parton, moving toward a major tribute to the icon after an outpouring of public support for the beloved late country music legend's legacy.

Lee said he spoke with Parton's team about the proposal this week. Her team expressed appreciation for the support and is open to continuing the conversation, according to a joint announcement from the governor and the Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority.

The proposal would place Parton's name on the gateway to Music City, connecting the transportation hub with a woman whose music, philanthropy and deeply rooted connection to her home state made her perhaps its most celebrated figure.

TRUMP MOURNS DOLLY PARTON, ORDERS US FLAGS LOWERED NATIONWIDE AFTER COUNTRY MUSIC ICON DIES

"Dolly Parton’s extraordinary life is forever woven into the fabric of our state," said Lee about the Tennessee native, who died Tuesday at 80 after a brief cancer battle. "From her rural mountain home in East Tennessee to global stages, Dolly carried the Volunteer Spirit with her.

"At a place where Tennessee welcomes the world, it is fitting that Nashville International Airport would bear the name of our state’s favorite daughter and greet travelers with the enduring legacy of Dolly’s music, generosity, faith, and kindness."

The announcement comes amid a groundswell of support for renaming the airport after Parton. A Change.org petition titled "Rename Nashville International Airport to Dolly Parton International Airport" had accumulated 155,501 verified signatures, according to the petition page.

DOLLY PARTON DEFIED COUNTRY MUSIC'S EXPECTATIONS FOR WOMEN AND BUILT A CAREER ON HER OWN TERMS: EXPERTS

The petition was originally launched in January 2025 by Lydia Popovich and Dan Dion, who argued that Parton's influence extended far beyond the music that made her famous, pointing to her philanthropy and her Imagination Library literacy program.

Following Parton's death this week, the organizers said tens of thousands of additional supporters signed the petition and renewed their effort to have Nashville's airport carry her name.

The campaign has also drawn support from Tennessee officials. State Rep. Todd Warner said in a response published on the petition page that he would introduce legislation supporting the change.

"Yes I will definitely introduce legislation to rename the BNA airport Dolly Parton International Airport! Thanks, TW," Warner wrote, according to the response reproduced by Change.org.

DOLLY PARTON'S LIFE IN HER OWN WORDS: FROM SMOKY MOUNTAINS POVERTY TO COUNTRY MUSIC IMMORTALITY

Nashville Council member Russ Bradford also said he would sponsor a resolution asking the Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority to consider the change, while stressing that the authority, rather than the council, has the ultimate say over the airport's name.

"I'm proud to sponsor a resolution asking the Metro Nashville Airport Authority to consider renaming BNA to Dolly Parton International Airport," Bradford said in a response published by Change.org.

The tribute carries particular resonance because Parton had previously resisted efforts to put her own legacy on a pedestal.

In 2021, Parton asked Tennessee lawmakers to withdraw a bill that would have allowed a statue of her to be erected on the grounds of the state Capitol.

STEVE DOOCY: THE DOLLY PARTON I SAW WHEN THE CAMERAS STOPPED ROLLING

"I am honored and humbled by their intention, but I have asked the leaders of the state legislature to remove the bill from any and all consideration," Parton said at the time in a post shared to social media.

She explained that she did not believe such an honor was appropriate while the country was confronting larger challenges, but left open the possibility that Tennessee might honor her in that way someday.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Given all that is going on in the world, I don't think putting me on a pedestal is appropriate at this time," Parton said. "I hope, though, that somewhere down the road several years from now or perhaps after I'm gone if you still feel I deserve it, then I'm certain I will stand proud in our great State Capitol as a grateful Tennessean."

The proposal to rename the airport will be discussed at the Metro Nashville Airport Authority’s next meeting on Sept. 17, according to their release.

World.title: Sleeper teams from each Power 4 conference: Who will exceed expectations this college football season?
World.content:
With college football beginning in earnest this Saturday, many fans are anxiously awaiting to see how the chips will fall in a wide open season in 2026.

Sure, on paper, there is a clear delineation between the teams who have everything to win a national championship and the rest of the field, but as they always say, "paper never played a football game."

With that in mind, I wanted to take a look at some of my favorite sleeper teams from each Power 4 conference.

PREDICTING EACH POWER 4 CONFERENCE CHAMPION AHEAD OF THE 2026 COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON

I already discussed who I think is going to win each conference, but what about the teams no one sees coming that could upset the established order.

These aren't necessarily teams that I would put money on to win their respective conferences, but they are certainly could if things break the right way.

Let's take a look at some power conference teams who are flying under the radar this season.

ACC - Virginia Tech Hokies

I wrote an entire article about how shocked I was to see the Hokies not in the preseason top-25, and I was even more shocked to see they were projected to finish 8th in the ACC.

I understand it hasn't exactly been a bed of roses for Virginia Tech since legendary coach Frank Beamer retired, but the Hokies — at least to my eye — have everything they need to finish in the upper echelon of the ACC this season.

For starters, landing head coach James Franklin was an absolute coup.

RANKING THE TEN BEST COLLEGE FOOTBALL COACHES IN THE COUNTRY AHEAD OF THE 2026 SEASON

I know I haven't been the most vocal defender of Franklin, but I still think he's a hell of a coach who will benefit from a change of scenery and a slightly less competitive conference.

The Hokies also rank top-five in the country in returning production and will feature Franklin's handpicked signal caller Ethan Grunkemeyer under center.

Grunkemeyer was forced into action after Penn State starter Drew Allar was lost for the season midway through 2025, and that experience will be invaluable for Virginia Tech this season.

A soft start to their schedule could provide the perfect "ramp up" into the meat of their slate in late October, and I wouldn't be shocked at all to see the Hokies push teams like SMU and Louisville for that silver medal spot in the ACC this year.

Big 12 - Houston Cougars

Everyone knows about Texas Tech and the stockpile of talent they have out in Lubbock, but I'm keeping my eye on another team on the opposite end of the Lone Star State to make some noise in the Big 12.

I'm surprised I haven't heard more about the Cougars during the preseason hype sessions, considering they won 10 games and finished in the top-25 last season, but perhaps this is right where they want to be.

Houston has all the ingredients to challenge the Red Raiders for the conference crown, including a great coach in Willie Fritz, an ascending defense, and one of the most experienced rosters in the Big 12 heading into 2026.

A massive early-season showdown looms between the Cougars and the Red Raiders in September, and if Houston is able to keep that game close or even win it, it could be the statement they need to let everyone know they are for real.

Other than the aforementioned date with Texas Tech, Houston avoids many of the other heavy hitters in the Big 12, including BYU and both Arizona schools, so another 10-win season could be in the books in H-Town.

Big Ten - Washington Huskies

I think the world of Washington head coach Jedd Fisch, and even wanted him to replace Billy Napier at Florida before Jon Sumrall was hired, so it's no surprise I believe he and the Huskies could achieve big things this year.

Looking at Fisch's trajectory, both at Arizona and now at Washington, will give fans a glimpse into what they could expect from the Huskies in 2026.

THREE TEAMS RANKED OUTSIDE THE TOP-12 OF THE COACHES POLL WHO WILL MAKE THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF

The Wildcats went from one win to five wins to 10 wins in three seasons under Fisch, and the current Washington head coach had win totals of six and nine in his first two seasons in Seattle, respectively.

With dynamic quarterback Demond Williams Jr. returning as well as a roster that ranks in the top-15 nationally in returning production, Fisch has all the pieces in place to make a legitimate run at a Big Ten title or, at the very least, put together a remarkable season in the Pacific Northwest.

Washington avoids Michigan and Ohio State this year and will play Penn State and Indiana at home.

A forgivable schedule could help the Huskies outperform their preseason expectations and have a lot of critics eating crow by season's end.

SEC - Mississippi State Bulldogs

As far as SEC sleepers go, I've seen plenty of love for programs like South Carolina, Auburn, and even Kentucky, but for my money, I believe the Mississippi State Bulldogs will shock plenty of fans and media pundits alike in 2026.

Jeff Lebby enters his third season as the head coach in Starkville, and many will view his 2025 season as a failure upon first glance.

The losing record will cause many to believe the rebuild is behind schedule, but a closer look shows that the Bulldogs were a few bad bounces and missteps away from an eight-win season.

Mississippi State took both Texas and Tennessee — two top-25 teams — to overtime, and were a terrible interception in field goal range away from beating Florida in The Swamp.

The Bulldogs are a sneaky talented team, shockingly ranking in the top-20 of the 247Sports Team Talent Composite, as Lebby has done a remarkable job upgrading the personnel at Mississippi State.

Sophomore quarterback Kamario Taylor was a highly-touted player coming out of high school and will unlock Lebby's offense with his combination of plus athleticism and uncanny arm talent.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

I'm not picking the Bulldogs to win the SEC outright, but don't be surprised if the Cowbell Clangers are spoiling a ton of talented teams' chance at winning the league this season.

World.title: 'Veronica Mars' star Jason Dohring traded Hollywood for farming
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

"Veronica Mars" star Jason Dohring has stepped away from acting to focus on a new passion.

During a recent appearance on the "Don't Do Nothing" podcast, the 44-year-old actor shared that he developed an interest in gardening around four years ago and told his agents, "I'm just going to go farm for a minute."

"I just got an interest in it and I've kind of the last three years I built like, I'm on my third farm now and we're just making great food for people cause I really realized that people are getting sick from the food that they're eating," he said.

He first began planting in Los Angeles, before developing a 14-acre farm in West Virginia, where they planted 4,000 trees, including apples, cherries, pears, peaches and nectarines, noting he probably planted "3,500 of them myself."

'THE THORN BIRDS' STAR RACHEL WARD TRADED 'EMPTY' HOLLYWOOD FOR FARM LIFE IN AUSTRALIA

The actor now lives on an 11-acre farm in Florida with his wife, Lauren Kutner, and their four kids, noting he moved there because of the weather. He said that when farming in California, they weren't allowed to drill a well and would run out of water.

"L.A. is crazy. [You can go] eight, nine months with no rain. You know what I mean?" he said. "That's when I when we moved to Florida I was like we get infinite rain. We have infinite manure. Like you know you could farm for free."

Dohring is proud of his Florida farm and the regenerative farming method he uses, which involves growing the crops without chemicals. Through this method, he says that on his farm, "stuff is starting to get much better."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"There was this old guy and he's like, ‘Are you the owner?’" he said about a recent experience on his farm. "And he's like, ‘I've been praying to God that the gate was open so I could come in here and see this cause I've been in agriculture since I was 12. I've never seen anything like this before.’"

Dohring first rose to fame playing Logan Echolls on "Veronica Mars" opposite Kristen Bell, for three seasons, from 2004 to 2007.

He starred in several other projects, including "Moonlight" and "The Originals," before returning to film the "Veronica Mars" feature movie in 2014 and the one-season revival in 2019. His last acting gig was four episodes of "SEAL Team" in 2021.

While he has stepped away from acting for now, he admits, "I'll probably jump back into it at some point," adding he has already done a short film for a friend.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"I love art, and when I get around art, even talking about this is exciting to me," he said. "I think there's something in everybody that is aesthetic, meaning beautiful or wants to create."

The actor married Kutner in 2004, shortly before "Veronica Mars" premiered. The two first met and became friends while in high school, with Dohring saying their friendship is the foundation of their marriage.

Since getting married, the couple have welcomed four children: son Owen, and daughters Lily, Ainsley Mae and Isla Avery.

"My wife and I were married 20 years ago today," he wrote on Instagram in July 2024. "We have had an amazing life together, including raising four incredible children. I consider her my best friend."

World.title: LGBTQ group reveals which Dem nominee is sponsoring Halloween event featuring drag shows
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

As the Trump administration’s efforts have choked off federal funding for LGBTQ groups, Keisha Lance Bottoms, former mayor of Atlanta and Georgia's Democratic gubernatorial nominee, is sponsoring an upcoming Halloween event open to children that will include drag shows.

"From 5-8, the little monsters roam free trick-or-treating through spooky trails and glowing Halloween worlds, and when night falls, the hallo queen show explodes with music, costumes and pure Halloween spectacle," ColGay Pride, an LGBTQ+ group based in Columbus, Georgia, said in a video.

Notably, the group’s programming states that the "adults-only" portion of the night, which includes the drag shows, will begin after 9 p.m.

Even so, Lance Bottoms’ support of the Halloween event, which includes a haunted walk, s’mores, an adult-and-kids costume contest — all centered around gender expression — adds to her record of supporting LGBTQ-related content around children.

POWERFUL LGBTQ+ GROUP'S ENDORSEMENTS COULD TANK VULNERABLE DEMS OVER RADICAL YOUTH TRANS AGENDA

ColGay Pride describes its goal as "promoting diversity, inclusion and equality for the LGBTQ community in Columbus and the surrounding areas and create a supportive and affirming environment through our programs and events."

The group, which is throwing its final Halloween celebration after 13 years, said President Donald Trump’s federal funding cuts had made it dependent on individual contributions.

"We are closing our doors next year," the group wrote.

"It has become far too difficult to raise money when our financial aid was cut off completely under Trump, when our own citizens — the very people we have served for twenty years — do not donate. Sometimes you simply reach a point where enough is enough."

The group thanked Lance Bottoms for her support in a post to Facebook with a "digital sponsorship certificate."

It’s unclear how much she contributed to the event.

Bottoms' gubernatorial bid has been complicated by political liabilities. The Campaign Finance Commission fined her $37,000 in 2021 for accepting over $60,000 in contributions that exceeded legal limits and $110,000 that exceeded debt caps.

She also announced that she would not pursue re-election as mayor of Atlanta amid a COVID-19 crime during which homicides spiked by 58% over levels from the year before.

In addition to those controversies, Bottoms has received criticism from conservatives for her stances on gender policy.

GOP FRONTRUNNER IN KEY GUBERNATORIAL RACE FORCED TO ANSWER ABOUT HIRING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS: 'I DON'T KNOW'

Recently, in a gubernatorial debate, the former mayor said she would have vetoed the Riley Gaines Act, a piece of legislation that banned biological men from competing in women’s sports.

"I believe that decisions about who competes and how people compete shouldn’t be happening at the state Capitol. I don’t support the government making decisions about who should compete in athletics. I believe that decision should be left to respective athletic associations," Bottoms said.

That comment, in particular, has become a key campaign quote for her opponent, Rick Jackson, a businessman and the Republican nominee to replace outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp, as they set out to attack Bottoms' far-left positions on issues of gender and sexuality.

"Keisha Bottoms and the other Democrats said they’d have vetoed the Riley Gaines Act. They won’t protect girls’ sports, but they will open the floodgates for woke ideology in our schools. We’re going to make sure they don’t get the chance," the campaign said in a post to X, highlighting the debate moment.

Bottoms’ sponsorship of the upcoming Halloween event isn’t the first time she has supported drag-themed activities.

In 2019, as mayor, she invited Ms. Terra Cotta Sugarbaker, a drag queen, to host a story hour after the Fulton County library system removed a scheduled "drag queen story time" from its events.

"Ms. Terra Cotta Sugarbaker and all our LGBTQ friends are always welcome at Atlanta City Hall. How about we host your next story hour? Let’s make it happen!" she wrote in a post to X.

RILEY GAINES AND MYKAYLA SKINNER SEND MESSAGE TO SIMONE BILES ON WOMEN'S SPORTS DEBATE AFTER SCOTUS RULING

The Bottoms campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the upcoming event, what was included in her sponsorship or whether it was appropriate to have children present for events centered around sexuality and gender expression.
