World.title: García Luna corruption case wins $5.8M for Guerrero schools: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

💰 García Luna case yields $5.8M for Guerrero schools : UIF chief Omar Reyes Colmenares said Mexico received US $5.8 million this week from its civil suit victory over the Weinberg family — ex-Security Minister García Luna’s alleged frontmen — in a Miami-Dade court. Sheinbaum said the funds will go to schools in Guerrero’s disadvantaged Montaña region.

: UIF chief Omar Reyes Colmenares said Mexico received US $5.8 million this week from its civil suit victory over the Weinberg family — ex-Security Minister García Luna’s alleged frontmen — in a Miami-Dade court. Sheinbaum said the funds will go to schools in Guerrero’s disadvantaged Montaña region. 🇲🇽 Mexico is ‘Doing very well,’ Sheinbaum says ahead of second report: Sheinbaum declared Mexico is “doing very well” almost two years into her six-year term. Her positive assessment of the current state of affairs came ahead of the presentation of her second annual government report next Tuesday.

Sheinbaum declared Mexico is “doing very well” almost two years into her six-year term. Her positive assessment of the current state of affairs came ahead of the presentation of her second annual government report next Tuesday. 🚣 Gold for rower Kenia Lechuga: Sheinbaum congratulated Nuevo León native Kenia Lechuga on her gold medal in the women’s lightweight sculls at the 2026 World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam, saying that as a former rower herself she felt “special affection” for the win. Mexican rowers also won gold in the women’s lightweight double sculls and bronze in the men’s lightweight sculls.

Why today’s mañanera matters

Today’s mañanera was significant as the federal government was able to demonstrate that its successful civil suit against former Security Minister Genaro García Luna — now imprisoned in the United States — is reaping monetary rewards.

Also of note was President Claudia Sheinbaum’s positive assessment of the current state of affairs in Mexico almost two years into her six-year term. Her favorable evaluation of the prevailing situation came four days before she is scheduled to present her second annual government report (segundo informe de gobierno) in a speech in Mexico City.

Sheinbaum: US $5.8 million recovered in García Luna case to go to schools in Guerrero

Omar Reyes Colmenares, head of the federal government’s Financial Intelligence Unit (UIF), told reporters that on Tuesday of this week, Mexico received US $5.8 million in funds recovered in the case involving García Luna, who in 2024 was sentenced to 38 years in prison in the United States after he was found guilty of collusion with the Sinaloa Cartel.

He noted that the UIF filed a civil suit in Florida aimed at recovering public money that was diverted out of Mexico in a corruption scheme involving García Luna and members of the Weinberg family. Members of the Weinberg family have been identified as frontmen for García Luna, who served as security minister during the 2006-12 government led by former President Felipe Calderón.

Reyes highlighted that a court in Miami handed down a ruling in May in favor of the Mexican state and against the Weinberg family. As part of the ruling, Judge Lisa Walsh in Miami-Dade County ordered members of the Weinberg family and related companies to pay US $578.5 million in damages to the Mexican state for losses incurred as a result of their involvement in corruption schemes.

“As a result of this process,” said Reyes, “the Mexican state received US $5.8 million on Aug. 25, 2026.”

The UIF chief said the money was obtained from the recovery of a surety bond and “the liquidation of 12 properties located in Florida, United States, and linked to the Weinberg family.” He noted that Mexico is awaiting the liquidation of other assets in order to recover additional funds diverted out of the country by García Luna.

Later in the press conference, Sheinbaum said that the $5.8 million in recovered funds that Mexico received this week would be allocated to schools in the Montaña region of the southern state of Guerrero.

“It’s around 100 million pesos that is going to be used in [one of] the most disadvantaged areas in the country,” she said.

Mexico is doing ‘very well,’ Sheinbaum says ahead of her second annual report

A reporter reminded Sheinbaum that in her first annual report speech — delivered at the National Palace on Sept. 1, 2025 — she said that Mexico and her government were “doing well” and would do “even better.” He subsequently asked the president how her administration is doing 12 months later.

“Mexico is doing better, Mexico is doing well,” Sheinbaum said.

“We’re doing very well — with the difficulties that any country can face, but we’re doing well,” she said.

@Claudiashein afirmó que México progresa positivamente en economía, reducción de la violencia y bienestar social, rumbo a su Segundo Informe de Gobierno. Algunos spots de campaña serán difundidos en radio, televisión y redes sociales. Las piezas muestran sus giras de… pic.twitter.com/pu8YEMBrT4 — Nota Central (@notacentralmx) August 28, 2026

Sheinbaum said she is “very optimistic” about Mexico’s economy and declared that Mexicans’ quality of life is improving. She also pointed out that violence has declined — a statement supported by a 30.8% annual reduction in homicides in the first seven months of 2026.

Sheinbaum subsequently spoke about her government’s raison d’être, saying that the reason why “we’re here” is to “create well-being for the people of Mexico.”

On Wednesday, the president presented economic data that she said was indicative of the strength of the Mexican economy. She highlighted the record foreign direct investment Mexico received in the first half of 2026, quarter-over-quarter economic growth of 1.4% in the second quarter of the year and the USD:MXN exchange rate, which at the time was below 17.

Sheinbaum congratulates world champion rower

The president congratulated Mexican rower Kenia Lechuga, a Nuevo León native who on Thursday won gold in the women’s lightweight sculls at the 2026 World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam, Netherlands.

“Many congratulations,” Sheinbaum said, adding that as a former rower herself, she reserved “special affection” for a victory by a Mexican rower.

Lechuga, who had previously won silver and bronze medals at World Rowing Championships, wasn’t the only Mexican rower to win gold in Amsterdam on Thursday. Aylin Ibarra and Melissa Márquez won the women’s lightweight double sculls, while Aléxis López placed third to secure the bronze medal in the lightweight men’s sculls.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: How Mexico City can solve its 400-year water crisis
World.content:
Following a bout of heavy rains in September 1629, water rose through the streets of Mexico City and did not recede. The city had just spent 22 years digging a drainage channel through the mountains, the Desagüe de Huehuetoca, meant to solve a problem the closed, mountain-ringed basin had faced for centuries: nowhere for excess water to go.

The project failed. Parts of the city stayed flooded for years and more than 30,000 people died, mostly from disease in the standing, sewage-laced water.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by ABC News (@abcnews)



The city kept making the same trade for four centuries after that: draining the water to survive and turning every success into a new, worse problem.

A city that traded its lake for a sinking foundation

Before the Spanish conquest, Tenochtitlán sat on an island in Lake Texcoco, its neighborhoods built with the lake rather than against it. Colonial and then Porfirian-era engineers kept draining it instead, culminating in the Gran Canal del Desagüe around 1900. Draining the lake solved flooding and erased the city’s water supply at the same time, so the city turned to pumping the aquifer beneath the old lakebed’s soft, clay-rich sediment.

Pumping that aquifer releases the pressure holding the clay open. The clay compacts, causing the ground to drop. A 2021 study published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth measured subsidence near 50 centimeters a year in the worst areas, and found the sinking no longer tracks current pumping rates: It is now driven by decades-old compaction that cannot be undone, even if every well stopped tomorrow.

That uneven sinking has warped the Gran Canal itself, leaving stretches of the drainage system sloping the wrong way. Mexico City has sunk roughly 30 feet across the lakebed zone, and engineers now run pumping stations just to lift sewage back up to where gravity can take over — the same 1607 trade, repeated at greater cost.

The newest version, the Túnel Emisor Oriente, finished in 2019 after 11 years of digging, carries wastewater 62.5 kilometers (39 miles) to Hidalgo state, where it irrigates the Mezquital Valley. Only about 36% of the city’s wastewater gets treated at all; the nearby Tula Valley region now draws 90% to 100% of its own aquifer from decades of Mexico City’s former runoff.

What survives to reach a kitchen tap

Mexico City’s water is treated properly at the source. What happens after is where the system fails.

Official figures from Mexico City’s water agency, the Sistema de Aguas de la Ciudad de México (SACMEX), put network-wide leak loss at roughly 40%, while researchers studying intermittent, low-pressure water systems in general have documented exactly how contamination gets in through a leaking network: a crack or joint, a nearby contaminant source, and a pressure gradient pulling inward.

Rooftop reservoirs, also known as tinacos, exist precisely because city pressure is not continuous, and a small pilot study in Guadalajara found contamination rates more than double after water sat in a home’s storage tank versus straight off the network.

Water contamination

Two boroughs carry a documented, more specific version of this.

In Iztapalapa, two named SACMEX/UNAM wells have shown arsenic and heavy-metal levels exceeding Mexico’s own drinking-water standard since they opened; separately, UNAM researchers found microplastics, Giardia muris and E. coli in the borough’s water.

SACMEX’s own 2020 data recorded arsenic violations across 28 wells in Tláhuac, Tlalpan, Coyoacán, Iztapalapa, Iztacalco and Azcapotzalco, signifying a documented national pattern: Only 1 in 10 Mexican treatment plants is even equipped to remove arsenic or fluoride.

Stressing the system

Meanwhile, large companies are also extracting from the same stressed basin. CONAGUA’s public registry shows Coca-Cola FEMSA holds a well concession in Cuauhtémoc, where it extracts 1.13 billion liters a year. PepsiCo’s bottler holds another in Iztacalco, extracting 511 million liters.

Nationally, Coca-Cola and PepsiCo’s Mexican bottlers have extracted roughly 14.7 billion and 25.7 billion liters, respectively, since 1994.

What none of the public record shows is what becomes of the 15% to 30% of that water any industrial reverse-osmosis system inevitably rejects as concentrate, a limit set by the physics of the membrane itself.

Where the hope is

The subsidence side of this cycle has already been broken elsewhere.

Tokyo sank roughly 4 meters before two laws, the 1956 Industrial Water Law and the 1962 Law on Regulation of Groundwater Use in Office Buildings, made new wells prohibitively expensive to drill while the government subsidized cheaper surface-water infrastructure as the replacement. Groundwater pumping in the city’s 23 wards peaked in 1964 and has fallen since; subsidence in the most heavily regulated districts was brought close to zero.

Venice stopped pumping groundwater entirely and now draws its drinking water from the Italian mainland instead, sinking at about 1 millimeter a year, down from a rate that once threatened the city outright.

Neither city undid the damage already on the books. Both proved the mechanism itself can be stopped, and both did it with a law, not a technology.

Legal remedies vs. a household fix

The legislative move mirrors Tokyo’s. Sustained public pressure on regulators, not new technology, is what got its fix passed. Here, that looks like contacting a local representative directly, and backing investigations like “Veneno en mi agua,” or “Poison in my water,” that keep this issue on the public record instead of letting it fade after one news cycle.

A household’s own move is smaller and immediate: A fix goes under the sink.

An ultrafiltration membrane, at roughly 0.01 microns, physically blocks the bacteria and parasitic cysts responsible for most water-borne illness here, the exact risk documented above. It runs on the building’s own water pressure: no pump, no electricity and a 100% water recovery rate, so there is no reject stream at all. The water that enters the membrane is the water that leaves the tap, only cleaner. That combination — no pump, no electricity, no wasted water — also makes it the cheapest of these options to buy and run.

Reverse osmosis, run at home, sends roughly 3 liters down the drain for every liter it produces, a smaller version of the same tradeoff bottlers make at industrial scale. Given how much of this city’s wastewater exits the basin rather than getting treated and returned, that reject water is likely gone from the Valley of Mexico’s own water cycle for good, unlike ultrafiltration, which never enters that path at all.

Ultrafiltration

Garrafón delivery carries its own documented risk: Independent testing found the majority of samples in one Mexico City study contaminated with coliform bacteria, and nearly a quarter with E. coli, in an industry that grew 85% between 2012 and 2018.

Ultrafiltration is the one choice in this entire chain that does not ask the aquifer for anything extra to keep a household safe. It does not fix the leaking network, the sinking ground, or the four centuries of trades that got the city here. It is the one piece of the cycle a single kitchen can opt out of today, without waiting on a General Water Law that has been stalled in Congress for eight years, or a recharge program that exists as exactly one working pilot against a documented crisis.

Andrew D. Daily lives in Roma Norte, where he runs a water filtration company and mexicocitytravel.com, a simplified guide for visitors. Before meeting his wife and relocating to CDMX, he worked 11 years in Los Angeles, CA, as a television Production Manager on shows like Shark Tank, The Voice, and Miss Universe.

World.title: Meet Jacinto Canek, the Maya rebel who rose against Spanish rule in Yucatán
World.content:
The people of Cisteil were tired. After years as a Spanish district, they depended heavily on the municipality of Yaxcabá, located in what is now the state of Yucatán. Despite being a relatively small town, it had a fiery population that wanted to free itself from the Spanish yoke.

Cisteil lasted no more than eight years under this abusive regime. Little did the Spanish know that this small Yucatecan town would spark a major Maya anti-colonial uprising, led by a Maya man named Jacinto Canek.

From student and Maya physician to revolutionary leader

Long before Miguel Hidalgo began the Mexican independence revolts in Dolores, in what is now the Bajío region, southeastern Maya communities were already seeking to rid themselves of Spanish invaders.

Despite his standing as a prominent figure of Maya resistance, little is known about the early life of Jacinto Uc de los Santos Canek. Born in the 18th century, he led the “most important Maya rebellion in Yucatán during the colonial era,” according to the Great Maya Museum in Yucatán.

Documentary evidence shows he was born around 1731 to a poor family in the southeastern state of Campeche. Historical records indicate he studied Latin, history and Christian doctrine at the Convento Grande in Mérida before being expelled for his rebellious nature. Canek had a strong knowledge of Christian doctrine, joined a religious organization in his hometown of San Francisco de Campeche and practiced traditional Maya medicine learned through oral tradition.

After the 1761 rebellion, “Jacinto Canek chose a name of historical significance for the Maya,” according to a study by Robert W. Patch from the University of California, Riverside. He proclaimed himself king of the movement to reclaim “political and religious domination of the Yucatán Maya.”

Thousands of Indigenous people recognized his authority and viewed him as an incarnation of Kukulkán, the sacred serpent of the Maya pantheon. Researchers note the movement sought to revitalize Maya culture after two centuries of colonialism, with revolutionaries believing the days of Spanish rule were numbered.

Jacinto Canek: Kukulkán and Christ, embodied in a Maya revolutionary

No other significant anti-colonial movement had taken place in present-day Mexico to this point. However, as a review of a criminal trial resulting from the rebellion emphasizes, “it was a highly serious rebellion, with a strong anti-colonialist content.”

Beyond establishing stronger trade ties with former Maya chiefdoms, the people of Cisteil wanted to reclaim their culture, traditions and religion. “The Maya continued to believe in a cyclic version of history,” the study points out, “which led them to think that one day in the future they would overthrow the Spaniards.”

Canek took a name sacred to two religious traditions: Maya and Christian. From 1761 onward, he was known as Jacinto Uc de los Santos Canek Chichán Moctezuma. He embodied the man-god myth of Mesoamerican tradition, presenting a syncretic Maya-Christian figure blending Jesus Christ and Kukulkán. Under that name, he summoned the highest rulers of Cisteil to wage revolution.

How the Maya remember Jacinto Canek

Yucatán Governor José de Crespo y Honorato ordered the arrest of the revolt’s leaders to quell the movement. Spanish forces captured Canek and took him to Mérida, where he was condemned to be “broken alive” — having his limbs broken with iron bars — before being executed on Dec. 14, 1761. His body was burned to ashes after his death.

Many followers were killed alongside him. Following the execution, Spanish commanders suppressed the rebellion before it could spread beyond central Yucatán.

The Spanish then launched a campaign to delegitimize the revolutionaries, framing the event as a “drunkards’ riot,” according to UNAM records. Among the Maya, however, it remained “a noble uprising against colonial exploitation.”

Today, Canek is remembered as “one of the most significant figures in the history of Yucatán” and as someone who “lives in the hearts of the women and men of the Maya people.”

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: Supreme Court ruling lets Indigenous communities speak in constitutional trials for the first time
World.content:
For the first time, Mexico’s Supreme Court (SCJN) has opened a formal avenue for Indigenous peoples, communities, and Afro-Mexican communities to participate in constitutional disputes (known as controversias constitucionales) as interested third parties — a role that had previously been limited to only government bodies.

“Today is a historic day,” Chief Justice Hugo Aguilar Ortiz, who is of Mixtec Indigenous origin, said during the Tuesday ruling. “We are attending this appointment with history to see if we can correct in some way 200 years of exclusion and racism, and, among them, the judicial exclusion of Indigenous peoples and communities.”

With five votes in favor and four against, the SCJN recognized the participation of the Mazahua community of Crescencio Morales, in Zitácuaro, Michoacán, in two constitutional controversies brought by the municipal government, related to regulations and actions connected to a prior consultation on indigenous self-government.

In its ruling, the SCJN concluded that the Mazahua community “must be recognized as an interested third party, in order to remove obstacles to its effective access to justice and ensure its full participation in a process whose resolution may directly affect its collective rights and interests,” Minister Arístides Guerrero García said.

An interested third party is any person or entity that has a contrary interest to that of the complainant in an amparo trial or constitutional dispute. Even though they are neither the plaintiffs nor the defendants and thus can’t initiate the trial, they can join ongoing disputes as an interested third party when a ruling by the SCJN could affect their rights or interests.

Historically, only entities, powers or governing bodies were able to act as third parties in constitutional disputes.

That doesn’t mean that Iindigenous communities weren’t able to defend their rights. They could, through other means. What the new ruling established is the opportunity to join a constitutional controversy promoted by an authority, meaning they can consult the file, submit arguments, and defend their rights.

The court cited articles 2 and 17 of the Mexican Constitution as the basis for the new ruling.

Article 2, reformed in 2024, recognizes Indigenous and Afro-Mexican peoples and communities as subjects of public law, with their own legal personality and assets. Together with the right of access to justice under Article 17 of the Constitution, the SCJN ruled that those groups have a procedural voice if the outcome of the constitutional controversy affects their legal sphere.

Three ministers voted against the ruling, arguing that granting a recognition that is not explicitly provided for in the Constitution, “directly implies an overreach of powers” ​​and amounts to legislating.

“This decision breaks the separation of powers,” Minister Espinosa Betanzo said.

Meanwhile, Minister Ríos González, who also voted against the ruling, added that the votes against the ruling do not imply a stance contrary to the rights of Indigenous peoples.

With reports from La Jornada

World.title: Costa Rica Limits 12-Hour Shifts to Private Firms as Deputies Shield Public Workers
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

COSTA RICA · POLITICS

Key Facts —What happened: Deputies voted to exclude public-sector employees from Costa Rica’s planned 4×3 reform of the Labour Code. —How it works: The 4×3 scheme allows 12-hour shifts on four days a week, in exchange for three full days of rest. —Who it applies to: Only private companies running 24-hour production cycles would be able to use the longer shifts. —The catch: The reform is still a bill that has not passed, so the new shifts do not legally exist yet. —The backdrop: Homicides hit a record 905 in 2023, but 2026 is tracking below 800 for the first time since the surge. —What comes next: Deputies keep debating the bill, which the government sells as an investment magnet after 20 years of trying.

Costa Rica’s long-fought 4×3 labour reform now covers private firms only, after deputies voted to keep the state’s own workers out of 12-hour shifts. The vote lands in a tense week, with a Wall Street Journal investigation on drug violence rattling the country even as killings decline.

What the deputies decided

The Legislative Assembly approved a motion that expressly excludes public-sector employees from the 4×3 reform. The change was reported on 28 August by the San José daily La República.

The 4×3 scheme would amend the Labour Code, known locally as the Código de Trabajo. It lets staff work 12 hours a day for four days, then take three full days off.

After the vote, the schedule would apply only to private companies with 24-hour production cycles. State workers stay on their current schedules whatever happens to the bill.

Juan Manuel Quesada, deputy whip of the governing party Pueblo Soberano, defended the carve-out. He said it dismantles the fear campaign that unions and the opposition Frente Amplio party built around the project.

He named union leader Albino Vargas directly. Critics, Quesada said, can no longer claim the state will impose 12-hour days on its own employees.

Why the government wants 12-hour shifts

The official case is economic. Quesada argues the schedules will raise competitiveness, attract investment and create jobs under clear rules.

The target is firms that run around the clock, from call centres to medical-device plants. The country has debated versions of this reform for more than 20 years.

For foreign readers, the stakes are familiar. The country competes for nearshoring investment against Mexico and its Central American neighbours, and flexible shifts are part of the pitch.

Unions answer that 12-hour days erode rest and family life, however many free days follow. The public-sector exclusion removes their loudest argument, but not their opposition.

A maximum-security prison and the drugs war behind it

The labour fight unfolds against a security debate. The government is building a maximum-security prison modelled on El Salvador’s giant Terrorism Confinement Centre, known as CECOT.

The logic is a regional one. Governments from San Salvador to Quito now promise voters order through mass incarceration, and San José is testing that model in a stable democracy.

Not everyone buys it. Robert Muggah of the Igarapé Institute, a Brazilian research group, told the Wall Street Journal that the country faces embedded transnational organisations, not street gangs, and that building prisons will not resolve it.

Stephen Madden, who directs the country’s Drug Enforcement Police, counters that the strategy works. He points to a hundred new officers over two years and drug seizures back at 2021 levels.

The Wall Street Journal alarm, and what the numbers say

The Journal’s report, published on 27 August and reported from the port city of Limón, describes a political civil war. It sets President Laura Fernández and her party against the judiciary over drug violence.

The paper traces the surge to the Moín container terminal, opened in 2019 outside Limón. The US State Department has called Costa Rica the leading transshipment point for South American cocaine since 2020.

Its headline figure is a 50 percent rise in homicides since 2020, close to Mexico’s murder rate. The official record supports the climb, from 570 killings in 2020 to a record 905 in 2023.

What the framing misses is the current year. The country counted 520 homicide victims as of 24 August, against 570 in the same stretch of 2025, the Tico Times reported.

The daily average has fallen from 2.5 killings in 2023 to 1.9. The Judicial Investigation Agency, the police body known as the OIJ, projects a 2026 close between 693 and 766.

The decline is uneven. Cartago, Puntarenas and Limón provinces edged up this year, while the other four provinces fell.

The political fight is real, whatever the trend. Fernández, in office since May, accuses the judiciary of infiltration by organised crime and has moved to cut its budget by tens of millions of dollars.

Attorney General Carlo Díaz warned the cuts favour organised crime. The UN special rapporteur on judicial independence has publicly registered concern, and citizens have marched in support of the courts.

What to watch from here

The first marker is the bill itself. The 4×3 project still needs final approval before any 12-hour shift becomes legal.

The second is the union response. Strikes and street protests have killed labour reforms in Costa Rica before.

The third is the year-end homicide count. A close below 700 would strengthen the government’s hand, while a late surge would strengthen the Journal’s.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Costa Rica’s 4×3 shift law? It is a proposed reform of the Labour Code that would allow 12-hour shifts on four days a week, in exchange for three days of rest. It targets private companies with 24-hour production cycles. Are public-sector workers included in the 4×3 reform? No. Deputies approved a motion that expressly excludes public-sector employees, so state workers keep their current schedules even if the bill passes. Is the 4×3 law already in force in Costa Rica? No. The reform remains a bill under debate in the Legislative Assembly. No 12-hour shift under the new scheme is legal yet. What did the Wall Street Journal say about Costa Rica? The Journal reported that drug killings have fractured the political system, setting President Laura Fernández against the judiciary. It linked the violence to the Moín container terminal, opened in 2019. Are homicides in Costa Rica rising or falling? Both, depending on the baseline. Killings rose about 50 percent from 2020 to a record 905 in 2023, but 2026 is tracking between 693 and 766, the lowest since the surge began.

World.title: Cuba Takes Its Hunger Blockade Claim to the UN Security Council
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

CUBA · GEOPOLITICS

Key Facts —What happened: Cuba told the UN Security Council on 25 August that US sanctions are driving hunger on the island. —The trigger: New US measures hit nine Cuban state firms in mining, metals, construction and trade. —The humanitarian case: UN data show food production down 60 percent and infant mortality more than doubled since 2018. —The catch: The Security Council cannot lift US sanctions, so Havana’s move is diplomatic pressure, not a legal remedy. —Washington’s line: US officials say the measures target the Cuban government and its revenue, not the population. —What comes next: The fight shifts to the UN General Assembly’s annual vote on the embargo later this year.

Cuba has carried its confrontation with Washington to the UN Security Council, accusing the United States of deepening hunger on the island through its decades-old embargo and a fresh round of sanctions on Cuban firms and officials.

What Havana told the Security Council

The Cuban government used a statement to the United Nations Security Council on Tuesday, 25 August, to sharpen its case. It warned against the use of hunger as a weapon of war.

Conflicts, inequality and unilateral coercive measures are aggravating global food insecurity, the statement argued. Havana then tied Cuba’s own worsening food situation directly to US economic, commercial and financial restrictions.

Those restrictions are what Cuba calls the blockade. Washington calls the same policy an embargo, in place in various forms since the early 1960s.

The framing matters. Havana is no longer arguing only about sovereignty and trade law, but about food, medicine and energy reaching ordinary Cubans.

The sanctions that triggered the escalation

The Security Council intervention came days after Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez attacked Washington over the new measures. The latest measures targeted nine Cuban state-owned entities in mining, metals, construction, trade and imports.

Senior officials of the Cuban Institute of Friendship with the Peoples, known by its Spanish acronym ICAP, were also sanctioned. Its president, Fernando González Llort, is among them.

Rodríguez said the measures are particularly affecting containers carrying food, medicines and medical equipment. That includes supplies bought by Cuba’s private micro, small and medium-sized enterprises, the businesses Washington says it wants to encourage.

He aimed his fire directly at US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The policy, Rodríguez said, is designed to damage Cuba’s economy and stop Havana from guaranteeing basic services.

Energy starvation and a deepening crisis

Behind the diplomacy sits a severe shortage economy. Cuba struggles with fuel, electricity, food and medicine, and the shortages have worsened through 2026.

A US executive order from January 2026 tightened Cuba’s access to fuel. UN human rights experts later described the effect as energy starvation with severe human-rights implications.

The UN Human Rights Office reported in June that food production had fallen 60 percent. Medicine supplies stood at just 30 percent of normal levels.

The same reporting put infant mortality at 9.9 per 1,000 births, up from 4 in 2018. Childhood cancer survival rates have fallen to 65 percent.

Power cuts make everything worse. In some areas blackouts have lasted 20 to 22 hours a day, idling irrigation, refrigeration, hospitals and public transport.

The reform paradox at the heart of the dispute

The confrontation now carries a contradiction that both sides acknowledge. Washington presses Cuba to open its centrally controlled economy, while Havana says US sanctions make exactly those reforms harder.

The Associated Press reported this month that Cuba has widened space for private business, imports and exports, foreign investment and even private banking. Yet the measures, Cuban officials argue, scare away the investors those reforms are meant to attract.

Cuba’s ambassador to the UN, Ernesto Soberón Guzmán, put the question plainly. Why impose new sanctions, he asked, just as Havana opens sectors of the economy to private participation?

Fuel and electricity shortages, he added, are discouraging investors and tourists alike. Tourism was once Cuba’s biggest source of foreign currency after professional services exports.

Washington rejects the hunger charge. US officials say the measures pressure the Cuban government and close revenue loopholes, rather than deliberately depriving the population.

What to watch from here

Do not expect the Security Council to act. The United States holds a veto there, which is why Havana’s move is about narrative, not enforcement.

The real stage is the UN General Assembly. For more than three decades it has voted overwhelmingly, every year, to demand an end to the embargo.

What has changed is the argument. Hunger and medicine shortages now sit at the centre of Cuba’s case, backed by UN humanitarian data rather than Cuban government figures alone.

For foreigners trying to read the standoff, that is the shift to track. The question is no longer only whether the embargo is legal, but whether its civilian cost has become the bigger story.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Cuba tell the UN Security Council? In a statement on 25 August 2026, Cuba warned against hunger as a weapon of war. It linked its worsening food situation to US economic, commercial and financial restrictions, which Havana calls a blockade. Which new US measures triggered the complaint? The latest measures targeted nine Cuban state-owned entities in mining, metals, construction, trade and imports. Officials of the friendship institute ICAP, including president Fernando González Llort, were also sanctioned. How bad is Cuba’s humanitarian situation? UN reporting in June 2026 put food production down 60 percent and medicine supplies at 30 percent of normal. Infant mortality has risen to 9.9 per 1,000 births, from 4 in 2018. Can the UN Security Council end the US embargo on Cuba? No. The United States holds a veto on the Security Council, so Cuba’s move is diplomatic pressure. The annual UN General Assembly vote against the embargo is similarly non-binding. What is the US position on the sanctions? US officials say the measures pressure the Cuban government and close revenue loopholes, not the population. Washington says it wants economic reform, while Havana argues the measures are undermining the very reforms under way.

World.title: Honduras Courts US Investment for Ports and Energy as Remittances Reach US$7.7 Billion
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

HONDURAS · ECONOMY

Key Facts —What happened: President Nasry Asfura signed a US agreement on 5 March 2026 funding a study of a coast-to-coast transport corridor for Honduras. —How big: Family remittances reached US$7,692.2 million in January to July 2026, up 11.2 percent on the same months of 2025. —What it means: Washington wants the country’s ports, energy and roads built with US technology, explicitly free of Chinese influence. —The catch: The US money pays for feasibility studies, not construction, so no investment has actually been committed yet. —Who it touches: About 1.8 million Hondurans live in the United States, and their transfers equal roughly a quarter of GDP. —What comes next: Consultant ShorelineHudson studies the ports of Puerto Cortés and San Lorenzo, then proposes rail standards and a financing plan.

Honduras is pitching itself to Washington as a nearshoring bet, with a US-funded study for a coast-to-coast corridor and ports on two oceans. At home, remittances reached US$7,692.2 million in the first seven months of 2026, up 11.2 percent on the year.

What Washington signed in Arlington

On 5 March 2026, the US Trade and Development Agency hosted President Nasry Asfura in Arlington, Virginia. The agency, known as USTDA, funds project preparation in emerging markets, always with an eye on US exports.

The two sides signed an agreement to accelerate an overland corridor linking the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean. The signing came ahead of President Donald Trump’s Shield of the Americas Summit in Miami.

USTDA will pay for a feasibility study covering new port and rail infrastructure. Deputy director Thomas R. Hardy said the goal is secure US trade routes, built with American technology and free of Chinese influence.

The money goes to CONFI, the state commission charged with building an interoceanic railway. CONFI has picked Hudson-Arvon LLC, a New Jersey firm trading as ShorelineHudson, to run the study.

The consultants will examine bottlenecks at two ports. One is San Lorenzo, on the Pacific Gulf of Fonseca, and the other is Puerto Cortés, the country’s main Caribbean gateway for container cargo.

The study will also design an inland rail terminal to ease congestion at Puerto Cortés. It then recommends rail standards and a financing plan built around US suppliers.

That supplier list is the commercial point of the exercise. USTDA names locomotives, freight wagons, container-handling equipment, terminal operating systems and security systems.

An old dream with a new sponsor

The interoceanic railway is one of the oldest ideas in national politics. A first attempt in the nineteenth century collapsed in debt, and the project has resurfaced in almost every decade since.

What is different this time is the sponsor. The United States now frames the corridor as a supply-chain security project, not just a national development plan.

The corridor study sits inside a wider courtship of the new government. On 14 May, Ben Black, chief executive of the US International Development Finance Corporation, met Asfura in Tegucigalpa.

Black travelled with a delegation led by Caleb Orr, the State Department’s top economic affairs official. He named energy and port modernisation as priority sectors for US investment.

Asfura, who took office at the start of 2026 after a Trump-backed election win, needs the capital. His government has moved to rejoin ICSID, the World Bank’s arbitration body, to reassure foreign investors.

It has also extended the Temporary Import Regime, the tax-incentive scheme that anchors the country’s maquila export industry. Road repairs are the visible domestic priority, after a slow start drew public criticism.

Remittances keep climbing, but the pace is cooling

The other half of the economy is money sent home by migrants. Family remittances reached US$7,692.2 million between January and July 2026, the Central Bank reported.

That is 11.2 percent more than in the same period of 2025. It keeps remittances far ahead of exports, tourism and foreign investment as the country’s top source of foreign currency.

The flows equal roughly a quarter of gross domestic product. Some 98.5 percent of the money originates in the United States, where about 1.8 million Hondurans live, with or without papers.

Growth is still in double digits, but it is cooling. Remittances jumped 25.3 percent in 2025 to a record US$12,212 million, and the central bank expects moderation this year.

The regional picture shows the same pattern. Remittances to the three Northern Triangle countries, Honduras, Guatemala and El Salvador, reached US$24,554.6 million in the first half of 2026, up 7.8 percent, according to International Organization for Migration data.

Mothers receive more than 37 percent of the transfers. Over 80 percent of the money goes to food, health and education, the central bank says.

The 1 percent tax and the deportation risk

Two US policy shifts hang over the numbers. Since 1 January 2026, the United States has applied a 1 percent tax to remittances sent from its territory.

The levy has not stopped the flows, but it raises the cost of sending money home. The central bank also lists a US slowdown and rising deportations as persistent risks for this year.

That combination explains the official caution. In January the bank projected about US$10,670 million for all of 2026, below the record 2025 total, precisely because of migration policy.

The January-to-July figure already covers 72 percent of that projection. Households, in other words, are beating the official forecast even as Washington tightens the screws.

What to watch from here

The first marker is the ShorelineHudson study itself. Neither USTDA nor CONFI has published a deadline for its conclusions.

The second is whether American interest becomes committed money. Delegations and feasibility studies are cheap, while financed ports and railways are not.

The third is the remittance trend into the final quarter. December is traditionally the strongest month, and December 2025 alone brought US$1,106.3 million.

For now, the country offers Washington a friendly government and a strategic corridor. In return, it asks for the one thing studies cannot deliver, which is construction.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Honduras and the USTDA sign in March 2026? On 5 March 2026, the US Trade and Development Agency signed an agreement with Honduras to fund a feasibility study for an overland transport corridor connecting the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean. How much did the country receive in remittances in 2026? Family remittances reached US$7,692.2 million between January and July 2026, up 11.2 percent on the same period of 2025, according to the Central Bank. Who is paying for the interoceanic corridor study? The USTDA is funding the study through CONFI, the state railway commission. CONFI selected the New Jersey firm Hudson-Arvon LLC, trading as ShorelineHudson, to carry it out. Why does the United States care about Honduran ports? Washington wants secure supply-chain routes in the Western Hemisphere built with US technology. USTDA deputy director Thomas R. Hardy said the routes should remain free of Chinese influence. What risks face Honduran remittances in 2026? The Central Bank lists the 1 percent US tax on remittances, a possible US slowdown and rising deportations as persistent risks for 2026.

World.title: Brazil Taps Senator Cid Gomes to Steer Redata Data Center Tax Bill to a Vote
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

BRAZIL · TECHNOLOGY

Key Facts —What happened: Senate chief Davi Alcolumbre named Cid Gomes rapporteur of Brazil’s data center tax bill. —What comes next: Gomes wants a floor vote next week, during the Senate’s concentrated session starting August 31. —The prize: Redata suspends federal taxes on data center equipment for five years, then can erase them. —The cost: The government expects R$5.2 billion (US$1.01 billion) in forgone revenue in 2026 alone. —The catch: The tax break has been legally dead since February, when the original decree expired unvoted. —Why it matters: Global cloud firms are expanding in Brazil, and investors say tax certainty decides where servers go.

Brazil’s Senate has put Senator Cid Gomes in charge of the data center tax bill, and he wants a floor vote next week. It is the bill’s best chance since the original incentive decree died unvoted in February.

What the Senate president decided

Senate President Davi Alcolumbre picked Cid Gomes, a senator from the north-eastern state of Ceará, as rapporteur of Bill 278/2026 on August 27. The choice was first reported by Agência iNFRA and confirmed by Correio Braziliense.

The rapporteur is the senator who steers a bill through the upper house. He writes the official report, negotiates the final text and, in practice, decides whether a bill moves or sleeps.

Gomes told Agência iNFRA he would make “every effort to reach a consensus and vote it next week”. He expects to publish his report on the eve of the vote, with the exact day set by Alcolumbre.

The slot is the Senate’s esforço concentrado, a concentrated voting week that starts on August 31. In these marathon weeks, party leaders clear priority bills in back-to-back sessions before recess or elections.

The scheduling is part of a wider deal between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and the heads of both chambers. Lula wants a package of priority bills passed before Brazil’s October general election.

What the bill actually does

Redata is short for Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter, a special tax regime for data center services. It targets the machines that fill a data center, not the building.

For five years, the regime suspends federal taxes on information-technology equipment bought in Brazil or imported. That covers servers, storage and networking gear destined for a company’s fixed assets.

Three levies are suspended. The import tax applies to goods with no Brazilian-made equivalent, the IPI industrialized-products tax covers listed goods made in the Manaus Free Trade Zone, and PIS/Cofins are federal contributions that fund social programs.

Once a company meets all conditions and the equipment is delivered, the suspension turns into a permanent exemption. Suppliers that manufacture equipment for an enabled data center can also join the regime.

The regime covers cloud computing, high-performance computing and the training and running of artificial-intelligence models. That scope is why Big Tech and AI investors are watching the vote so closely.

The conditions attached to the tax break

The regime is not a free lunch. Companies must cover all of their contracted electricity with clean or renewable sources, either through supply contracts or their own generation.

That condition is Brazil’s selling point. More than 86 percent of the country’s electricity already comes from renewable sources, a fact the bill’s lower-house rapporteur, deputy Aguinaldo Ribeiro, cites constantly.

Firms must also keep water use for cooling at or below 0.05 litre per kilowatt-hour, measured annually. They must publish a sustainability report and be fully up to date with federal taxes.

The text passed by the lower house adds two more commitments. Companies must reserve 10 percent of processing capacity for the Brazilian market and spend 2 percent of equipment value on research and development.

Twenty-two amendments await in the Senate, according to Exame magazine. One, by Senator Laércio Oliveira, would make natural gas an eligible energy source, which would weaken the green condition.

Why the bill slept for six months

The regime was born in September 2025 as a provisional measure, a presidential decree with immediate force. Under Brazilian law, such decrees die if Congress does not convert them into law in time.

This one expired on February 25, 2026, without a vote. Hours earlier, the Chamber of Deputies had approved an identical stand-alone bill, written by government leader José Guimarães, to keep the policy alive.

The bill then reached the Senate and stopped. Alcolumbre, locked in a political dispute with Lula at the time, pulled it from the agenda, and it sat untouched for six months.

For months, the expected rapporteur was Eduardo Gomes, a senator from the opposition Liberal Party. The switch to Cid Gomes, an ally of the government, signals that Lula now wants the bill passed, not parked.

A legal wrinkle remains. Brazilian electoral law restricts new tax breaks in an election year, but the government argues the cost is already written into the 2026 budget law, which softens the problem.

The Ceará angle, and what it costs

Cid Gomes is the leader of the PSB party bloc in the Senate and a former governor of Ceará. He is one of the most experienced deal-makers in the north-east, Brazil’s fastest-growing data center frontier.

His state has attracted significant data center investment, according to BNamericas. He filed nine amendments to the original decree and sat on the congressional committee that studied it.

The treasury, meanwhile, counts what it gives up. The government estimates forgone revenue of R$5.2 billion (US$1.01 billion) in 2026, plus R$1 billion (US$194 million) in each of the two following years.

Supporters answer that the investment dwarfs the cost. Industry projections cited in Congress put global data center spending in the trillions of dollars this decade, and Brazil wants a bigger slice.

What to watch next week

The first signal is Gomes’s report, due on the eve of the vote. Watch whether it accepts the natural-gas amendment or keeps the bill’s renewable-only condition intact.

The second is the text itself. If the Senate changes a single comma, the bill returns to the Chamber of Deputies, and the election calendar leaves almost no room for a second round.

The third is the state-level piece. A parallel cut of up to 90 percent in the ICMS state sales tax on equipment depends on a deal among state finance secretaries, stalled since last year.

The market is not waiting. Alibaba Cloud opened its first South American cloud region in Brazil this week, and investors keep repeating the same message: money follows tax certainty.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Redata bill in Brazil? Bill 278/2026 creates Redata, a special tax regime that suspends federal taxes on data center equipment for five years. Once companies meet the conditions, the suspension becomes a permanent exemption. Who is Cid Gomes? Cid Gomes is a senator from Ceará state and leader of the PSB bloc in Brazil’s Senate. Senate President Davi Alcolumbre named him rapporteur of the Redata bill on August 27, 2026. When will Brazil’s Senate vote on the bill? Cid Gomes says he wants a floor vote next week, during the concentrated session that starts on August 31, 2026. Senate President Davi Alcolumbre will set the exact day. How much would the Redata regime cost Brazil? The government estimates R$5.2 billion (US$1.01 billion) in forgone revenue in 2026. It expects a further R$1 billion (US$194 million) in each of the two following years. What must companies do to qualify for Redata? They must buy all their electricity from clean or renewable sources, meet a water-efficiency limit for cooling, publish sustainability reports and be current on federal taxes.

Sources: Agência iNFRA, Correio Braziliense, Metrópoles, Tele.Síntese, Exame, CNN Brasil, BNamericas. Exchange rate: US$1 = R$5.15 (August 28, 2026).

World.title: Police await CCTV after 77-year-old woman killed crossing Philip Goldson Highway
World.content:
Police await CCTV after 77-year-old woman killed crossing Philip Goldson Highway

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are awaiting surveillance footage as they investigate Thursday’s fatal traffic accident that claimed the life of 77-year-old Burrell Boom resident Erlene Gillett.

The accident occurred shortly before 11:30 a.m. on August 27 in the vicinity of Mile 2 on the Philip Goldson Highway.

Police say Gillett was attempting to cross the highway when she was struck by a Dodge Caravan being driven by a man whose name has not been released.

The vehicle has since been impounded as part of the investigation, while a sample was obtained from the driver and he was served with a Notice of Intended Prosecution.

During Friday’s police press briefing, Assistant Superintendent Stacy Smith said investigators have received assurances that surveillance footage from an establishment in the area may have captured the accident. That footage is expected to help police establish the exact circumstances surrounding the collision, including whether other motorists may have stopped to allow Gillett to cross.

Smith urged pedestrians to use designated crossing areas where available, but stressed that motorists also have a responsibility to remain alert, even when travelling within the speed limit.

Local media reports say Gillett was crossing the highway in front of My Lights when she was struck by a southbound minivan.

The investigation continues.

World.title: Police indicate inmate has died following apparent suicide attempt while in police custody
World.content:
Police indicate inmate has died following apparent suicide attempt while in police custody

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have indicated that an inmate who reportedly attempted to take his own life while in custody has since died, though police say further details on the case are still being gathered.

The matter arose during Friday afternoon’s police press briefing when reporters sought an update on the condition of the inmate.

Assistant Superintendent Stacy Smith indicated that her understanding was that the inmate had died, but said she had not yet received a complete briefing on the investigation.

Smith also indicated that a post-mortem examination was expected and said police hope to provide additional information on the matter by Monday.

Reporters raised concerns about the circumstances because the deceased was in the custody of the state at the time of the incident, placing a duty of care on the institution responsible for him.

Police did not provide the inmate’s identity, the facility where the incident occurred, or further details surrounding the apparent suicide attempt during Friday’s briefing.

The investigation remains ongoing.

World.title: International News: Missing persons near 2,000 in Nepal flood disaster
World.content:
International News: Missing persons near 2,000 in Nepal flood disaster

By Zoila Palma: The number of people reported missing after devastating flash floods in Nepal has surged to 1,924, according to the country’s disaster relief agency, as rescue teams continue searching areas devastated by a massive flood wave.

At least 517 foreign nationals are among those reported missing, although authorities have issued varying figures as the situation continues to develop, BBC reports.

Nepal’s reported death toll has risen to 579, while at least five people have died in Tibet, where 558 others are reported missing. Information from Tibet remains limited, with reports largely coming from Chinese state media as rescue and recovery operations continue near the Nepal-Tibet border.

The disaster has left widespread destruction in its wake, with one rescue worker describing the scene near the border as “nothing but ruins.”

Rescue teams are now working in extremely difficult terrain near Gyirong Port, where roads have been destroyed and dense forests and steep cliffs have hampered access.

China’s state broadcaster CCTV reported that firefighters from Tibet and Sichuan reached the area on Friday, including six Tibet fire and rescue personnel, 15 members of a Sichuan rescue team and a rescue dog.

World.title: Belize and regional partners strengthen Agricultural Disease surveillance
World.content:
Belize and regional partners strengthen Agricultural Disease surveillance

By Zoila Palma: Belize and other member countries of the International Regional Organization for Agricultural Health (OIRSA) have agreed to strengthen regional surveillance and coordination to protect agricultural production and trade from emerging diseases and pests. The agreement was reached during the 97th Extraordinary Meeting of the International Regional Committee for Agricultural Health (CIRSA) held today in Guatemala City.

The meeting brought together Ministers of Agriculture and other senior representatives from Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama and the Dominican Republic.

Belize was represented by Luis Alex Balona, Minister of State in the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries. The meeting was chaired by Guatemala’s Minister of Agriculture, Livestock and Food, María Fernanda Rivera.

Among the major agricultural health threats discussed were African Swine Fever, Fusarium Wilt Tropical Race 4 and Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza. Regional authorities noted that these diseases can cross borders and cause significant impacts on agricultural production and international trade. To address the risks, countries agreed to maintain constant surveillance and strengthen standardized prevention and response protocols, particularly at borders, ports and airports.

The meeting also examined the growing impact of extreme weather events on agricultural health. Changes in rainfall patterns and rising temperatures can create favourable conditions for the emergence and spread of pests and diseases, making regional cooperation increasingly important. Authorities emphasized that coordinated action is essential to protect farmers and the communities that depend on healthy and resilient agricultural systems.

CIRSA members also reviewed efforts to strengthen OIRSA as a regional institution, including progress toward approving its 2026–2036 Strategic Plan, a new Investment Policy and updated organizational regulations. These measures are intended to improve the capacity of member countries to detect, prevent and respond to agricultural health threats while protecting food production and regional trade.

World.title: Belize hosts regional Fruit Fly meeting as 50-year Medfly Control programme reaches milestone
World.content:
Belize hosts regional Fruit Fly meeting as 50-year Medfly Control programme reaches milestone

By Zoila Palma: Belize hosted the XII Meeting of the Fruit Fly Commission on August 27, 2026, in Placencia, bringing together senior representatives from the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), Mexico’s SENASICA, Guatemala’s MAGA, the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries (MAFSNGI), and the Belize Agricultural Health Authority (BAHA).

The annual meeting serves as a key platform for regional coordination under the Trinational Agreement between the United States, Mexico and Guatemala to prevent and control the spread of the Mediterranean fruit fly (Medfly) into North America.

Commissioners reviewed achievements, assessed emerging risks and priorities, and agreed on the joint work programme and budget for 2027, with the continued protection of the Medfly-free areas of Belize and Petén, Guatemala remaining a priority.

This year’s meeting also marked the 50th anniversary of the regional Medfly programme and Belize’s national programme, which began in 1976 with support from the USDA.

Over the past five decades, BAHA’s plant health teams have maintained Belize’s Medfly-free status through ongoing surveillance and rapid response efforts, helping protect agricultural production and preserve access to international markets for commodities that are hosts of the pest.

The milestone also provided an opportunity to recognize BAHA officers whose technical expertise and dedicated fieldwork have contributed to the programme’s success, with staff receiving awards for their service.

The meeting concluded with Chief Executive Officer Servulo Baeza signing the 2027 Cooperative Agreement between Belize and the United States, securing continued technical and financial support for the country’s Medfly prevention and control efforts.

World.title: Ministry of Agriculture and FAO train officers to protect Coconut Industry from pests and disease
World.content:
Ministry of Agriculture and FAO train officers to protect Coconut Industry from pests and disease

By Zoila Palma: The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), in partnership with the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries (MAFSNGI), has concluded a five-day Training of Trainers Workshop focused on coconut pest and disease management.

The training, held in Belmopan, forms part of FAO’s technical cooperation programme supporting the revision of Belize’s National Rural Development Strategy, with a specific focus on the coconut sector.

The initiative also supports the global “One Country One Priority Product” (OCOP) initiative, which promotes green enterprise and sustainable development within Belize’s growing coconut industry.

Participants included members of the Ministry’s fruit tree programme team, district extension officers and officers from the Caribbean Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI) involved in coconut production.

During the first four days, participants received technical training on integrated pest management strategies for major threats to coconut production, including the coconut weevil, red mites and red ring disease. The sessions covered pest and disease identification, host recognition and modern management techniques to strengthen the ability of agricultural officers to diagnose problems quickly and provide farmers with appropriate guidance.

The workshop concluded with practical field and laboratory exercises, where participants identified mite infestations and signs of fungal diseases in coconut plantations and learned laboratory techniques for confirming red ring disease in infected plant tissue.

The trained officers will next take these practices to farmers across the country, with district-level training sessions scheduled for September and October 2026 as Belize works to protect smallholder livelihoods, strengthen sustainable farming and build climate resilience in the coconut sector.

World.title: New Corozal Wellness & Community Health Resource Center inaugurated
World.content:
New Corozal Wellness & Community Health Resource Center inaugurated

By Zoila Palma: A new hub dedicated to strengthening community health services was officially launched in Corozal, bringing together the Government of Belize, UNICEF Belize, the Ministry of Health and Wellness, HECOPAB and the Government of the Republic of Korea.

The Corozal Wellness & Community Health Resource Center is expected to serve as a central space for health knowledge, training and community engagement.

The center will provide community health workers, volunteers, youth leaders and health professionals with access to resources and opportunities to build their skills. The initiative aims to strengthen community-based health services and help ensure that essential information and support reach families and communities that need them most.

During the launch, UNICEF Belize Representative Sajid Ali highlighted the critical role communities play in building a stronger health system. The initiative recognizes that health workers, volunteers and community leaders all have an important part to play in ensuring that health services effectively reach people, particularly those who may otherwise face barriers to accessing care and information.

UNICEF Belize expressed appreciation to the Government of the Republic of Korea and all partners who contributed to the initiative, emphasizing the importance of making reliable health information accessible to everyone.

The new resource center is expected to support continued collaboration and capacity-building as Belize works to strengthen community-based healthcare.

World.title: Ministry of Health and PAHO host National Epidemic Intelligence Planning Workshop
World.content:
Ministry of Health and PAHO host National Epidemic Intelligence Planning Workshop

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Health & Wellness, in collaboration with PAHO/WHO, conducted a National Epidemic Intelligence Planning Workshop to strengthen early warning and response to public health threats.

The Ministry noted that multisectoral partners, including the Department of Environment, Immigration, Civil Aviation, the Forestry Department, and the Belize Agricultural Health Authority, joined the Ministry of Health & Wellness to review national capacities, identify gaps, and prioritize actions for a National Epidemic Intelligence Plan.

“Strengthening Belize’s epidemic intelligence capacity helps detect threats to human health early, including infectious diseases, chemical hazards, and environmental hazards. Early detection enables timely prevention and response, helping to reduce the impact of these threats on Belize’s population,” the Ministry explained.

The Ministry says that together, they are strengthening coordination, information sharing, and timely action to protect the health of all Belizeans.

World.title: PM says he has no power to keep Cooper’s Pen residents on land
World.content:
Prime Minister Andrew Holness speaking to residents in Cooper's Pen, Trelawny on Friday, August 28, 2026. (Photo: Horace Hines)

TRELAWNY, Jamaica – Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness told residents of Cooper’s Pen in Trelawny, whose houses were demolished earlier this month, that he has no power to keep them on the land.

He made the revelation to the residents during a tour of the community Friday, accompanied by Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett and Member of Parliament for Trelawny Northern, Tova Hamilton.

Before beginning the tour of the demolished area, the prime minister spoke with residents and told them he would meet with them again after the tour.

He said he would announce possible solutions following the tour.

On August 11, some 20 houses were demolished in the community, leaving roughly 20 families homeless and affecting approximately 40 families overall.

Since the demolition, residents have staged two separate demonstrations calling for the prime minister’s intervention and assistance.

– Horace Hines

World.title: Courage under fire
World.content:
Firefighters battle the inferno at Super Parts Limited on Hagley Park Road on Thursday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Employees of Superior Parts Limited and a taxi driver battled to save millions of dollars worth of motorcycles and cars on Thursday as a raging fire tore through the company on Hagley Park Road in St Andrew, while firefighters were hampered by a lack of water amid the severe drought that has triggered water restrictions in sections of the island.

Although firefighters from seven stations in Kingston and St Catherine responded, the majority of the stock was destroyed in the midday inferno that sent thick black smoke into the air and created traffic snarls on Hagley Park Road and adjoining thoroughfares.

In the midst of the chaos and destruction, 71-year-old Leroy Terlon used a forklift to remove numerous wooden boxes from the premises and placed them on the road.

“I had to put out the energy and the effort to get certain things saved. I have been here for 20 years and I helped to build the company to where it is now, with labour and loyalty. This event shouldn’t have happened,” Terlon told the Jamaica Observer as he sipped a cold beer at a nearby gas station following his heroics.

He said he was cooling off after his exposure to the intense heat.

“This hurts me. This company is like mine. If I talk about it, tears will come to my eyes. I have been there for so long. It hurts me. I don’t have liquid cash in the business, but I have years of service,” he added as he received congratulatory messages from friends for his bravery.

Other employees also rushed to move stock from the building, while taxi operator Kemal Dunn used his car to tow motor vehicles from a car mart adjoining the burning property.

“I just saw it and said I had to help. I knew it would spread because Superior has a lot of boxes,” he told the Observer.

“I was just driving past. My uncle owns a car dealership up the road. This car dealership just started. For a trying man, I decided to just assist him as best as I could,” Dunn explained.

“Only one car got damaged out of more than 30 that were there. I helped them rescue a good 20 of them. I used my car to pull out some. We used a wire to jump-start others because they were parked for a good while and they had no power to start. I am glad I helped them to minimise the loss.

“I was just watching the electric wire. The fire, you just have to know how to stay a good distance because you are going to feel the heat. The wires were sparking and gashing.”

“I love to help a person and he can pass it on to a next person. I am not going to take my phone and video when I can help,” he added, taking an apparent jab at the many onlookers who stood recording the fire with their cellphones.

Dunn said he banged on the windows of neighbouring houses to ensure that no humans were inside.

“All of these things are material things that can be replaced. A lot of people won’t have a job tomorrow, but they still have life,” Dunn reasoned.

As the fire raged, people in a number of adjoining residential and commercial premises moved out as many supplies and furniture before the flames spread.

One Superior Parts employee, who wished to remain anonymous, speculated that welding sparked the blaze.

“There was welding going on around the back. The fire started around that side. Nobody is allowed to smoke on property, so we believe it started with the welding. We don’t see any other way the fire could have started,” the worker said.

Amid the devastation wrought by the fire, police were kept on their toes by onlookers who wanted to get close-up shots to post on social media. Cops were heard repeatedly telling them to remove from the area for their safety.

Other onlookers were heard venting that the motorbikes were being destroyed and the police did not allow them to go in and grab one for themselves.

Throughout the ordeal, power lines caught fire, sending sparks flying and forcing people to take cover. At the same time, numerous loud explosions were heard coming from the premises.

Three firefighters were reportedly injured during their attempt to put the blaze out.

The Observer was told that the Jamaica Fire Brigade had received a call alerting it to the fire at 12:08 pm. Units from Trench Town initially responded, but according to a firefighter who requested anonymity because he was not authorised to speak to the media, the magnitude of the fire was so great that units had to be requested from other stations.

“There were units from York Park, Half-Way-Tree, Rollington Town, Port Royal, Stony Hill, Portmore, and Spanish Town,” the firefighter said, while pointing to the difficulty they experienced accessing water at the scene.

“The water challenges were expected because of the drought conditions. A lot of the hydrants have no water or low water pressure and it was a massive fire,” he added.

Up to 6:00 pm, the fire had not been fully extinguished.

World.title: Sandals Foundation head Heidi Clarke honoured with 2026 Skift IDEA Trailblazer Award
World.content:
CLARKE... I believe the success of any business should also be measured by the opportunities it creates for others to rise, empowering generations and strengthening communities

IN recognition of her far-reaching impact, Sandals Foundation Executive Director Heidi Clarke has been selected to receive the prestigious ‘Trailblazer Award: Women Shaping the Future of Travel,’ as part of the 2026 Skift IDEA Awards.

The Skift IDEA Awards are the travel industry’s way of recognising excellence in design, creativity, and innovation with winners being a beacon of where the industry is heading.

Presented in partnership with Women Leading Travel, the Trailblazer Award honours a woman whose career demonstrates exceptional leadership, resilience, and influence in shaping the future of travel.

Clarke, who heads the philanthropic arm of Sandals and Beaches resorts, has harnessed the power of tourism to strengthen communities and expand opportunity across the Caribbean.

Since the launch of the not-for-profit Sandals Foundation in 2009, Clarke has led initiatives that improve lives across the Caribbean, with a focus on education, community development, and environmental conservation in the nine islands where Sandals and Beaches resorts operate.

Under her care, the foundation has touched more than 1.8 million lives, supporting more than 2,600 schools, close to 200 large-scale conservation initiatives, and mobilising more than 32,500 volunteers across the region, among other extraordinary projects.

“It is truly an honour to be recognised, and I am immensely proud of what our team, together with our incredible partners, has made possible,” said Clarke.

“I believe the success of any business should also be measured by the opportunities it creates for others to rise, empowering generations and strengthening communities. Tourism has an extraordinary footprint, and when we harness that reach with purpose it can be a tremendous force for positive change across our Caribbean region,” added Clarke.

Her work has championed tourism as a force for positive, lasting change, bringing together communities, governments, non-profit organisations, businesses and travellers to address local needs and strengthen the destinations that sustain the industry.

Born and raised in Jamaica, she has spent nearly two decades developing programs that strengthen communities, expand economic opportunity and advance environmental stewardship throughout the Caribbean.

“Heidi is a true champion for the Caribbean and has dedicated her career to creating opportunities for its people and building a stronger future for the region,” said Adam Stewart, executive chairman of Sandals and Beaches Resorts and president of Sandals Foundation. “She leads with tremendous heart and purpose, and with an unwavering belief in the potential of our Caribbean communities. Her work through the Sandals Foundation is at the heart of who we are at Sandals Resorts and Beaches Resorts, and reflects our deep and enduring commitment to the region we call home. This recognition is incredibly well-deserved, and we could not be prouder of Heidi and the contributions she continues to make,” added Stewart.

The Skift IDEA Awards are now in their eighth year. The 2026 winners were evaluated through an initial review by the Skift Editorial Team, followed by an independent judging panel of travel and business leaders representing top hospitality organisations.

World.title: Dancehall gets recognition from the JUNO Awards
World.content:
2025 JUNO nominee Skystar.

AHEAD of the 2027 staging of the JUNO Awards, Canada’s equivalent to the Grammys, the Canadian Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences (CARAS) has introduced a series of category and eligibility updates.

These updates, according to CARAS in a press release shared with the Jamaica Observer, are designed to better reflect Canada’s music community and to provide clear, meaningful pathways for artistes to have their work recognised.

The category Reggae Recording of the Year has been renamed Reggae/Dancehall Recording of the Year. The reggae category was first instituted in 1985 as Best Reggae/Calypso Recording. For the 1994 staging, the category was renamed Best Reggae Recording, with the name Reggae Recording of the Year coming into effect in 2003.

Canada-based dancehall artiste Phenique is pleased with the evolution of the JUNO Awards.

“I’m excited to see the JUNO Awards continuing to evolve and recognise the diversity within today’s music. I think these changes create more opportunities for artists across different genres to have their work recogniSed and celebrated. It’s definitely a positive step forward,” Phenique told the Jamaica Observer on Tuesday.

Recording artiste, broadcaster and curator of the weekly Reggae North Canadian Reggae/Dancehall Top 20 chart, Tony Anthony, believes that the inclusion of dancehall is long overdue.

“The inclusion of Dancehall in the JUNO Awards’ Reggae/Dancehall Recording of the Year category is a significant and long-overdue step forward for our community. Industry professionals and supporters within the reggae and Dancehall community have advocated for Dancehall to be properly recognised on one of Canada’s biggest music stages. This announcement is not just a change in the name of a category—it is an acknowledgment of the cultural impact, creativity and contribution that Dancehall has made to Canadian music and to the broader music industry. This is an important milestone, but also a reminder that our community must continue to advocate for both genres and ensure that its artists receive the respect, visibility and opportunities that come with being recognized as a vital part of Canada’s music industry,” Tony Anthony disclosed.

2025 JUNO nominee dancehall artiste Skystar, who is originally from the Kingston 20 area, sees the revamping of the reggae category to include dancehall as a step forward.

“I’m excited to see the JUNOS expanding the conversation to officially recognise dancehall. Reggae is deeply rooted in Jamaican culture, but Dancehall has grown into a powerful global movement that continues to influence music, fashion, language and youth culture around the world,” he noted. “For artists like myself who represent the next generation of Jamaican music here in Canada, this recognition matters. It tells us that the sound, culture and evolution of our music are being seen and valued. I believe this is a great step forward, and I hope we continue creating space for the many different sounds and generations that make Reggae and Dancehall so powerful. Respect to the JUNOS for recognising the culture.”

However, Carrie Mullings, former chair of the Reggae Committee for the JUNO Awards, says dancehall music was always submitted for consideration.

“During my time with the JUNO’s (17 years, 12 as a chair) the category already consisted of dancehall submissions when you read the category description. As much as it is nice for the word Dancehall to be included in the category title it was never excluded. I feel these small steps are good but the bigger conversation in my opinion is the fact that an album body of work and a single can be submitted in the same category. We should be addressing the reason the category has not been split into 2, 1 for Reggae/Dancehall Recording of The Year (for single submissions) and 1 for Reggae/Dancehall Album/EP of the Year. As our music grows, collectively we should express our needs for expansion and recognition. Reggae/dancehall has walked the JUNO Red Carpet since 1985, please acknowledge our culture’s growth and award it accordingly,” said Mullings.

Other category changes for the 2027 JUNO Awards include:

Rap: Melodic Rap Recording of the Year and Rap Recording of the Year will replace Rap Album/EP of the Year and Rap Single of the Year.

Electronic/Dance: Electronic/Dance Single of the Year and Electronic/Dance Album/EP of the Year will replace Electronic Album of the Year and Dance Recording of the Year.

Contemporary Christian/Gospel: Contemporary Christian/Gospel Recording of the Year will replace Contemporary Christian/Gospel Album of the Year, with singles, EPs and albums now eligible.
