The submission for awards and songs for consideration for the 2027 staging of the JUNO Awards will open on September 21 with November 5 being the final submission date.

The 56th annual JUNO Awards will be broadcast live from Canada Life Centre in Winnipeg, Manitoba, on Sunday, April 4, 2027. JUNO Week runs from April 1 to 4, 2027.

World.title: Nation’s Choice makes $1-billion hotel bet
World.content:
Nation’s Choice chief executive Donald McDonald shows pallets of frozen products inside the company’s Clarendon cold-storage facility, part of a roughly $1-billion investment aimed at expanding capacity for the hospitality sector.

Nations Choice has invested about $1 billion in new cold storage capacity as the Jamaican food company positions itself for increased demand from the hotel sector while preparing to export locally manufactured products across the Caribbean.

Guyana is expected to be the first export market early next year, Chief Executive Officer Donald McDonald said, with Barbados, St Lucia and the Cayman Islands also among the countries being targeted.

The Clarendon-based company imports and distributes frozen and chilled seafood, meats, poultry and vegetables, but has been steadily increasing manufacturing as it builds the Nations Choice name into a consumer brand.

“We are preparing ourselves now to start exporting from Jamaica some of the products that we manufacture,” McDonald told the Jamaica Observer in an interview on Wednesday. “We have gone into some markets, done some market surveys, and there is a lot of interest in some of the products that we do manufacture.”

The planned exports would include burgers, bacon, ham and pickled products made in Jamaica. Nations Choice already moves some branded products into other Caribbean countries but McDonald said those goods are produced or packaged outside Jamaica. That activity accounts for only about one to two per cent of the company’s business.

Nations Choice has invested an estimated $4 billion since starting in 2011 with two containers and five products, McDonald said. The company now employs more than 300 people and handles about 200 stock-keeping units.

The larger cold storage facility represents an investment of about $1 billion and can hold about four million kilogrammes of product. A separate picking room, which is not included in that investment, has capacity for about 1,500 pallets. The operation runs around the clock.

McDonald said the investment was made with Jamaica’s expanding hotel pipeline in mind. Hospitality already accounts for about 20 per cent of Nations Choice’s business, with the remaining 80 per cent coming from the wider local market, including institutions and consumers.

He expects between 8,000 and 9,000 hotel rooms to come on stream over the next two years, which he believes will create additional demand for food suppliers.

Government filings reported in July identified 13 hotel projects facilitated by Jamaica Promotions Corporation (Jampro), that are expected to add 8,943 rooms, although the developments have varying completion timelines and some have been delayed.

“I think that presents a great opportunity for growth in servicing that sector,” McDonald said. “That is why we’re interested in building this new cold storage, positioning ourselves to be able to service the hospitality sector.”

The bet on hotels comes while that part of Nations Choice’s business is still recovering from Hurricane Melissa. McDonald estimated that the company’s hospitality business was down about 30 per cent in November and December as a number of properties closed, particularly in western Jamaica.

The impact was partly offset in the months that followed as hotels that remained open operated at high occupancy because fewer rooms were available. Nations Choice also supplied protein and frozen vegetables to Central Kitchen during its hot meal operations following the hurricane.

McDonald said the company has not yet fully re-established its hotel business because some properties remain closed while others are only now reopening.

Nations Choice is also putting more weight behind products it makes itself. Manufacturing began in 2017 with pig tail and mackerel and has since expanded to burgers, ham, bacon and other processed foods.

McDonald said the company now produces about 29,000 burger patties each week, while locally manufactured products account for roughly 15 per cent of what it distributes.

Over the past three years Nations Choice has also increased the number of products sold under its own brand in supermarkets, moving beyond its traditional business-to-business model supplying hotels, restaurants, wholesalers and institutions such as schools, hospitals and prisons.

Its locally manufactured range includes curried goat and jerk pork burgers, with chicken bacon due to be added in early September.

“We are launching a chicken bacon,” McDonald said.

Those locally made products are also being lined up for the regional push. Nations Choice already supplies Guyana with goods sourced from other jurisdictions, McDonald said, but is now preparing to supply the market with products manufactured in Jamaica.

“I would say we have broken in already because we are already moving products there from other jurisdictions,” he said. “It is just a matter of moving products now from Jamaica there, which is what we are preparing ourselves to start doing.”

World.title: MORE WITH LESS
World.content:
WELLINGTON... it is even more important that the fans come out and support the competition (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

DESPITE ISSA working with one of its smallest sponsorship budgets for schoolboy football in recent times, President Keith Wellington believes this season could be one of the best yet, thanks to a revamped structure across the various competitions.

The launch of the prestigious under-19 high school football season was held on Wednesday, with the daCosta Cup set to begin next Saturday while the Manning Cup kicks off four days later.

However ISSA will execute the competitions with less sponsorship dollars this year, which Wellington says is down to a little over $40 million.

Long-time sponsor Wisynco, which supported the competition for more than a decade through its various brands, has not returned this year after investing $37.3 million in last year’s season. Bert’s Auto Parts has also not returned after coming on board in 2025.

KFC; Kirk Distributors through its brands Kendel and Cetamol; and Charles Chocolate, through its brand Ping Pong, have remained on board while Happy Ice has joined as a new sponsor, just weeks after former Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) Operations Manager Omar McFarlane was named CEO.

While grateful for the current partnerships Wellington says fan support will be crucial this season to help offset the sponsorship shortfall.

“It has and will have a significant impact on schoolboy football in terms of what we are hoping to do. That is why it is even more important that the fans come out and support the competition,” he said. “This is their thing; it’s the fans’ thing. They want to see schoolboy football each year, they want to see their schools participate, and their support in coming and paying $500 at the gate, those little contributions will help to support their schools.”

“We provide all the schools with playing gear, we provide the referee fees for everybody, and obviously we have to find venues when it comes to the latter stages of the competition so we need the support of the general public.”

This season will be one of the most unique in the near-120-year history of schoolboy football. The top 15 teams from both the Manning Cup and DaCosta Cup have earned byes into the second round, with nine teams from the Manning Cup first round and 21 from the daCosta Cup first round advancing to join them.

Wellington says this could lead to a more competitive season compared to previous years.

“We are hoping that the first round — where the teams we believe are more equally matched — will be a lot more competitive and the best teams will advance. And they advance having played [5, 6, 7 games already] to compete against the more established programmes who may have played a lot more practice matches.”

The formats of the knockout competitions, the urban area Walker Cup, and the rural area Ben Francis Cup have also changed, with the top 32 teams now competing. For the past seven years the semi-finalists of the Manning and daCosta Cup were unable to compete.

The all-island knockout tournament, the Champions Cup, will have its format decided during the season.

“We are happy that most persons are comfortable with the changes and are happy to see the changes. What we need to do now is to ensure that we execute properly and that we get the support, not just from the teams involved but from the supporting cast — the students, the general public, and corporate Jamaica, to ensure that we have a successful season,” said Wellington.

Excelsior High will look to defend their Manning Cup title while St Elizabeth Technical (STETHS) will look to retain their daCosta Cup title. Clarendon College are the only team from either competition to have successfully defended their title since 2018.

Manning Cup seeded teams: Excelsior, Jamaica College, St Catherine, Wolmer’s Boys’, Campion College, Charlie Smith, Calabar, St Jago, STATHS, Kingston College, Tivoli Gardens, St George’s College, Eltham, Mona, Vauxhall.

daCosta Cup seeded teams: STETHS, Glenmuir, Clarendon College, Dinthill Technical, Cornwall College, Kemps Hill, Maggotty High, Old Harbour, Garvey Maceo, McGrath, Ocho Rios, Christiana, Manchester, Manning’s, William Knibb

World.title: BYD welcomes ATTO 8
World.content:
The 2027 BYD ATTO 8 was launched over two days — Saturday, August 22 at Kingston Polo Club and Sunday, August 23, with a test drive day at the Police Officers’ Club, St Andrew.

BYD JAMAICA, the arm of ATL Automotive Group responsible for the BYD line of new energy vehicles, rolled out the red carpet for the latest addition to its model line-up, the ATTO 8, with two days of activities this month.

“It’s a dream come true to have the ATTO 8 on Jamaican shores,” Sloane Jackson, head of business, BYD Jamaica, told the Jamaica Observer’s weekly Auto magazine.

The vehicle was launched on Saturday, August 22, at Kingston Polo Club with the opportunity to test-drive it the following day, Sunday, August 23, at Police Officers’ Club, St Andrew.

Jackson explained that the ATTO 8 was not a given, and that it was a process to bring it to market from China, having seen it last April at Auto Shanghai 2025. He and his team were privy to a special and private unveiling of the vehicle.

“One of the things they showed us that wasn’t unveiled at the show, but unveiled to us as the BYD team, was the new Tang. What they told us was that it would be called the Sealion 8 in some markets, and the ATTO 8 in our region, available as a full EV and as a hybrid. We were initially told that we might get it,” Jackson said.

After the revelation that it would be available in right-hand drive, as it was going to be sold in the Australian and South African markets, Jackson felt it would be a great fit for the Caribbean region and his Jamaica portfolio.

The ATTO 8 is a mid-sized SUV, using BYD’s hybrid technology. Currently, it is only available in one trim level, DM-p, which makes it an all-wheel-drive plug-in hybrid vehicle. The drivetrain is similar to the BYD Shark pickup. Under the bonnet of the ATTO 8 is a 1.5-litre turbocharged four-cylinder engine. The petrol engine is paired with two electric motors — front and rear — for a total power output of 536bhp. The 35.6kWh battery is rated to deliver 152km of pure electric range, with a combined range up to 1,400km. It can be charged externally at 11kWh for AC, and DC fast-charged at 72kWh using the CCS2 port. The ATTO 8 can also do Vehicle-to-Load to run attached electrical devices.

On the performance front, 100kph can be reached in under five seconds, with a top speed of 200kph.

Beyond its speed and range as a seven-seat SUV, the ATTO 8 is packed with the technology expected from BYD. There’s wireless charging and USB ports throughout a spacious cabin that features integrated multi-colour ambient lighting, premium materials, double-layer glass for the front doors, and a 21-speaker sound system.

For family use, there is a maximum 1,960-litres of cargo capacity, powered seating — including the ability to control the front passenger from the second row, and even amenities such as a massage function for the second row. There are driver aids for safety and convenience, while the BYD infotainment offers up its usual wide range of interactivity.

Jackson said that the sales numbers of the ATTO 8, to date, have justified its addition to the showroom floor, as it comes at a time when rising fuel prices are driving the automotive consumer’s buying habits, gaining BYD’s line-up of electric vehicles and hybrids even more attention. This was a sentiment mirrored by Mark Dommisse, managing director, ATL Automotive Group.

“We are exceptionally lucky to host this brand in our portfolio. I would say that BYD is the heavyweight champion of the Chinese brands around the world, and that has definitely shown today. When we took on the brand two years ago, I think there was a lot of curiosity from the general public and a lot of questions. Every time the name BYD was asked, it was always with a question mark; nowadays it’s a mainstay brand that everybody knows. It’s trendy, it’s sexy, and they’re bringing out new products left, right, and centre. We’re certainly very happy with the sales volume. We’re very happy with the return on investment, and we’re honoured to hold the brand,” he said.

Beyond the launch, guests were given free rein to examine the ATTO 8’s features to the fullest, while being treated to food, drink, and activities, including creating a signature car fragrance.

The 2027 ATTO 8 DM-p is now available from BYD Jamaica at $15 million, with the EV model expected to arrive next year.

“All that is available to us in right-hand drive is the hybrid. The EV model should be coming in the middle of 2028, which will have the most powerful single electric motor ever built, with the option of 1,000 bhp,” said Jackson.

World.title: Fire engulfs Superior Parts dealership on Hagley Park Road
World.content:
A fire has engulfed the Superior Parts dealership on Hagley Park Road in St Andrew. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Firefighters are now battling a blaze that has engulfed the Superior Parts dealership on Hagley Park Road in St Andrew.

The cause of the fire is not yet known but the incident happened around midday. At least two units from the Jamaica Fire Brigade are on location.

There have been no confirmed reports of casualties.

More to come.

World.title: Ousted Ukrainian defense chief Fedorov takes advisory role with Italy
World.content:
Fedorov, who called for wartime elections after being pushed out of government in President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s latest reshuffle, also stressed that he is not decamping to Rome. “My main focus remains unchanged,” he wrote, adding he will continue working in Ukraine on projects to strengthen the country’s defense and attract international resources.

Crosetto first offered the position in July, saying he called Fedorov the day after his dismissal and asked: “When would you like to come to Rome to work with me as an adviser?” He praised Fedorov as an innovator who had “completely changed the rules of the game on the battlefield.”

The former minister was dismissed in mid-July after roughly six months at the helm of Ukraine's defense department amid tensions with the country’s military leadership and policy disputes. His removal triggered rare wartime protests.

He has since sharpened his criticism of President Zelenskyy, calling for elections earlier this month despite Russia’s ongoing invasion and warning that Ukrainians “cannot endlessly live” without understanding how major decisions are made.

Zelenskyy has rejected the idea, warning that wartime elections could “destroy” the country.

World.title: Climate and AI to loom large in von der Leyen’s State of the Union
World.content:
During Friday's discussion with the cabinet chiefs, Seibert linked the expected focus on climate to the damage caused by floods and wildfires over the summer, according to the two officials, who were briefed on the gathering. They were granted anonymity to discuss the closed-door talks.

The climate focus comes as von der Leyen’s Commission tries to defend its 2040 emissions-cutting target while responding to mounting pressure from industry and national capitals to limit the economic cost of the green transition.

The discussion also touched on how to present AI’s impact on jobs. Von der Leyen’s team has asked the Commission’s relevant policy units, in particular DG Connect, to provide fresh statistics for the speech on the number of jobs likely to be lost and created as AI adoption spreads, according to one of the officials.

Seibert also raised migration as a likely topic in the address, referring to the crisis in the Spanish autonomous city of Ceuta, according to one of the officials. The Commission is expected to revamp the mandate and operations of EU border agency Frontex, a third official said.

The Commission president's speech is expected to include references to social policy around the 10th anniversary of the European Pillar of Social Rights next year, alongside Ukraine and enlargement, according to one of the officials. But the topics have yet to be finalized.

The meeting was the second major opportunity for commissioners to get their priorities name-checked, with their cabinets having already submitted two- to three-page pitches to Seibert. The Commission's policy units, known as the directorates-general, also submitted documents outlining the topics they want von der Leyen to cover.

World.title: What it’s like to live through Kyiv’s constant air raids
World.content:
Kyiv has survived more than 20 air raid alerts since Thursday night. Some were an hour long, while others lasted for up to 10 minutes.

Indeed, every alert, as Russia continues its persistent destruction of millions of books, food warehouses and liquor factories, also means everything has to stop until we hear the words: “Air raid alert is over.” Dozens of trains are delayed, and businesses shut down and wait, losing customers and money.

But “survivors must still go to work,” as we like to joke bitterly. People are still expected to commute, even though Kyiv’s subway has stopped running between the left and right banks of the River Dnipro. Sleep-deprived civilians need to walk for hours, squeeze themselves into buses, or get stuck in traffic on bridges, just to get to work and back home. Transport chaos overground means even more danger for people stuck in large groups all around the city.

But our wartime economy, on which we need to rely more and more due to the slowing of foreign aid, cannot afford to stop.

“The country’s defense spending is constantly growing, and this requires maximum mobilization of domestic resources,” said Hlib Vyshlinsky, the executive director of the Center for Economic Strategy think tank based in Kyiv. “The policy of zero tolerance for the risk to the life and health of civilians under constant missile and drone strikes becomes irrelevant, because the state is still not able to protect them at 100 percent.”

As a Kyivan, I can tell you that this terror sends your mental stability into a spiral.

World.title: Indian PM Modi expected to attend December European Council
World.content:
Narendra Modi shakes hands with António Costa prior to a meeting in New Delhi on December 19, 2019. | Prakash Singh/AFP via Getty Images

Participation would enable signing of EU-India trade deal, which opens up market of 2 billion people.

BRUSSELS — Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is planning to attend the EU summit in December, according to two officials familiar with the discussions.

The visit would come after the EU and India concluded negotiations on a free-trade agreement and signed a security and defense partnership in January.

"We are working on it," said one of the officials when asked to confirm that Modi would join leaders in Brussels on Dec. 17-18 for the European Council’s final scheduled meeting of the year. The visit hasn't been officially confirmed and plans may change.

World.title: France opens door to fighter jet cooperation with Sweden
World.content:
The French comments are the clearest overture made to Stockholm since the high-profile failure of a next-generation fighter jet project between France, Germany and Spain, known as the Future Combat Air System (FCAS). The decade-long program faltered due to disagreements between France's Dassault Aviation and Germany's Airbus Defence and Space, and ultimately collapsed last spring.

The competition between Paris and Berlin to attract Stockholm is one of the most closely watched developments in the aerospace sector. POLITICO previously reported that Germany had already reached out to Sweden.

The Nordic country's defense champion Saab makes its own fourth-generation Gripen fighter — although the warplane's engine uses core technology from American company GE Aerospace. Engines for France's Rafale fighter jets are locally made by Safran.

"Dassault builds its own aircraft, and Saab builds its own: two competitors with fairly similar approaches who respect one another. There was cooperation in the past," the official said, stressing however that "nothing formal has been agreed" on fighter jet cooperation.

Sweden is expected to decide on the next steps for its warplane program by September 2027.

World.title: Belgium makes helmets compulsory on faster e-scooters
World.content:
The Brussels government recently reversed its decision to ban shared e-scooters from its streets as of September 2026. | Nicolas Maeterlinck/BELGA MAG/AFP via Getty Images

The mandate targets models capable of going between 20 and 25 km/h, citing head-injury risks.

Belgium will make helmets mandatory for riders of faster e-scooters from Sept. 1, the federal mobility ministry said Friday.

Under the new ministry announcement, helmets will be compulsory for users of motorized personal transport devices with a maximum design speed that “exceeds 20 kilometres per hour,” regardless of how fast they are actually traveling.

Riders can wear either a moped helmet or a bicycle helmet, provided it protects “the temples and the back of the head.”

World.title: The US got Meta to change Instagram and Facebook. Europe wants in.
World.content:
The settlement on Wednesday details a series of changes that Meta needs to make to Facebook and Instagram over the next 10 years, including limiting daily time for minors on the platform, checking ages of users more rigorously and disabling cosmetic filters for teens.

It has upped the ante for Brussels’ social media regulators.

“Ironically, 9 measures out of 12 are covered by the [Digital Services Act], our law since 2023. U.S. courts are going faster than the EU Commission. We must ENFORCE DSA NOW!” former European Commissioner Thierry Breton, who negotiated and enforced the EU's social media rulebook up to 2024, wrote on X after the news of the settlement.

German center-right lawmaker Andreas Schwab told POLITICO that Meta in the U.S. now "has even to go beyond what it offers to the European consumers.” Schwab, an architect of one of the EU’s Big Tech laws, the Digital Markets Act, called for Meta's policies in the two jurisdictions to be aligned.

The European Commission in July accused Meta of breaching EU rules under the Digital Services Act by running addictive design features on Facebook and Instagram. In April, it accused Meta of breaking the same rules for not doing enough to keep under-13s off its platforms. The EU's investigation into addictive design and minors is more than two years old but has yet to yield concessions from the company or penalties for non-compliance.

Spanish center-left European Parliament lawmaker Laura Ballarín Cereza asked the Commission on Thursday why Meta has committed to making changes only for U.S. users while it is in a discussion with EU authorities over the same issues. How will the Commission “ensure that EU citizens are not left with weaker protections than those in the US,” she wrote.

World.title: Former Iceland prime minister to pro-EU voters: Your referendum doesn’t matter
World.content:
“If I become foreign minister or prime minister later, have I fulfilled this simply by asking the EU, ‘what are you willing to give us?’ And is my job done?” wondered Gunnlaugsson. “They can’t explain how to honor the vote if it’s a ‘Yes,’” he said, referring to the current Social Democrat-led government.

The right-wing politician rose to prominence during the 2008 financial crisis as the spokesperson for a campaign against using Icelandic taxpayer money to bail out the country’s largest bank and repay foreign creditors in the U.K. and the Netherlands. He founded the Centre Party in 2017.

Gunnlaugsson describes his party as “small ‘c’ conservative and centrist” — though some of his opponents disagree.

“People sometimes call us populist, and it always annoys me because I always see myself as anti-populist. I’m always talking about things that are difficult to explain, and I’m always annoyed about how politics is becoming all about just the surface and easy ideas,” said Gunnlaugsson.

In June of this year, however, his Centre Party joined the European Conservatives and Reformists group in the European Parliament, which includes right-wing nationalist parties that often receive the populist label, such as Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy and Poland’s Law and Justice party.

A geopolitical vote

On Aug. 29, Icelanders will answer either “Yes” or “No” to the question: “Should negotiations on Iceland’s membership in the European Union start again?”

World.title: Norway mourns king Harald V as crown prince Haakon becomes king
World.content:
Norway is mourning King Harald V after the monarch died aged 89 at Oslo University Hospital’s Rikshospitalet at 6:35 a.m. local time on Friday, according to the Royal Palace. Hundreds of people gathered outside the palace to lay flowers and wreaths, while church bells rang across the country at noon. The Norwegian Royal Standard was flown at half-mast as officials and members of the public paid tribute to a king who had reigned for more than three decades.

 

Harald became king in January 1991 following the death of his father, King Olav V. His reign spanned a period of strong economic growth, fuelled in large part by Norway’s oil and gas industry. Known for his modern and modest approach to the monarchy, Harald remained a widely respected national figure as the country’s head of state.

Crown Prince Haakon, 53, has succeeded his father as King Haakon VIII. He has adopted the motto “All for Norway” (Alt for Norge), the same words used by his great-grandfather, King Haakon VII.

Norway’s monarchy is largely ceremonial, with political power resting with the country’s elected parliament. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre signed the book of condolences at the Royal Palace, saying the country had been left with “a deep sense of gratitude” for Harald’s long service.

World.title: Europe's royal houses and world leaders mourn the death of Norway's King Harald V
World.content:
European monarchs and world leaders paid tribute to Norway's King Harald on Friday, after the royal palace announced his death at the age of 89.

 

Harald was the continent's oldest reigning monarch. His son Haakon automatically succeeded him to the throne.

Here are some of the main tributes from across the continent and further afield.

Danish and Swedish monarchs

The kings of Denmark and Sweden called Harald an "extraordinary" leader and good friend who unified his country.

"Both as head of state and a successful athlete, he was an outstanding representative of his country. He gave 'All for Norway'," Sweden's King Carl XVI Gustaf said, referring to Harald's royal motto.

Denmark's King Frederik X said the late monarch was "an extraordinary man" who "joined duty and responsibility with presence and compassion."

People gather in Palace Square to mourn Norway's King Harald V following the announcement of his death in Oslo, 28 August, 2026 AP Photo

Dutch royal family

The Dutch royal family recalled "unforgettable" journeys with King Harald around Oslo and the rest of Norway.

"We cherish the memory of our special friendship with him in our hearts. King Harald served his country with love, pride, and conviction," the family said in a statement.

Belgian royals

Harald's "humour, humanity and sincerity made him a truly special man," Belgium's King Philippe and Queen Mathilde said.

"Generations of Norwegians grew up with him. For decades, he was a familiar and reassuring presence, a beacon of stability for his country. He fulfilled his role with unwavering dedication, loyalty and dignity," they said in a statement.

The Norwegian flag flies at half-mast at the Norwegian Embassy in Copenhagen, 28 August, 2026 AP Photo

Spain's royal family

Spain's royal family hailed King Harald as an "example of responsibility, dignity, simplicity, and tireless dedication to the service" of his country.

"With respect and admiration for him, as well as deep sadness, we offer our condolences" on the king's death, they wrote on social media.

Britain's King Charles

Britain's King Charles III hailed a "dear cousin" who he said had served "with unwavering dedication, guiding Norway through times of great change with warmth and humility."

"As Norway mourns the loss of so towering a figure, my whole family join in remembering a much-loved kinsman and friend whose kindness, compassion and deep sense of duty echoed from across the sea and across the decades," the king said in a statement, personally signed Charles R.

French president

Harald "worked tirelessly throughout his reign to strengthen the ties uniting Norway and France," Emmanuel Macron wrote on X, recalling a "warm welcome" on his visit to Oslo in June 2025.

Ukraine's President

"His Majesty embodied dignity, wisdom, and an unwavering commitment to his country," said Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a statement.

"Ukraine will always remember his steadfast support and solidarity with the Ukrainian people during the darkest days of Russia's aggression."

Italy's PM

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, in a post on X, called Harald: "A monarch who served his nation with equanimity, authority and a deep sense of institutional duty, helping to strengthen the ties between Norway and Italy throughout his long reign."

Swiss president

The Swiss president Guy Parmelin wrote in a post on X that Harald "will be remembered for his steadfast leadership and devoted service to his country".

Canada's PM

"Canada mourns with you," said a statement from Mark Carney, offering the condolences of his government.

"I had the privilege of meeting his Majesty last March in Olso and he spoke of the ties between our nations with great warmth and affection."

NATO, EU chiefs

Harald "showed himself to be a dedicated leader," posted Mark Rutte, head of the NATO alliance that includes Norway.

"His own military roots made him a champion of the Norwegian military and a long-time friend of NATO," he wrote online.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that Harald "served his country with warmth, humility and an unwavering sense of duty."

UN chief

A spokesman for UN Secretary General António Guterres said he was "deeply saddened" by the king's death.

"He will be remembered for his engagement for children's welfare and environmental issues, his support for diversity and calls for generosity," the statement added.

Jordan's royal family

Jordan's Royal Hashemite Court said it mourned the passing of King Harald "may his soul rest in peace."

The court "expresses the deepest sympathies of His Majesty and the Jordanian people, as they stand with Norway and its people at this difficult time."

King Abdullah ordered his court to observe three days of mourning, a statement from the court added.

World.title: Number of missing in Nepal floods passes 2,400 as UNICEF says 17,000 children need aid
World.content:
The number of people missing in Nepal and China surpassed 2,400 on Friday, underscoring the scale of the disaster days after a tsunami-like wall of water and debris swept away villages and killed hundreds.

 

Rescuers were battling through mud even as the threat of new floods loomed, with emergency teams recovering 586 bodies so far and some of the dead swept downstream as far away as India.

The new figures came as Nepal's disaster authority added 933 hydropower workers to a missing persons list already including trekkers and pilgrims to Tibet's sacred Mount Kailash.

Relatives have crowded hospitals in Nepal's capital in a painful hunt for their loved ones, with posters on the walls bearing photos and names of the missing.

"Today is the third day and we don't know anything. Hopefully he is in a safe place," Samjhana Thing, 27, told the AFP news agency referring to her brother. "We lost everything. He is our everything."

The US Geological Survey said the disaster, the deadliest for Nepal since a 2015 earthquake, was caused by a glacial collapse that triggered a vast flow of icy debris.

A damaged electric pole leans after flash flooding in the Devighat area of Nuwakot district in Nepal, 28 August, 2026 AP Photo

The deluge of ice and mud also caused huge lakes to form and one of these formations has become a direct threat to emergency workers scouring the region for survivors.

Nepali police urged all rescuers to "immediately move to a safe location", saying it had received information that "a water dam has burst again on the Tibetan side."

In Tibet, China was forced to suspend its rescue operation at the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of renewed flooding on Friday, before saying the threat had eased.

State broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by immense piles of debris began overflowing toward where rescue teams were headed, but later said the water level of the pool had dropped.

Rescue operations were therefore "proceeding in an orderly manner", it added.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, who chaired a meeting on rescue efforts, offered Beijing's help to Nepal's emergency operations.

People walk along a street lined with damaged structures after flash flooding in the Devighat area of Nuwakot district in Nepal, 28 August, 2026 AP Photo

Swept away

Emergency teams had been racing to retrieve survivors from affected zones, where the widespread devastation meant food and water supplies were running out.

The Nepali military located people trapped in the tunnel of Trishuli 3A hydropower project, where they were working to find a way in to extract the survivors.

"Two helicopters have been dispatched but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel," army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP.

Some 350 workers and residents have been brought to safety from the site, he added, but efforts were ongoing to rescue more than 100 people trapped in the same area.

Workers clear debris in the aftermath of a flash flood in the Devighat area of Nuwakot district in Nepal, 28 August, 2026 AP Photo

Workers rescued from other dam projects along the Trishuli valley described a disaster that unfolded with terrifying speed.

Buddha Tamang told AFP he survived only because he was inside a tunnel at the dam where he worked when the flood struck.

"The senior officers working on the other side, they were all swept away," Tamang, who was airlifted on Thursday after being marooned for more than 24 hours, said.

Aid trickles in

Aid began to reach some survivors in Nepal on Friday, as the full scope of the devastation continued to emerge and survivors sought shelter at makeshift army relief centres.

Children who have been separated from their families are being given shelter as attempts are made to reunite them with families.

The UN's agency for children UNICEF said at least 17,000 children are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance, while 18 schools have been destroyed and another 20 damaged.

The International Red Cross estimates that at least 93,000 people have been affected and are in “great need.”

Also on Friday, the European Union promised €2 million in aid for Nepal with European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen writing on X that the "immediate humanitarian aid" would help "deliver life-saving assistance to families and communities hit hardest."

World.title: Ceuta warns it is 'on the brink of collapse' as Spain seeks Frontex and Europol help
World.content:
Spain has asked the European Commission (EC) for the support from Frontex and Europol to assist with the screening of migrants who are staying irregularly in Ceuta, according to several Spanish media outlets.

 

Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska has asked the EC for Frontex, Europol and the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) to "reinforce the device set up to address the management of the triage and subsequent processing of the personal files of the immigrants who still remain in Ceuta irregularly."

The Interior Ministry also demanded the extension of Operation Minerva, a joint initiative of the Spanish police and the EU border protection agency Frontex.

Madrid ask that that operation run until 2 September until "the situation created in the autonomous city is resolved."

Madrid also asked for the " assistance of the European Union Agency for Asylum in conducting interviews and providing interpreters" in order to triage migrants.

Due to space limitations in Ceuta, this process is expected to be carried out electronically.

Migrants who crossed from Morocco into Spain return to a beach after being expelled from the area the previous day, 21 August, 2026 AP Photo

The Interior Ministry announced on Friday that Ceuta's border would be reinforced with a package of "extraordinary" measures such as extending the Tarajal and Benzú breakwaters, a permanent system of maritime containment buoys, aerial surveillance with drones, light intervention vessels and remotely operated underwater devices.

At the same time, Ceuta's Assembly unanimously called on the central government on Friday to act "immediately and without further delay" arguing that the city is in an "extreme situation, on the verge of collapse."

The Board of Spokespersons, together with the non-affiliated MPs, unanimously approved on Friday an institutional declaration calling on the government to adopt urgent measures one month after the mass entry of at least 72,000 migrants from Morocco.

"Ceuta has lost its way of life and its calm. We do not have much time to avert disaster," Ceuta's President Juan Vivas warned.

The declaration calls for a return to their countries, "in accordance with the law" of those who took part in the mass entry and are still in Ceuta. It also backs citizens' right to demonstrate, as long as it is done "peacefully and in an orderly manner," and condemns violent incidents recorded in recent days.

"No one can or should take the law into their own hands. The defence of Ceuta and the interests of its people can only be pursued through legality," Vivas said.

Migrants who crossed from Morocco into Spain are escorted by Spanish police to temporary shelters after being cleared from a beach in Ceuta, 20 August, 2026 AP Photo

Appeal for calm

Meanwhile, Spain's interior minister called for calm on Friday after residents of Ceuta clashed with police during protests against migrants who have remained in the North African enclave following a mass influx.

Tensions have been high in the territory of 80,000 people since at least 72,000 people crossed into Ceuta over several days in July, triggering a Europe-wide migrant alert.

Spain's leftist government says most have since left the enclave of 18.5 square kilometres but thousands remain wandering the streets and sleeping on beaches.

Demonstrations have intensified in recent days, with some protesters clashing with police on Thursday at a beach where migrants have been sleeping. Some of their belongings were burned.

Migrants who crossed from Morocco into Spain are escorted by Spanish police to temporary shelters after being cleared from a beach in Ceuta, 21 August, 2026 Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

A soldier was injured in a separate incident on Thursday when migrants threw stones at troops, while 12 Moroccan migrants were arrested.

Two more arrests were made after migrants attacked a police officer, sources said.

"Violence is not the answer," Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told parliament on Friday.

"I call for calm and an end to any form of violence, because...violence is not the way to resolve any problem with the complexity" of that facing Ceuta, he added.

Right-wing and far-right parties have demanded that all the migrants be rounded up and sent back to their home countries.

Grande-Marlaska accused them of "inciting hatred and confrontation" in Ceuta.

The government has warned that each individual must be identified to determine whether they are entitled to asylum or subject to deportation, while unaccompanied migrant children require special protection.

Ceuta and Melilla, another small Spanish territory in North Africa, form Europe's only land border with Africa.

World.title: Bayeux Tapestry: Macron to open landmark London exhibition next Wednesday
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron will travel to London this Wednesday 2 September to open an exhibition at the British Museum devoted to the Bayeux Tapestry, an 11th-century work depicting William the Conqueror's conquest of England, the Elysée announced on Friday.

 

Macron will also have a "first in-depth exchange" with the new British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, on Thursday, the presidency said.

He is also expected to "have the opportunity to greet King Charles", a presidential adviser added, without giving further details.

The main purpose of the visit is "the opening of the exhibition marking the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum", an event described by a presidential adviser as "a particularly significant moment" for Franco-British relations and personally championed by the current occupant of the Elysée.

The French leader wants to highlight this "exceptional loan" of the piece, which left France for the first time in more than 900 years when it was transported to London under tight security.

On Friday, the British Museum unveiled some sections of the work depicting the 1066 Battle of Hastings and the invasion led by William the Conqueror's Norman army.

The exhibition will be open to the public from 10 September to 11 July 2027; 100,000 tickets have already been sold for the first four months.

The French president, who will be accompanied by his wife, Brigitte Macron, is "very much looking forward" to seeing the tapestry displayed "in optimal conditions".

In London, the 70-metre-long linen embroidery will be shown flat for the first time, rather than hung vertically as it has been in Bayeux for decades.

According to the British Museum, this exhibition layout makes it easier to grasp the full scale of the work.

This historic move from Bayeux in Normandy prompted protests from experts who feared irreversible damage to the tapestry, which had already been weakened by 30 unstabilised tears and nearly 10,000 holes. An online petition circulated at the time of Macron's decision, calling on the relevant French authorities to abandon the loan.

The journey nevertheless took place in optimal conditions, and the French Culture Minister, Catherine Pégard, visiting London in mid-July, said she was delighted to see the thousand-year-old embroidery "in very good condition".

The French leader's visit will be the first by a head of state or government from the European Union since Andy Burnham took office last month, following the resignation of Keir Starmer, with whom Macron had worked closely and forged warm personal ties.

"The president had built a very friendly and extremely effective relationship with Prime Minister Starmer, particularly on the Ukraine and Middle East files," a presidency official said.

Coordination with his successor is expected to be "equally important and regular". "Contact was established immediately" with Burnham, the presidency added, also highlighting his first steps in office, including a swift trip to Kyiv to demonstrate his support for Ukraine.

World.title: Greenland to open truth commission over forced contraception of Inuit women scheme
World.content:
Greenland said on Friday it would establish a Truth and Reconciliation Commission on Denmark's forced contraception of thousands of indigenous Inuits, after experts failed to agree on whether the scheme constituted "genocide."

 

The forced contraception campaign is one of the darkest chapters in Greenland's history with its former colonial master Denmark.

From the 1960s to 1990, more than 4,000 Greenlandic women were forced to wear a contraceptive coil, or intrauterine device (IUD), in the vast majority of cases without their consent or that of their parents if they were minors.

Girls as young as 12 were affected, some of whom were never able to have children afterwards.

"We cannot say, on behalf of the government, whether there was genocide. This is something we can continue to debate," Greenland's Justice Minister Marianne Paviasen told reporters.

Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the priority now was to "begin the healing process."

Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen in Marienborg, 27 April, 2025 AP Photo

"We will set up a reconciliation commission," he vowed, saying he wanted to cooperate with Denmark on the matter.

In Copenhagen, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen also sounded a conciliatory note.

"We will handle the political process together with the government of Greenland. The most important thing for me is that we find the right path together," she said.

A four-member commission was tasked in August 2024 with shedding light on the scheme.

The experts were unable to agree on a unanimous conclusion, presenting two different reports instead.

"One states there was no genocide at all, while the other says there might have been," Paviasen said.

The reports did however agree that the contraception programme may have violated multiple human rights and the rights of Indigenous peoples.

Meeting in the Parliament Hall at Folketing Hall at Christiansborg in Copenhagen, 27 August, 2026 AP Photo

'Not just about history'

One of the victims, Henriette Berthelsen, told the AFP news agency before the reports were presented that the conclusions were skewed from the start since no Greenlandic Inuit was appointed as experts.

"For me, this is not just about history or politics. It's my body, my life and my right to self-determination," she said.

"And once again, I see that it is others who will investigate and define what was done to me and to other Inuit women."

On Thursday, the Danish parliament agreed that women affected by the forced contraception campaign can claim compensation from Copenhagen, an initiative pushed by Frederiksen, who presented Denmark's official apology last year.

Media coverage of the case has revived trauma that had been buried for decades.

A person skis in Nuuk, 6 February, 2026 AP Photo

"I realised everything it had cost me, all those hospitalisations, those surgeries, the schooling I missed and, above all, those pains I had never associated with that damn IUD," said Kirstine Najarak Berthelsen.

"It was buried so deeply in my subconscious...Everything that happened to people is beyond imagination if you haven't experienced it yourself," she added.

By the late 1970s, one in two Greenlandic women of childbearing age, at least 4,070 women, had been fitted with an IUD, according to an investigation presented in September 2025.

The scandal came to light when one of the victims spoke out in the media about the trauma she experienced.

A podcast series in 2022 then revealed the full extent of the campaign.

Henriette Berthelsen has long called for a Truth and Reconciliation Commission to be established.

The 68-year-old psychologist said that would make it possible to "acknowledge what happened."

"I believe that only then will we be able to begin to heal and move forward - not as adversaries, but as human beings and as peoples equal in dignity."

Nuuk and Copenhagen are also shedding light on several other painful chapters from the past, including children adopted without their parents' consent.

World.title: Céline Dion concerts: Canadian star returns to Paris after six years away from the stage
World.content:
Two weeks before Céline Dion's first concert in Paris, "Dionmania" is reaching a new high in the capital. Outside the Royal Monceau palace hotel on Avenue Hoche, a crowd has gathered to welcome the singer.

 

On Friday 28 August, Céline Dion arrived in Paris to begin rehearsals for the first leg of her historic series of concerts. Her schedule is tight, with 16 shows planned between 12 September and 17 October.

In all, the singer has scheduled three concerts a week, on Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays. Each will bring together more than 30 000 spectators in a venue that has been sold out for months. A further ten concerts are also planned for May 2027.

Paris, the stage for a long-awaited comeback

Fans turned out in force to welcome the star. It is worth noting that, apart from a performance at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games, she has not sung in France for almost ten years. Her last series of concerts dates back to 2017.

Yet the love story between Céline Dion and France remains strong. In total, 15 of her 27 studio albums have been recorded in French. It is therefore no surprise that the singer has chosen Paris for her big return to the stage.

Addressing the crowd that had gathered outside her hotel, she told BFM TV: "I have always felt supported from day one and this is a story that continues. It really is my second home, I appreciate you being here, thank you so much."

For six years, Céline put her performances on hold for health reasons. The star has had difficulty singing because of stiff person syndrome, from which she suffers.

World.title: Fans welcome Céline Dion outside her Paris hotel as she prepares to launch a 16‑show arena residency
World.content:
Canadian music superstar Céline Dion has arrived in Paris, around two weeks ahead of the start of her highly anticipated concert residency. A crowd of fans gathered outside the Royal Monceau, where she will stay during her time in the capital. Admirers who saw her described her as “in better shape”, “relaxed” and “as beautiful as ever”, saying they were “very happy” to see her up close.

 

The 58-year-old star waved, blew kisses and briefly stopped to greet the crowd, telling reporters she felt supported and describing Paris as her “second home”. Asked what song she would open the concerts with, Dion kept the choice secret.

The Paris residency marks her return to a major concert run after she cancelled her Courage World Tour following her diagnosis with stiff-person syndrome, a rare neurological disorder she revealed publicly in 2022.

The concerts will be held at the Plenitude Arena in Nanterre, west of Paris, formerly known as Paris La Défense Arena, which can accommodate up to 40,000 spectators. Dion last performed in the French capital in 2024, when she sang “Hymne à l’amour” at the opening ceremony of the Paris Olympics.

The 2026-2027 residency will feature 16 shows in September and October, followed by a further 10 concerts in May 2027.

World.title: US arrests far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos
World.content:
Yiannopoulos, a far-right commentator, was an early supporter of Donald Trump and his immigration crackdown, but they have since fallen out. DHS said he was an "illegal alien" who overstayed his visit in the US.

US authorities have detained right-wing commentator Milo Yiannopoulos and plan to deport him, the Department of Homeland Security said on Friday.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents arrested the British provocateur at New Orleans International Airport on Thursday for overstaying in the US, the department said, describing him as an "illegal alien from the United Kingdom."

"Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an Immigration Judge on July 22, after failing to show up for his immigration hearing," the agency said. "He will remain in ICE custody pending removal. "

ICE directed family and legal representatives to contact the agency’s office in Alexandria, Louisiana, which serves as a deportation hub for international flights.

Far-right activist Laura Loomer, who routinely takes credit for action against those who have fallen out with the US president, posted about the incident shortly after.

"I was the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the US illegally where he incited violence against President Trump and worked for Marjorie Traitor Greene," Loomer wrote on X, referring to the former US congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene who stepped down after a feud with Trump.

Loomer went on to say that she "reported him to ICE and the FBI."

Yiannopoulos previously supported ICE

Once a Donald Trump supporter and advocate of the president's immigration crackdown, Yiannopoulos has since fallen out with the Trump movement.

Yiannopolouos first gained notoriety in the early 2010s as a writer for right-wing website Breitbart News, where he played a key role in the "Gamergate" anti-feminist harassment campaign.

He resigned from Breitbart in 2017 after a video of him appearing to condone pedophilia resurfaced online. He later apologized for the remarks.

Yiannopolouos continued to espouse far-right views, including calling for a stop to immigration and mass deportations.

As recently as June last year, he said California "needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections ​and government buildings, with on the ⁠spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally."

Celebrity news website TMZ suggested that Yiannopoulos may had been in New Orleans ahead of a scheduled performance by Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West. Yiannopoulos has worked for Ye in various capacities, first as part of his aborted 2024 presidential campaign, followed by a brief stint at fashion label Yeezy, and most recently as a personal spokesperson.

World.title: Spain asks EU's Frontex for help in processing Ceuta migrants
World.content:
Of the over 70,000 migrants who illegally crossed into Ceuta from Morocco in late July, some 5,000 still remain in the Spanish exclave. Ceuta residents have been angrily protesting their continued presence.

Spain has asked for help from the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) in processing migrants who crossed into Ceuta last month and still remain in the North African Spanish territory.

Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska sent a request to Beate Gminder, the European Commission's director general for migration and home affairs, to help with screening migrants in Ceuta.

Madrid has also requested 10 more Frontex officers to help with the screening.

Frontex is the European Union agency responsible for managing the bloc's external borders and fighting cross-border crime.

Why is Spain asking for help with the Ceuta migrants?

Over 70,000 migrants crossed from Morocco to Ceuta illegally in late July. The incident triggered a massive EU migration emergency and brought Spain's leftist government much criticism.

Though the majority of people were quickly sent back to Morocco, at least 5,000 migrants still remain in the Spanish territory of roughly 80,000 residents.

Madrid cannot deport the remaining migrants quickly as a collective return without individual assessment is prohibited under international law and Spanish court rulings.

Unaccompanied minors at risk of sexual assault in Ceuta To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rising anger against migrants in Ceuta

Ceuta's residents loudly reject the migrants' continued presence and have made their voice heard via protests which have sometimes turned violent.

Spain has ruled out moving the migrants into the mainland as that would invite further criticism from the opposition as well as some EU members.

Migrants have set up camp on Trampolin Beach, where some tents have been attacked and set on fire amid the residents' rising anger.

On Thursday, protests turned violent with 12 migrants arrested after stoning an army vehicle, injuring one soldier and other migrants. Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that 11 migrants were expelled from the territory, citing sources from the city's main court.

Anti-migrant protests took a violent turn this week Image: Antonio Sempere/AFP

World.title: Austria museum heist: Thieves snatch diamond necklace
World.content:
The stolen necklace, studded with 673 precious stones, belonged to Egypt's Queen Nazli. It was being displayed as part of the museum's exhibition for designs by France's Van Cleef and Arpels.

Two men walked into Vienna's Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) as visitors only to storm out with a priceless 200-carat platinum and diamond necklace worth several million dollars, police said on Friday.

The broad-daylight heist on Thursday, the latest in a series of high-profile thefts to have hit European museums in the past year, triggered a search that grew beyond Austria's borders.

What do we know about the heist?

The two robbers bought tickets to enter the museum.

But once inside, they made their way to the temporary exhibition for French designers Van Cleef and Arpels and "smashed a glass display case" with a hammer before "fleeing with the jewelry in an unknown direction," according to a police statement.

Police added that they did not wear masks and could be clearly seen on surveillance cameras.

A police spokeswoman told the German DPA news agency that one of the robbers was carrying what is believed to be a real firearm.

She said visitors and security staff were in the room when the display case was smashed, adding that it was understandable that the security staff did not stand in the way of the armed perpetrator.

The MAK museum confirmed the theft but did not comment further. On its website, the museum continues to promote its exhibition , which is due to run until September 27.



The stolen necklace, made of platinum and 673 precious stones said to weigh over 200 carats, was designed for Egypt's last royal family Image: Landespolizeidirektion Wien/dpa/picture alliance

What do we know about the stolen necklace?

The stolen necklace belonged to Egypt's now-deposed Queen Nazli and was designed for her in 1939 for her daughter's marriage to the future Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, whose family has also since been removed from power.

It is made of platinum and 673 precious stones said to weigh over 200 carats.

Van Cleef and Arpels describes the necklace on its website as a "triumph of white jewelry."

The case is only the latest in a string of heists to have hit European museums in recent month.

The most high profile was last October's Louvre museum break-in in Paris, which saw thieves snatching in jewellery worth $102 million (roughly €88 million) in under eight minutes. Museum thefts have also been reported in Italy and Spain.

World.title: Germany news: Baltic summit plans hybrid-threat task force
World.content:
08/28/2026 August 28, 2026 Finance Minister Klingbeil calls on Trump to end 'irresponsible' Iran war

Finance Minsiter Klingbeil (right in picture), Chancellor Merz and other leading German politicians are getting back to business after the summer break this week Image: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil is the guest on this Friday's "Interview der Woche" political podcast by public broadcaster ARD.

Much of the interview revolves around domestic policies directly in Klingbeil's ministerial wheelhouse, like the sugar tax, planned income tax reforms, and Germany's difficult economic situation more generally.

But when the discussion turned to fuel prices in Germany, which are nearing their all-time highs from much earlier in the year once again, the Social Democrat (SPD) leader Klingbeil wasted no time in pointing to the external factors in play.

"First of all you have to say that this is the fault of Donald Trump, who started this irresponsible war in Iran," Klingbeil said. "These are the effects, which people are now feeling at the fuel pumps. Therefore the most important thing — and I will be in the US next week for the G20 finance ministers' summit — and the most important message to the US is: Bring this war to an end. That's the first point."

Klingbeil said that the second issue should be to address oil companies "profiteering" as a result of the unrest in Iran and the Gulf, arguing that consumer prices were not a fair reflection of the oil prices or economic fundamentals.

He said he wanted the question of windfall taxes on oil companies to once again be discussed at an EU level.

"The oil companies are making gains on the back of this geopolitical situation," Klingbeil said. "They are filling their pockets and that needs to be stopped, which is why I'm lobbying for the windfall tax and am saying that the proceeds that are raised should be redirected to consumers — which could be achieved by reducing fuel prices."

For a two-month period, Germany dipped its taxes on gasoline and diesel to try to relieve the pressure on prices at the pumps. But this measure expired without renewal in July and prices have since returned close to their highest-ever levels, from earlier in the year. Other smaller factors like the low water levels on the River Rhine impacting freight transport have also played a more minor role in driving up prices in some parts of the country.

World.title: What next? Kurds say yes, Druze still say no to united Syria
World.content:
The Druze minority in Sweida, Syria, is now the only group that hasn't accepted central government authority. How does the end of an independent Kurdish area impact Druze plans for a different, divided kind of Syria?

This week, Syria's Kurdish minority agreed to dissolve what had been their almost 14-year-long experiment in independent rule.

During the Syrian civil war, which began in 2011, the Kurds consolidated their authority over a large part of northeastern Syria, and wanted to maintain that after the civil war ended. But as Kurdish leader Mazloum Abdi said this week, "circumstances have changed."

Kurdish fighting forces, which go by the name of the Syrian Democratic Forces, or SDF, will now be integrated into the general Syrian military, and the oil-rich area they ruled will come under the authority of the central government.

All this means that Sweida province, home to much of Syria's Druze minority, is now the only area not to have accepted the authority of the central government.

The Druze are ethnically Arab and one of Syria's many religious minorities, making up around 3% of the population Image: Fahd Kiwan/AP Photo/picture alliance

End of idea of 'decentralized Syria'

There is no doubt that the change in the situation with Syria's Kurdish community will affect what is happening in Sweida, experts say.

When Omer Ozkizilcik, a nonresident senior fellow at US think tank, the Atlantic Council's Syria Project, met with Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri in early 2025, the Druze leader said he was in daily phone contact with Abdi.

"He said that they were coordinating all their efforts and that they had a similar political vision for Syria — that is, decentralized with autonomous regions," said Ozkizilcik. "He basically repeated the Israeli approach, where they believe Syria should be divided, with an autonomous zone on the coast for the Alawite [minority], for the SDF in the northeast, and then in the south for the Druze. That shows that al-Hijiri's political vision was highly dependent on his alliance with the SDF."

That idea is no longer feasible. "Basically it puts an end to this vision of a fragmented, weak and decentralized Syria," the Ankara-based analyst argued.

That is also probably the reason why, earlier this week, al-Hijri again emphasized the Druze ties to Israel, Ozkizilcik suggested.

On Monday in Sweida, al-Hijiri declared the Druze an "inseparable part of the state of Israel."

"Even in terms of our beliefs, we share common ground," he said.

Observers have pointed out while al-Hijiri (pictured) has said the Druze have common interests with Israel, it's not the same as linking religions Image: Ali Haj Suleiman/Getty Images

​​​​​​But it's clear that having Israel annex Sweida would be very difficult for a number of reasons, including geography and demographics. Sweida is also still dependent on the central Syrian government. Despite it being impossible for government forces to enter the area, Sweida still receives public services, salaries, pensions, power and water from Damascus.

What caused the rift?

The exclusion of government forces began after intercommunal violence in Sweida in July 2025. Fighting started between Druze and Bedouin locals. Government forces arrived, ostensibly to quell the violence, but they too were then accused of attacking Druze communities.

A report by the United Nations found over 1,700 people died as a result of the clashes.

The event resulted in deep Druze mistrust of the new Syrian government. Even locals who had been in favor of a united Syria began to question whether it might not be better to have a semi-autonomous Druze state.

"There has been a complete erosion of trust," Lubna al-Basit, a Sweida activist, told DW. "Before discussing solutions, the reality today is that the government must be held accountable for the massacres committed in Sweida."

Another Druze, now based in the US but who wished to remain anonymous for security reasons, believes the new Syrian government is more radical than it looks.

"They're trying to behave in way that appeases the West," he told DW. "But you know, we have this joke. They're indicating to go left when they're turning right. For the Druze, the priority would be security, dignity and a chance for prosperity. I don't think many people see that as attainable under the current Syrian government."

The UN report also said that Druze, Bedouin and government-allied forces may all have committed war crimes in July 2025 Image: Izettin Kasim/Anadolu/picture alliance

In September, a road map to repair relations was formulated with Jordanian and American negotiators. But Druze allied with al-Hijiri rejected the plan, and the central government hasn't done much to bring July 2025 perpetrators to justice. In June, the UN's special envoy to Syria said no progress had been made on the road map.

Since last year, Syria's central government "has dealt with the [Sweida] issue on the premise that a large-scale military confrontation would not resolve the crisis," researchers at the Syrian Center for Security and Defense Studies, or MISDAD, wrote in a paper this month .

Any such confrontation "would have deepened the rift with the local community and given external actors greater room to intervene or exploit the tension. Therefore, the Syrian government opted for a more cautious approach, based on calming the situation on one hand, and utilizing the state's security, administrative, and economic tools on the other."

Basically, the researchers at MISDAD continued, the Syrian government is waiting it out, hoping that increasing prosperity elsewhere in the country and the problems al-Hijiri's factions already have running the province's public services, will bring Sweida back to the fold.

A memorial service in Sweida: The crisis of Druze trust in the Syrian central government is severe after last year's violence Image: Shadi Al Dubaisi/JNA/ZUMA/picture alliance

A 'small authoritarian regime in Sweida'

What isn't likely to happen is any kind of revolution, Ozkizilcik explained.

"The issue here is that al-Hijiri has the guns, Israeli financial support and Israeli military advisers from the Israeli-Druze community," he continued. "There is basically a small authoritarian regime in Sweida that's controlled by al-Hijiri, so it would be very difficult for the Druze community to rise up against him."

Opponents of al-Hijiri have been forced out of the province, abducted or killed, there's been fighting between different Druze militias, and there have even been some small civilian protests. Reports say al-Hijiri loyalists have also stopped Druze civil servants from working with ministries in Damascus.

Ozkizilcik and other observers believe a resolution to the situation in Sweida won't come down to what al-Hijiri wants anyway.

Just as American military support — or rather, its withdrawal — for Kurdish forces was integral to the new resolution between the central government and Syrian Kurdish forces, what happens with the Druze community next is also likely to come down to external forces.

Some have argued that the situation in Sweida was a way for Israel to pressure Syria as the two governments tried to negotiate a new security agreement. Throughout 2025, senior Syrian and Israeli politicians were involved in talks, with mediation from the US, to potentially reactivate a 1974 disengagement agreement. However, these fell apart late last year.

Since the overthrow of the dictatorial Assad regime in Syria in late December 2024, the US has said it is in favor of a unified Syria. Israel appears to want the opposite, arguing that a divided Syria won't pose a threat.

"The real decision maker [on Sweida] will be Israel, not al-Hijiri," said Ozkizilcik. "Once — or if — there is a potential security deal between Syria and Israel, then I believe we will also see a political solution to Sweida and the Druze."

World.title: Germany: Man gets life in jail for US tourist's rape, murder
World.content:
The crime was unsolved for over three decades before new DNA proof made it possible to arrest and convict the now 81-year-old. His victim, Amy Lopez, was 24 at the time of her murder.

A German court on Friday sentenced an 81-year-old man to life in prison for the rape and murder of a US tourist over 30 years ago.

Amy Lopez was 24 when she was raped and killed by the convicted man in 1994.

Hans S., whose last name is not given as per Germany's privacy laws, was only arrested earlier this year, when police were finally able to identify him using new DNA technology.

What do we know about the US tourist's murder?

Lopez's body was found near the historic Ehrenbreitstein Fortress in Germany's western city of Koblenz in September 1994 by children playing in the area. Her corpse bore stab wounds, severe head injuries and injuries consistent with strangling.

The regional court in Koblenz found that Hans S. had lured her into a secluded building, falsely promising to show her the way to a hostel, only to tie her up, rape her and then stab her nine times.

The court found that Hans S. had been "looking for a victim to rape" and that Lopez "was tragically in the wrong place at the wrong time."

The defendant confessed to the crime in general terms.

The courtroom was full of observers right through to the final day of what the judge called an "extraordinary case." Among those in attendance, were Amy's father and brother.

"Of course, the verdict cannot undo what happened, nor can it bring Amy back," said lawyer Kathrin Kienle, who represented the victim's family.

"But Amy's father and brother have told me that, in fact, they were never able to find any inner peace throughout this whole time whilst the perpetrator remained at large."

How was the defendant identified after 30 years?

The defendant had been known to authorities for other sexual offenses, serving prison sentences that lasted up to several years. Some of the incidents took place after 1994, with the most recent being in 2005.

His DNA had been on file since his 1999 conviction of attempting to rape a 16-year-old girl.

Though the genetic date had been later deleted, police managed to obtain a new saliva sample from the suspect, which matched a DNA trace found on Lopez's clothing.

His lawyer said he voluntarily provided the DNA sample because "he finally wanted clarity," describing his crime as "an enormous burden" on him.

The defendant was arrested at a nursing home in Koblenz at the end of February 2026.

After the verdict, defense lawyer Volker Klein said he did not intend to lodge an appeal or seek a review.

World.title: Uganda: World's 'youngest monarch' dies aged 34
World.content:
Oyo Nyimba, once recognized as the world's youngest reigning monarch, has died in his mid-30s. As one of Uganda's traditional monarchs, he took the throne of the Tooro kingdom in 1995, aged just 3.

Oyo Nyimba, a Ugandan king of the traditional pre-colonial kingdom of Tooro, has died aged just 34, the prime minister of Tooro announced late on Thursday.

"It is with profound sadness and a heavy heart that I announce the passing of His Majesty Omukama of Tooro, King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV," Tooro's regional leader Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki said on social media.

What is the role of traditional monarchs in Uganda?

Uganda is a republic, ruled by a parliament and a nominally-elected head of state, longstanding President Yoweri Museveni, who's been in power since 1986.

But the country retains several traditional monarchies that still preside over their kingdoms as they were constituted in the pre-colonial period. Their power is largely symbolic but they wield considerable cultural and social influence.

Although they were banned after independence from British colonial rule in 1962 by a republican president who said he wanted to unify the nascent country, Museveni reinstated the traditional monarchs in 1993.

Oyo Nyimba was arguably the most recognizable among them, not least because of his unusual story, taking the throne at the age of just 3 in 1995.

Oyo Nyimba frequently took an interest in youth development and issues affecting younger people during his reign Image: Nicholas Kajoba/Photoshot/picture alliance

What did officials say about Oyo Nyimba's death?

Regional leader Akiiki said that the king had died late on Thursday, without giving a cause of death. He said an official statement with further details, including the funeral and mourning arrangements, would follow later.

He called on the people of Tooro to "remain united, calm and prayerful during this difficult time."

Akiiki also issued one surprising claim about the unmarried young king, who since a very young age had been seen as perhaps Uganda's most eligible bachelor.

"The continuity of the Crown is assured," he said. "His Majesty leaves behind a Prince as heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of the Tooro kingdom."

Ugandan opposition leader Bobi Wine also issued condolences online.

Oyo Nyimba's death triggered an outpouring of grief online and widespread national coverage in Uganda.

The Queen Mother of Tooro Kingdom Best Kemigisa was often close by her son's side, particularly earlier in his reign. Here she was accompanying him to the Kabira International school in the capital Kampala in 2006. Image: Mike Odongkara/dpa/picture alliance

Who was King Oyo Nyimba of Tooro?

Born on April 16, 1992, Oyo was the second-born child of the late Omukama Patrick David Matthew Kaboyo Olimi III and Queen Best Kemigisa Kaboyo, with two sisters.

He ascended to the throne of Tooro, an area in western Uganda near the border to Congo, in 1995 after his father's death.

His unusual status as a modern "boy king" led to considerable interest early in his reign, including from world leaders like former Libyan strongman Moammar Gadhafi, who repeatedly visited Tooro.

Oyo's mother was among his key advisers in his younger years, as was President Yoweri Museveni, who attended his coming-of-age 18th birthday party in 2010 in Fort Portal.

In 2025, the Guinness Book of World Records said he was still the youngest reigning monarch alive, its most recent renewal of the record.

He spent time in the UK at Winchester University to conclude his education. This time away from Uganda prompted a failed challenge to his position in 2015, when his cousin Prince David Kijanangoma declared himself the rightful king of Tooro, accusing Oyo of neglecting the region.

Oyo was known as a lover of sports, and a fan of London football club Arsenal. He took interest in causes including HIV prevention, environmental conservation, tourism and climate change, for instance when he embarked on a hiking expedition in the Rwenzori Mountains in 2022 to try to showcase Uganda's tourism potential and the risks of climate change.

Prior to the news of his death, a Ugandan government minister was quoted in local media as saying Oyo had been seriously ill and was seeking medical treatment in the US.
