World.title: US revokes ex-Iraq finance minister’s visa after FBI adds her to terrorism watchlist
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Trump administration has revoked former Iraqi Finance Minister Taif Sami Mohammed Al Shakarchi’s US visa after she was put on an FBI terrorist blacklist.

The US State Department announced the decision on Friday, stating Sami, Iraq’s finance minister from 2022 to July 2026, had her visa canceled after the FBI added her to its terrorist blacklist.

US authorities did not explain why they included her on the list.

Officials said that Sami had already departed the United States before his visa was canceled.

The action precludes her from returning on that visa.

The discovery comes weeks after Sami was implicated in a broader corruption probe in Iraq.

An Iraqi court summoned the former minister earlier this month, and she was allegedly put on a judicial wanted list as authorities probed charges against high political and government officials.

She was thought to be outside Iraq and had not been captured.

The summons is not a conviction, and Iraqi police have not shown Sami’s crime in court.

Her inclusion on the US terrorist blacklist is unrelated to the Iraqi corruption inquiry, and US officials have not publicly said if the two cases are related.

The action marks a significant shift in Washington’s approach to Sami.

Before becoming finance minister in 2022, she was named to the State Department’s International Women of Courage Award while working as Iraq’s deputy finance minister and budget director-general.

The department at the time recognized her as playing a key role in efforts to combat corruption in Iraq’s public finances.

At the 2022 award ceremony, then-Secretary of State Antony Blinken lauded Sami’s anti-corruption efforts, emphasizing her work exposing financial scams and defending public resources.

In October 2022, previous Prime Minister Mohammed Shia Al-Sudani’s cabinet appointed Sami as Finance Minister, and she served in that role until July of this year.

Her story has given the anti-corruption fight in Baghdad a worldwide dimension.

Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi’s administration has started a series of investigations, arrests, and asset seizures aimed at former and current officials to recoup public monies and strengthen state control.

The State Department has not publicly explained the information behind the FBI watchlist decision or announced any criminal charges against Sami in the United States.

The FBI’s public Most Wanted Terrorists list should not be confused with the larger terrorist blacklist maintained by the US government; Sami is not included on the public Most Wanted Terrorists site.

World.title: Nepal floods trauma ‘enormous’: Red Cross
World.content:
Geneva – The Nepal-Tibet flood disaster has left an “enormous” level of trauma, the Red Cross said Friday, with early estimates suggesting 93,000 people may have been affected.

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the world’s largest humanitarian network, fears the death toll from Wednesday’s disaster, already above 500, will continue to rise.

“Due to roads and bridges having been washed out and both cell coverage and electricity cuts, we have not yet been able to access some of the hardest-hit areas,” said David Fisher, the IFRC head of delegation for Nepal.

“The trauma of this event is enormous,” he told a Geneva press conference, speaking from Kathmandu.

“Thousands of homes have been destroyed or suffered significant damage. We believe that at least 93,000 people have been affected and in great need.”

Nepal’s Red Cross has begun providing emergency relief, including food, water, hygiene kits, mattresses and blankets.

The floods and landslides that struck Nepal and China’s autonomous Tibet region saw a tsunami-like wall of water bury homes, smash bridges and sweep away vehicles.

UN aid chief Tom Fletcher said on X that the United Nations was “moving at speed to save lives”.

Lila Pieters Yahia, the UN resident coordinator for Nepal, said drinking water was being airlifted into affected areas.

“The damage is just incredible,” she told the press conference, speaking from the field, adding that more than 40 bridges had been destroyed or badly damaged and “over 40 kilometres (25 miles) of road completely destroyed”.

She said search and rescue operations were the government priority.

– ‘Cascading hazards’ –

“We haven’t seen a mountain hazard event like this for a very, very long time,” Kamal Kishore, head of the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction, told the press conference.

“It’s really immense and we are still coming to grips with the extent the damage.”

He said the disaster was still unfolding in an ecosystem where one disaster could trigger “a range of cascading hazards”.

The UN children’s agency UNICEF, said at least 14 children were confirmed dead.

“Sadly, we’re only seeing the beginning of this tragedy,” spokesman Ricardo Pires told reporters.

“For those who survived, the emergency is far from over. Children now face increased risks of disease, malnutrition, violence and exploitation, as well as the psychological impact of what they have experienced.”

He said 18 schools had been destroyed and another 20 damaged, with an estimated 10,000 children urgently needing support to continue their education.

The World Health Organization said eight health workers were missing and six health facilities had been damaged.

“The priority is to ensure continuity of health services,” WHO spokesman Tarik Jasarevic said.

He said the UN health agency had delivered surgical masks and gloves and body bags to Nepal.

World.title: UEFA’s legal move ‘massive escalation’ in bitter Infantino feud
World.content:
Paris – UEFA’s intention to launch a legal suit accusing FIFA president Gianni Infantino of “criminal mismanagement” is a “massive escalation” of their feud, a former marketing director of the International Olympic Committee told AFP.

UEFA, European football’s governing body, has urged Infantino to resign over his now-abandoned plan to bring private investment into the World Cup.

On Thursday, UEFA withdrew “on a provisional basis” its threat to boycott FIFA tournaments, but not before dropping a bombshell by announcing it was “considering legal action arising out of and in connection with the FFE plan proposed by FIFA.”

“UEFA and other interested parties are preparing to bring criminal claims in Switzerland against Infantino and possibly other FIFA officials and advisors for criminal mismanagement,” read the legal document drawn up by UEFA’s US-based lawyers and to be filed in a court in Florida.

For Michael Payne, former head of marketing at the IOC, this could prove to be devastating for Infantino.

“UEFA’s legal threat, going after Infantino and FIFA for ‘criminal mismanagement’ is a massive escalation — a move no member federation has ever undertaken against a governing body for over a century,” he told AFP.

“Discovery, if the papers are ever released, will not paint a pretty picture, and open up a whole new focus around Infantino’s leadership and governance — or lack of.”

Terrence Burns, who served as brand and marketing strategist for two successful World Cup host bids, said it could affect Infantino’s hopes of being re-elected to a fourth and final term in Rabat next March.

“I think the legal threat is the better weapon of the two,” he told AFP.

“A boycott hurts the players and the fans, and it could make Infantino look like the victim.

“Going the legal route does the opposite because it’s aimed at him personally, not at the game, and it keeps the story alive on a timetable FIFA cannot control.

“And that’s the real point!

“It could run through the November nomination deadline (November 18 for candidates to declare) and into the March vote.”

– ‘Civil war’ –

Infantino has stayed put despite the onslaught of criticism from UEFA and two fellow confederations including CONCACAF, whose Canadian president Victor Montagliani is viewed as the likeliest challenger.

Neither Payne nor Burns are surprised, with the former saying: “Infantino has no choice but to tough it out — he has nowhere else to go.”

Burns, who has played a pivotal role in five successful Olympic bid city campaigns, says Infantino has an invaluable weapon.

“I think time is on his side, not UEFA’s,” said the American.

“Every week this drags on is another week he’s the president, meeting heads of state, doing deals, handing out the things a president can hand out.”

Burns believes the 56-year-old Swiss incumbent seems to have the numbers to be re-elected.

“It’s 211 votes, not three confederations, and he’s spent 10 years building that base one federation at a time,” said Burns.

“Saudi Arabia, Argentina, Mexico, most of Africa, and much of the Gulf are already with him.

“I think he’ll fight to the last day because fighting is the only strategy.”

Payne, who is credited with overhauling the IOC’s brand and finances in two decades as marketing supremo, says Infantino should learn from history.

“There is a very real risk of civil war — does that mean break away — or non-stop pressure on Infantino, paralysing his leadership, until he has no choice to eventually resign, as (Sepp) Blatter was forced to after his re-election,” said the 68-year-old Irishman.

Burns is more circumspect about the divisions.

“I’d stop short of civil war,” he said.

“Nobody wants to break the World Cup — too much money is riding on it, for everyone.

“To me, it feels more like a family feud over who runs the business, but it’s real, and it won’t fix itself.”

Burns, though, believes the two camps will learn you can’t always get what you want.

“The good news is a deadline is looming, and it is called the month of March,” he said.

“This cannot go on indefinitely; I think it will get solved in a way that leaves everyone with slightly less than what they wanted.

“As a pal of mine always says, ‘Welcome to the work week, boss; that’s how things get done!'”

World.title: Iraq debuts first tech pavilion at LEAP 2026 in Riyadh
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — For the first time, Iraqi technology and digital enterprises will exhibit in a dedicated national pavilion at Saudi Arabia’s LEAP 2026, providing a new platform for Iraq’s developing tech industry to seek collaborations and investment from Saudi Arabia and the broader Gulf.

The Iraq Pavilion will be held from August 31 to September 3 at the Riyadh Exhibition and Convention Center in Malham, bringing together Iraqi enterprises in artificial intelligence, fintech, digital transformation, logistics, media, and technology services in one location.

The premiere is noteworthy for Iraq’s young technology economy, as LEAP has grown into one of the region’s biggest meetings of technology businesses, entrepreneurs, and investors.

This year’s event is expected to draw more than 201,000 people, including 1,800 global technology companies, 600 startups, and 1,900 investors.

– LEAP 2026 –

The Iraqi delegation includes Media World, part of March Holding, alongside Nass Al Iraq Holding, Digital Transformation Company (DTC), NAI, Theki Tech, Qafia Creative Agency, Daman Digital Platform, Zaeem Express Delivery, Advenature, MATIC, Rabee Securities and Dofied.

The companies represent an expanding Iraqi private sector.

Nass Al Iraq Holding’s activities include telecoms, digital transformation, real estate, and advertising, with its technology subsidiary DTC focusing on digital transformation and Theki Tech providing infrastructure and smart-building technologies.

Media World links digital content suppliers with telecom carriers in regional markets, while NAI concentrates on business-oriented artificial intelligence solutions.

Qafiya provides advertising and creative services.

Financial technologies will also be significant.

Rabee Securities, one of Iraq’s biggest securities brokerage firms, has worked on key Iraq Stock Exchange listings, and Dofied is creating digital cash-collecting systems to replace paper-based records.

Meanwhile, Zaeem Express symbolizes Iraq’s fast-increasing logistics and e-commerce infrastructure, with its delivery network delivering over 50,000 packages each day throughout the nation, according to pavilion information.

The participation of LEAP investors might make the event more valuable for Iraqi entrepreneurs seeking Gulf finance and regional partners. T

he conference offers specific startup and investor programs that link entrepreneurs with possible investors and firms looking for new markets.

The pavilion also comes as Iraq’s and Saudi Arabia’s economic ties expand beyond their usual emphasis on oil and government-to-government collaboration.

Bringing Iraqi technology businesses directly into Riyadh’s economic ecosystem might assist in strengthening linkages in AI, finance, logistics, digital services, and venture capital.

For Baghdad, luring Saudi and other GCC funds into technology would help diversify an economy that is still largely reliant on oil and generate more chances for Iraq’s private sector.

Tahaluf organizes LEAP 2026, which is currently in its fifth edition, with support from Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and the Saudi Federation for Cybersecurity, Programming, and Drones. Saudi officials see the event as a key component of the kingdom’s efforts to transform Riyadh into a global technology and investment powerhouse.

The Iraqi Pavilion will be in Hall 3, Booth H3.G160, for the duration of the four-day event.

World.title: Norway’s new King Haakon VIII, popular face of shaken monarchy
World.content:
Oslo – As comfortable in a duffel coat as in ceremonial dress, Norway’s new monarch, King Haakon VIII, is the new face of a monarchy long praised for its modernity and modesty, but now beset by woe and scandal.

Haakon automatically succeeded to the throne Friday after his father, King Harald, passed away peacefully earlier in the day.

The 53-year-old informed the government in a meeting that he would keep the same motto as his father and grandfather: “All for Norway.”

He has increasingly seen his family’s affairs plastered across front pages: his wife’s lung transplant, revelations about her ties to convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, a rape conviction against his stepson, and the escapades of his eccentric sister and her American self-proclaimed shaman husband.’

“Everything will be fine with him when the time comes. It is reassuring to know that,” the late King Harald said of him in a book.

“I am fortunate that it is Crown Prince Haakon who has to take over,” Harald said, musing that his own father had probably been more worried about the succession

The tall, bearded and stately Haakon is as modest and measured as most Norwegians — reflecting a society that shuns opulence and ostentation.

Married to Mette-Marit, a commoner who was a single mother before their wedding, Haakon has focused his attention on issues that concern many of his generation, including environmental protection and fighting racism and homophobia.

“It’s important that we protect who we are and for Norway to be a country where we’re allowed to love and be with whoever we want,” he said the day after a bloody attack against the gay community in Oslo in June 2022.

Born on July 20, 1973, the prince attended state-run daycare and schools, in line with the wishes of King Harald and Queen Sonja, who were keen to see him grow up among “ordinary” Norwegians.

After a stint in the navy, he went on to earn a bachelor’s degree in political science at the University of California in Berkeley and a master’s in international politics at the London School of Economics.

– Scandals –

Haakon is a fan of skiing, surfing, and windsurfing, as well as music.

It was at a 1999 music festival at Kristiansand, in southern Norway, that he met his future wife, whose tumultuous past made headlines in the Scandinavian country.

At the time, Mette-Marit Tjessem Hoiby was a single mother of a young son named Marius, the fruit of an earlier relationship with a man with a heavy criminal record, including assault and cocaine possession.

Norwegians however quickly saw beyond her wild past. The couple went on to have a daughter expected to one day be queen, Ingrid Alexandra, born in 2004, and a son Sverre Magnus, in 2005.

But storm clouds were building on the horizon.

Haakon’s sister Princess Martha-Louise, a fan of alternative therapies, has repeatedly been accused of exploiting her royal title for commercial purposes.

She made headlines again by marrying a self-proclaimed shaman, Durek Verrett, in 2024, described as a dangerous “charlatan” by his critics.

Then his stepson Marius was arrested in August 2024 and sentenced to four years in prison in June 2026 for rape and assault. He has appealed.

Just days before the conviction, Haakon’s wife Mette-Marit, underwent a lung transplant for pulmonary fibrosis that was diagnosed in 2018.

The Norwegian media had in February already published troubling revelations about Mette-Marit’s friendship with Epstein in the early 2010s.

Even though the disgraced financier had already been convicted of soliciting a minor, Mette-Marit had been in frequent contact with him, their emails indicating a close relationship.

She said she had been “manipulated and deceived”.

“When you get married, it’s for better or for worse,” Haakon remarked in March during a televised interview the gave about the Epstein revelations.

The scandals have tarnished the royal family’s image and weakened its support in the Scandinavian country, though it remains broadly popular.

Haakon has nevertheless “shown himself to be a man who remains steady in the face of a storm, and that is a very valuable quality in a monarch,” Caroline Vagle, a reporter for magazine Se og Hor, told AFP.

“He has also had the best teacher he could possibly have had in his father,” she added.

In a poll conducted in March, nearly eight out of 10 Norwegians felt that he would make a good king.

World.title: All eyes on Warsh as Fed chair kicks off key central banking meeting
World.content:
Washington – Markets will be wanting much — but expecting little — from US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh as he kicks off the Jackson Hole central banking conference in Wyoming on Friday.

Warsh, appointed by US President Donald Trump and in office since May, will speak at 8:00 am (1400 GMT) at the remote and storied venue for monetary policy watchers.

Since 1982, policymakers and prominent economists have gathered in this valley ringed by mountains in Grand Teton National Park — known to most people more for its bison than for spirited debates on macroeconomics.

Fed chiefs traditionally use their first speech at Jackson Hole to lay out their vision for how they see the path for monetary policy and the central bank as a whole.

Since taking office, however, Warsh has been adamant about saying less, not more.

He has refrained from giving guidance on the direction interest rates may take in the world’s largest economy, and refused to share his views on the economic outlook or how surging inflation and other challenges should be tackled.

“I don’t think he’s going to do a complete 180 and all of a sudden, become a great communicator,” said Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon.

Daco said Warsh’s speech was likely to stand in contrast to ones from his predecessors, who often spoke about their vision of economic policy-making or current crises.

“(For Warsh) it’s likely to be one that remains quite abstract, focusing on the need to reform the Fed regime and the need to correct for the mistakes of the past,” he said.

“That may be the speech we get, which is quite low on content and low on policy.”

– ‘Now is the time’ –

The world’s largest economy has delivered robust growth despite facing significant challenges, including shocks from Trump’s tariffs and his war on Iran, which has sent global energy prices skyrocketing.

Both policies have fuelled inflation in the United States, which has remained above the Fed’s long-term two-percent target for more than half a decade.

On Wednesday, the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge clocked in at 3.7 percent, down 0.4 percentage points from May, when it hit a three-year high.

A quarter of voting members on the Fed’s rate-setting committee have called for the central bank to raise rates in order to take on the crisis. The majority held rates steady at their last meeting in July.

On Thursday, Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack — one of the dissenters — said the bank needed to raise now or face further pain later.

“I believe now is the time to act,” she told CNBC in Jackson Hole.

“The longer inflation stays above our objective, the harder it will be for us to bring it back down, and the more pain that individuals and businesses are going to be experiencing.”

Bernard Yaros, lead US economist at Oxford Economics, said markets wanted more from Warsh, particularly on how he views the economic outlook, but that investors were not holding their breath for him to be forthcoming.

Hammack pushed back against Warsh’s views on communicating less. While she did not name the Fed chair, responding to a question she said communication was a key responsibility to fulfil the duties of an independent Fed.

“Hand in hand with that independence comes accountability and transparency,” she said. “And I feel like it’s important for me, as a member of the committee, to talk about how I see the economy unfolding.”

World.title: Japan spent record $96 bn in yen interventions: ministry
World.content:
Tokyo – Japan spent 15.4 trillion yen ($96 billion) to boost the yen between late July and late August, the finance ministry said Friday, the largest monthly intervention on record.

The Bank of Japan intervenes in the market under the instruction of the ministry to ease economic damage from sharp fluctuations in exchange rates.

The yen has been weakening because of the gap between Japanese and US interest rates, high oil prices and concerns about Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s spending plans further swelling Tokyo’s enormous debts.

The finance ministry data released on Friday showed that the market interventions happened between July 30 and August 26, but did not specify exact dates.

On July 31, Tokyo and Washington carried out their first joint intervention in 28 years to boost the yen that had hit a four-decade low.

US President Donald Trump confirmed the concerted action aboard Air Force One early this month, calling it a “signal of friendship” with Japan, and “good for the world economy”.

The operation to buy yen came after the unit hit 163.99 per dollar last month, its weakest since 1986. On July 31, it soared to 157.40, the strongest since early May.

On Friday, the yen was at 159.6 against the greenback.

The July intervention was the first time since 2011 when the United States and Japan — and other G7 members — sold yen to stop it rising after a huge earthquake.

The last time Washington and Tokyo bought yen was 1998.

Experts say the Trump administration also acted to reduce the US trade deficit — a weak yen helps Japanese exporters — and to help Japan invest $550 billion in the United States as promised under a 2025 trade deal.

While good for its big exporters like Sony and Toyota, a weak yen inflates import costs for resource-poor Japan, especially oil just as the Middle East war strangles supplies from the Gulf.

The yen has been sliding despite previous interventions and comments by Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama that Japan was ready to act, remarks aimed at deterring investors from betting on the currency sliding further.

World.title: Iraq-Gulf trade faces Hormuz strain, IRIS says
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — According to a new report by the Institute of Regional and International Studies (IRIS) at the American University of Iraq, Sulaimani, Iraq risks losing some of its growing commercial ties with Gulf states as the Strait of Hormuz is disrupted, forcing Iraqi traders to seek alternative supply chains through Turkey.

According to the August Iraq Economic Review, Iraq’s economic integration with the Gulf has expanded in recent years as a result of a mix of big government initiatives and smaller commercial networks that link Iraqi enterprises to GCC ports, suppliers, and logistical companies.

The Hormuz crisis is now challenging both.

Qatar is cited as one of the most notable instances of the investment trend.

According to the research, Doha has committed more than $9 billion in energy, logistics, infrastructure, and real estate investments since 2023, excluding its interest in TotalEnergies’ Iraqi energy project.

Saudi energy interconnection projects, UAE engagement in Grand Faw Port, Qatari investments, and the Development Road are all steadily strengthening economic ties between Iraq and its Gulf neighbors.

According to the report, Iraqi participation in the GCC is not required for this integration, which may be achieved via bilateral investment, infrastructure, and private-sector collaboration.

However, the analysis highlights a less noticeable issue affecting Iraqi traders.

Businesses that formerly depended on the UAE, notably Jebel Ali, to import Asian commodities and industrial inputs into Iraq are now experiencing greater transportation and logistical expenses as a result of the Hormuz interruption.

Some have started going north to Türkiye, where existing land links provide a more dependable option.

The move might have long-term effects.

According to IRIS, economic connections among smaller merchants are based on suppliers, credit, and trust, so if such networks relocate to Turkey, they may not immediately return to Gulf routes, even if circumstances near Hormuz improve.

Türkiye is especially appealing since its manufacturers can provide items, including building materials, at costs and qualities appropriate for the Iraqi market.

Traders contacted for the research said that certain Gulf-made alternatives were too costly for their consumers.

According to the paper, Baghdad could react by engaging directly with chambers of commerce, trade groups, and transportation firms to identify the real challenges that businesses face, rather than depending only on high-level agreements with Gulf states.

It offers temporary tariff reductions, speedier customs processing, and freight assistance for lower-value commodities traveling via alternate Gulf routes, notably Fujairah.

It also suggests establishing an Iraq-GCC platform to provide merchants with information on freight prices, transit times, and the profitability of routes via Jebel Ali, Khorfakkan, and Turkish ports.

The study also emphasizes that Gulf investment will be contingent on circumstances inside Iraq.

Baghdad must strengthen administration, lower business costs, shield investment from the militia economy, and deliver promised infrastructure if the present wave of Gulf interest is to result in long-term economic integration.

IRIS cautions that the opportunity for action is dwindling. If more Iraqi enterprises develop suppliers, financial contacts, and transportation networks in Turkey, reestablishing the Gulf-oriented trade lines created over the last decade may become more challenging.

World.title: Flash floods put focus on India's glacial lakes
World.content:
An aerial view of damaged structures covered in thick mud and debris following the flash floods at Devighat in Nepalâs Nuwakot

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) disaster in Nepal Wednesday has renewed discussion on India's own strategy and preparedness to mitigate such risk with the presence of approximately 200 high-risk glacial lakes in the Himalayan regions.According to govt's survey of these glacial lakes, Himalayan ranges are host to as many as 7,500 of them - with 10% in Sikkim and of which 25 are considered very high-risk. The study found 4,700 of these glacial lakes situated in Ganga river basin with a catchment area estimated at over 2.5 lakh sqkm, projecting a colossal scale of devastation a single breach could cause.India suffered one of the worst GLOF disasters in recent times when on Oct 3, 2023, glacial rocks of 14.7 cubic meter collapsed in South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim, close to midnight, "generating a 20-m high displacement wave", wiping out several hydro power assets and settlements on its way downstream.Krishna Vatsa, member of National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), said the Nepal event illustrates a new dimension of Himalayan disaster risk, though the precise sequence of events is still being scientifically established. "These are cascading hazards: an ice or rock failure can become a debris flow, create a temporary lake and then generate a flash flood. Such events can develop extremely rapidly and may provide very little warning time downstream."India's National GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme has marked 195 at-risk glacial lakes and follows five key priorities (assessment, monitoring, early warning, mitigation, community awareness). It needs to be speeded up and scaled up immediately as a priority for national security," said Syed Safi Ahsan Rizvi, an ex-NDMA member.As a response to the Sikkim disaster, Centre had set up a high-level coordination committee on GLOF disaster risk reduction. The initiative, spearheaded by PM's principal secretary PK Mishra, was tasked to host multi-agency deliberations and surveys of such lakes and identify the high-risk ones. Govt also allocated Rs 150 crore for the National GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme for four Himalayan states having high-risk glacial lakes.The first meeting of the coordination committee on DRR was held in Nov 2024, when PM's principal secretary expressing his satisfaction on the group's "tri-focal lens: assessment, monitoring, and mitigation". The committee hosted regular meetings and received feedback, which were then formed as part of joint strategy between states and Centre. However, not much is known on follow up actions.Earlier, govt had claimed that multi-agency expeditions were conducted to assess all "A-category" lakes. The teams comprised scientists and officials from NDMA, Central Water Commission, Geological Survey of India, Centre for Development of Advance Computing, ITBP and the Army.

World.title: Government tightens norms for e-cycles, e-bikes
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The road transport ministry has proposed to tighten technical and safety norms for low-speed electric cycles and e-bikes with a maximum speed of 25 kmph and motor power below 600 watts.

Manufacturers of these would have to get vehicles certified by authorised testing agencies before they can qualify for exemption from the Motor Vehicles Act to be treated as âmotor vehicleâ.

At present, electric two-wheelers that have motor power below 250 watts are not treated as âmotor vehiclesâ and hence donât need registration. This definition is now being expanded to vehicles that have motor power up to 600 watts, which officials said is ârealisticâ.

All these vehicles will be required to use only lithium-ion batteries instead of lead-acid batteries.

As per draft amendments to Central Motor Vehicles Rules, such vehicles will have to be fitted with âsuitable brakes and retro-reflective devicesâ for visibility. The draft notification said for pedal-assisted electric bicycles, the motor assistance must progressively reduce and cut off once the vehicle reaches 25 kmph or when the rider stops pedalling.

The proposal is significant considering that low-speed electric two-wheelers have witnessed rapid growth as affordable urban mobility options, but many models have operated with limited regulatory oversight.

World.title: Junk foods will soon have labels warning of high salt, sugar and fat
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Junk foods will soon carry warning labels highlighting high levels of salt, sugar and fat, with the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) telling Supreme Court on Friday that it has agreed to red-coloured hexagonal warnings on the front of food packages to help consumers identify products high in specified nutrients of concern.

FSSAI conveyed its position through a compliance affidavit filed before Supreme Court in response to the court's Aug 13 order on front-of-pack labelling (FoPL).

The move comes after the court pushed Centre to act on the issue, saying, "If the Union does it on its own, well and good, otherwise we shall proceed to pass further directions."

Under the framework, products high in specified nutrients would carry prominent red hexagonal warnings reading "HIGH FAT", "HIGH SALT" and/or "HIGH SUGAR", as applicable.

FSSAI has agreed to exempt single-ingredient foods such as ghee, edible oil, salt, sugar, jaggery and honey from the proposed warnings, subject to applicable food safety and labelling regulations.

The regulator has agreed to implement FoPL in phases, giving the industry time to reformulate products. Phase I would cover products high in two or more specified nutrients, while Phase II would extend warnings to products high in any one specified nutrient.





Do warning labels work?

The framework is based on nutrient thresholds specified under the Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024, issued by ICMR-NIN. The affidavit follows the Supreme Courtâs observations on public health, particularly amid concerns over the rising prevalence of childhood obesity. The court said front-of-pack labelling could help consumers make informed purchasing decisions.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The case stems from a PIL filed by NGO 3S and Our Health Society, which approached Supreme Court through advocate Rajiv Shankar Dwivedi, seeking front-of-pack labelling to help consumers make informed choices.

FSSAI said the system is intended to provide a âsimple, prominent and easily comprehensible warningâ to consumers about food products high in specified nutrients of concern. It also cited international examples, including Chile and Canada, where front-of-pack labelling has been adopted.

Supreme Court had considered options including coloured indicators, interpretative words, numbers, letters, symbols and percentages for front-of-pack labelling and directed Centre to take a decision and place it on record.

World.title: Clean energy push unfair on developing nations: CJI Surya Kant
World.content:
NEW DELHI: CJI Surya Kant Friday told Commonwealth countries it was unfair that industrialised nations, who took two centuries to adopt clean energy, were asking nations in the process of industrialisation to move towards renewable energy within decades.

Speaking at the Commonwealth Secretariat in London, CJI Kant said, âCountries that are finally industrialising are being asked to move rapidly towards renewable power, and are often made to bear the brunt of criticism when they cannot move fast enough.â

âThe challenge, therefore, is to reconcile the urgency of the clean energy transition with the principles of fairness and shared responsibility that must underpin it,â the CJI said.

World.title: Nilekani committee seeks public ideas to fix exams
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The high-powered task force set up by Centre to overhaul Indiaâs public examination system opened a nationwide consultation on Friday, seeking suggestions from students, parents, teachers and other stakeholders on making high-stakes tests more secure, transparent and student-friendly.

The panel, headed by Infosys co-founder and technology expert Nandan Nilekani, was announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi last month amid heightened scrutiny of the examination system following NEET-UG paper leak controversy and youth protests over alleged lapses in the testâs conduct.

The announcement had come a day after Centre accepted the demands raised by the youth-led CJP, whose protests over NEET leak included calls for then education minister Dharmendra Pradhanâs resignation and withdrawal of FIRs against protesters.

âThe High-Powered Task Force (HPTF) on Reforms in Public Examinations wants to hear from students, parents, teachers â every citizen,â a senior official said on Friday.

The task forceâs mandate âto examine and recommend comprehensive reforms relating to conduct, security, design and governance of public examinations, including examinations conducted by National Testing Agency (NTA), the ministry of personnel said.





HPTF, which seeks âto benefit from the experience, knowledge and perspectives of stakeholdersâ, said the suggestions may dwell on the conduct and security of public exams as well as the examination design and assessment methodology.

Stakeholders may give inputs on better governance, accountability and institutional arrangements; as also systems to prevent, detect and redress examination malpractices, the ministry said.

The public consultation will remain open till Sept 13, with citizens allowed to send suggestions through WhatsApp, a dedicated website, email and a toll-free number.

Officials said the task force is examining reforms across the examination chain â from institutional processes and question-paper security to use of technology and strengthening of examination infrastructure.

It will also look at measures to improve accessibility and inclusion, while factoring in student well-being during the examination process.

âThe objective is to develop a public examination system that is robust, secure, transparent, equitable and future-ready,â the official said. The exercise assumes significance after repeated controversies surrounding national-level entrance and eligibility examinations raised questions over paper security, examination management and the ability of testing agencies to respond quickly to irregularities.

World.title: Second excavation phase at Kashmir Buddhist starts today
World.content:
ZEHANPORA (BARAMULLA): Excavations will begin Saturday on the second phase of Zehanpora, a Buddhist site in north Kashmirâs Baramulla. J&K chief secretary Atal Dullo will inaugurate the project.

The presence of a 2,000-year-old Buddhist civilisation at the site was discovered last year by Mohamad Ajmal Shah, a professor at University of Kashmir. It gained prominence after PM Narendra Modi mentioned it during his monthly radio programme Mann Ki Baat on Dec 28 last year.

The Prime Minister recalled that people had noticed tall mounds in Zehanpora for years without knowing about their significance. What were first believed to be unusual rock formations were later found to resemble three Buddha stupas seen in photos in a French museum.

According to Modi, the blurred photos, thousands of kilometres away, proved crucial as it showed three Buddhist stupas, helping archaeologists connect the dots and reconstruct Kashmirâs ancient past. The discovery reaffirms J&Kâs rich cultural legacy.

It all began in Oct 2023 when Shah was on a fellowship in France and came across the 100-odd old photos at Guimet Museum showing stupa domes in Baramulla. âI immediately realised I had visited the site.





What struck me was the domes in the photos looked much larger than what we see now,â said Shah, attached to the varsityâs department of Central Asian Studies.

Later, Shah requested J&K govtâs department of archaeology to fund the project and it agreed. Shah and his team started digging in Nov last year, initially discovering a hall identified as an apsidal (semi-circular) stupa.

Shah and his team also found iron/copper artefacts, needles, decorated objects and other materials.

âWe identified wall alignments through drone images and excavated precisely at those points. There is a strong possibility that many structures and artefacts still lie preserved beneath the ground,â Shah said.

Shah highlighted the possibility that the site was linked to the Fourth Buddhist Council (1st century CE). âKashmir was a major centre of Buddhism in ancient times. It was here that Hinayana Buddhism evolved into Mahayana Buddhism, giving the religion a new philosophical and cultural form,â he said.

Shah pointed out that the Chinese explorer Hiuen Tsang had mentioned Baramulla in his travel accounts. According to Shah, Tsang spent a night at Uskur, a Buddhist site near Baramulla town and visited several monasteries in the area. âThis suggests Tsang must have visited the monastery at Zehanpora as well,â Shah said.

World.title: Gen Z vs the khap panchayats: Old rules, new rebels
World.content:
Anchal, an M.A. student and a resident of Igra village, Jind district, posted a video on social media satirising khap panchayats, the powerful but unelected community bodies dominated by elderly men from landowning communities in Haryana. Imagining what a “Gen Z panchayat” might look like, she suggests in the video that elderly men face restrictions on playing cards, smoking hookahs and bidis, and wasting time, while tobacco sellers be fined. The money collected through such fines, she jokes, could be used to replace phones damaged or confiscated from girls.

Anchal was responding to a controversy that exploded after a khap panchayat member, Virender Dhull, a resident of Ikkas village in Haryana, made a remark about young women at the Naugama khap meeting in Jind on August 1. The comment that went viral was about women riding pillion with their fathers on two-wheelers, their legs astride, while using mobile phones and wearing clothes the khap thought unsuitable. He said their phones should be smashed. Dhull, a director of physical education at Jat Senior Secondary School in Jind, was hit by social-media criticism.

Over the past few weeks, several khap panchayats across parts of north Haryana have unleashed a series of resolutions, many against women. The khaps have opposed marriages within the community and live-in and same-sex relationships, while also resolving to fight drug abuse, online betting, and obscene social-media content.

Khap leaders insist they are not issuing diktats. They describe themselves as community elders offering guidance to the youth, and argue that their goal is to preserve social cohesion and protect families. Except, ostracisation will be a penalty for those who disregard these social rules. And the rules are targeted primarily at young women.

To many, especially the social-media-vocal Gen Z, the khaps’ message sounded like an attempt to regulate their personal choices in the name of tradition.

“Why are concerns over culture and social behaviour directed primarily at girls? If these restrictions are genuinely meant to protect society and preserve our culture, they should apply equally to men,” Anchal says.

Young women see the controversy as an enduring culture of social control over female agency, and have posted videos against the diktats. Several men too, like rapper Rahul Fazilpuria and content creator Paras Yadav, too, took to social media to condemn the resolution.

Naugama khap president, Jaivir Lohan, however, says Dhull’s remarks have been misrepresented. He maintains that the khap has not banned mobile phones for girls or prescribed what women should or shouldn’t wear. Parents, he says, should decide what is appropriate for their children, and the khap will intervene only if parents seek its help.

“The views expressed during the panchayat on women’s clothing and use of mobile phones was an individual’s opinion,” Lohan says. The Naugama khap has 42 members, all male.

Haryana’s over 130 khap panchayats have long carried an image of being stuck in time. Their decisions have frequently been criticised for restricting women’s autonomy, particularly their freedom to choose whom to marry, who to associate with, and how to live. They have largely kept women away from decision-making roles.

Khap state of mind

On August 9, 24 khap panchayats met in Jind’s Kandela village. Here, they passed a resolution disallowing women and men from marrying within the same gotra (clan) or cluster that their khap panchayats oversee. This diktat is based on their belief that its members are one extended social family. However, people are free to choose who they marry beyond this boundary.

Chanderbhan Nambardar, a khap member, says people within this network are considered brothers and sisters, irrespective of caste differences and, in some cases, gotra distinctions. For the khap, therefore, a marriage within these prohibited social boundaries is seen as a relationship crossing what the community considers a kinship boundary. Lohan says that same-gotra marriages lead to genetic disorders and weak offspring, because of a common gene pool.

The consequences, if the khap panchayat is disobeyed, are severe. Nambardar says that if a woman and a man who come under the 24 khap panchayats disobey, they will not be allowed to enter the area under their community-appointed jurisdiction. He acknowledges that the khaps have no legal authority, though.

The khaps also passed a resolution banning live-in and same-sex relationships, and content they felt was obscene, while also urging the government to regulate marriage by choice, or love marriages, as they are called in India.

Raghubir Nain, president of the Sarvjatiya Binain khap, in Jind, says the panchayat did not oppose love marriages, but wanted them to take place with parental consent and within accepted social norms. He refers to live-in and same-sex relationships as a “nai beemari (new disease)” in society. The Naugama khap has made similar demands.

Naugama khap spokesperson Umed Jaglan says they want the government to examine the social consequences of live-in relationships, particularly where a married person leaves a spouse and children to live with another partner. The khap argues that such relationships can damage families and traditional social institutions.

Khap leaders also say women are being included more in decision-making now, through special assemblies and women’s wings aimed at addressing social issues.

On August 23 in Jind, the Naugama khap panchayat convened its first ever women-led mahapanchayat. They too passed resolutions against love marriages and live-in relationships, but also against dowry and gun culture. A 21-member committee will spread the word and ensure compliance.

At a mahapanchayat, held in July at the Meham Chaubisi Chabutra in Rohtak, participants adopted resolutions against drug abuse, online betting, obscene social-media content, and the glorification of guns online. The gathering also decided to eliminate the use of hookah at community functions — an especially striking move in a State where the hookah has long been a symbol of rural social interaction. The mahapanchayat was chaired by Chaubisi Khap president Subhash Goyat and attended by prominent local artists, including Ajay Hooda.

Khap leaders say these social issues they take up rarely receive the same attention as their positions on marriage and relationships. Nambardar argues the khaps are “guiding lights” for the youth.

Gen Z hits back

On her YouTube channel, Leena Sharma (leena_yuvan7240) criticises what she describes the khap diktats, questioning how restrictions on women’s clothing, mobility, and behaviour can be imposed in the 21st century. She points out that women sitting astride a motorcycle is a matter of safety. She also questions khap resolutions, such as not allowing DJ music at weddings, asking why community bodies should dictate personal choices. Her larger argument is generational: cities may be changing, she says, but villages need to change too.

On Instagram, Garima (@garima.sees) talks about how the khaps were claiming that this was done to save “culture”, but it was just to control women. In a Reel with the caption “One of the reasons why Haryana is developing backwards,” she says the State grapples with one of the highest youth unemployment ratios and one of the lowest sex ratios in India. “Meanwhile, Haryana’s male youth is involved in drugs and crime, but no such panchayat is held for the betterment of these people. Na unkay liye kuch ban kiya jaata hai, aur na unkay liye kuch rules banaye jaate hain (Nothing for them is banned, nor are there any rules made for them),” she says on the video.

It’s not just women speaking against the diktat. Aman Kashyap, who holds a master’s degree in journalism from a university in Jind, asks, “When the Constitution grants girls equal rights, how can a panchayat decide to smash their phones or restrict their movements?” He calls these diktats illegal and contrary to fundamental rights, including the freedom of movement, expression, and privacy. He stresses that the views of a few khap members should not be seen as those of all of Haryana, noting that many students and their parents too had opposed the decisions.

Krishan Dalal, a reel creator with nearly 27.8k followers on his Instagram account @iamkrishan7, clocked 747k views on his post on the subject. In the Reel with some mixed messaging, he says, “Actually, ye buddhay hain gay (Actually, these old men are gay),” adding that, “Before they die, they want to come out of the closet….” He also says, with some misunderstanding, “Ye low testosterone mard ki pehli pehchaan hoya kare, ki jab kahin uska bas nahi chalta toh aurat ne sanskar aur sabhyachaar sikhane nikileya kare wo. (The first sign of a low-testosterone man is that when he cannot assert his authority anywhere else, he sets out to teach women about values and civilisation).”

Critics, however, point out that societal relationships are governed through individual rights and the law, rather than through community sanctions. A YouTube channel FlicksUnpacked has uploaded a Short under the title “Huge Decision by Haryana Khap on Love Marriages”. It addresses Khap members as “so-called dadajis (paternal grandfathers)”, accusing them of seeking attention and social-media fame.

The clip reflects a wider generational tension in Haryana and elsewhere: traditional community-based institutions continue to assert authority over matters of relationships and social conduct, while the youth increasingly uses digital platforms to challenge those norms and demand greater autonomy, equality, and individual rights.

Customs versus law

As they sit in a circle in a building set on 5 acres of land in Ramrai village, some of the men feel India’s laws must be in tandem with Haryana’s social customs.

“Couples entering into these relationships, which are against our social customs, are given security by law-enforcing agencies,” Jaglan says, referring to safe houses set up by the government to protect couples who have been socially ostracised and whose lives are sometimes in danger.

Jaglan says the Naugama khap has actively approached political and legal authorities seeking changes to the law. According to him, more than two years ago, a delegation first met then Haryana Chief Minister Manohar Lal Khattar, and later, in January 2025, met Union Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal. Among its demands were changes to the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, restrictions on same-gotra and same-village marriages, and legal action against live-in and same-sex relationships. Jaglan says the delegation was assured that its concerns would be placed before the Union Cabinet, but that no further action or response followed.

The khap also demanded changing the legal marriage age for women, with Jaglan recalling that some members had proposed reducing it from 18 to 16. He also points to its history of approaching political and judicial authorities, including earlier meetings with former Haryana Chief Ministers Devi Lal and Bansi Lal, as well as a representation before the Supreme Court.

The khap leaders see matters such as drugs, guns, and dowry as being interconnected with other parts of the social order, like marriage and relationships. Their critics see a dangerous blurring of the line between community advice and coercion.

Anti-women accusations

Nambardar rejects the accusation that khaps are anti-women. He points to the wider political system to explain why women remain under-represented in khap leadership. “Women became sarpanches in Haryana only in the 1980s,” he says, questioning the gap between political promises and reality. “Every political party talks about 33% reservation for women, but how many women are actually in the State Assemblies and Parliament?”

According to him, the problem runs deeper than the khaps themselves. Indian society, he says, continues to be patriarchal, with women still under-represented in politics, government, and employment. “So naturally, there are fewer women in khaps as well. But their representation is growing fast.”

Nambardar argues that several decisions taken by khaps have received support from women. For instance, during the wrestlers’ protest, when several women wrestlers from Haryana had accused BJP leader Brijbhushan Singh of sexual abuse, the khaps stood by the women.

The khap remains rooted in a Haryana where village identity, kinship, honour, and collective decision-making continue to carry enormous weight. But it operates alongside Gen Z that is increasingly connected to cities, smartphones, social media, new forms of work and relationships, and a legal system built around individual rights. That collision is producing uncomfortable questions on both sides.

In the first four months of 2026, Haryana’s Sex Ratio at Birth plummeted to 898 girls for every 1,000 boys.

World.title: Praggnanandhaa becomes first Indian to win Grand Chess Tour title
World.content:
He was trailing. And he was up against the World No. 2. And yet, there was almost a sense of inevitability to it. R. Praggnanandhaa duly defeated Fabiano Caruana and won the Grand Chess Tour.

After losing the first game, he bounced back in great style to win the multi-format final at St. Louis on Thursday (August 27, 2026). He became the first Indian to win the most prestigious tour on the chess circuit.

Caruana, in fact, was the champion of the Grand Chess Tour last year, and also in 2023. He had begun on the right note in the U.S. city, winning the opening classical game of the final against his 21-year-old rival from Chennai, whose blunder with his rook on the 28th move proved fatal.

Praggnanandhaa, however, came back strongly in the second classical game, in which he was in control before an error of judgment allowed his American opponent to draw after 95 moves. Caruana thus maintained his lead, 9-3 (a classical win carried six points).

The Indian, however, showed his supremacy in the faster time controls. He won both the rapid games — worth four points each — and thus took an 11-9 lead going into the blitz section. Caruana was in a must-win situation in the last blitz game, but Praggnanandhaa drew it with perpetual checks, giving him a 15-13 match victory.

He is indeed looking unstoppable on the chessboard. This is his second major success at St. Louis this month. Just a fortnight ago, he had won the Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz in spectacular style. He won the tournament by a margin of 1.5 points, over his nearest rival Javokhir Sindarov, this year’s World championship challenger. Praggnanandhaa was leading on all five days of the event.

Before Saint Louis, he had recorded a career-best performance at Norway Chess in Oslo, where he emerged as the champion after beating the World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen twice in his hometown. The five-time World champion has often spoken highly of him and once even named him as the player closest to him in style.

That is indeed high praise. Pravin Thipsay, India’s third Grandmaster, believes Praggnanandhaa has earned it. “He has a great sense of what is required to win, and it is not about a better position or a complex position,” Thipsay tells The Hindu over the phone from Mumbai. “He has a knack of where that initiative is and goes for non-simplification like Carlsen. And he goes beyond the book and is a very active player even when the positions are equal. He has become a very strong player practically.”

Praggnanandhaa’s recent successes have come after he went through one of the worst periods of his career. He was so badly out of form in the year’s most crucial event – the Candidates tournament in Cyprus, where he was placed seventh in a field of eight.

If he continues to play like this, he could be one of the favourites for the next Candidates. “Yes, he will be a great force,” says Thipsay.

World.title: Nepal flash floods LIVE: Death toll rises to 579; nearly 2,000 people still missing
World.content:
The death toll in the Nepal flash floods touched 579 on Friday (August 28, 2026), even as the search for nearly 2,000 missing people continued for the third day after the disaster struck.

Fears of a second wave of flash floods loomed large in Nepal after authorities issued a fresh warning on Friday (August 28, 2026) following an increase in the water level in the Bhotekoshi River area. The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said the rise in the water level at the same site raised the risk of another flood in the area.

WATCH | Why did the flash floods happen in Nepal?

At least 320 Indians remain missing, and around 400 others are stranded on the Chinese side following devastating flash floods along the Nepal-Tibet border, and India is ready to extend all possible help to Kathmandu in its rescue efforts, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said on Friday (August 28, 2026).

MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said 96 Indian nationals who were stranded on the Chinese side have safely crossed over to Nepal by land route. Twenty-one Indians arrived in New Delhi this afternoon, a day after they reached Kathmandu from the flood-affected areas of Nepal, he said.

Also Read | Danger from above: On the Nepal flood

A preliminary assessment suggested the collapse of a high-altitude glacier in Nepal was behind the mudslides and floods along the Nepal-China border, said China’s Foreign Ministry. Chinese authorities said 555 tourists had been evacuated from Gyirong county in Tibet. As of today, Chinese authorities had confirmed five deaths but added that more than 558 people were still missing.

World.title: Delhi HC issues show-cause notice to social media user over ‘contemptuous’ videos
World.content:
The Delhi High Court has issued a show-cause notice to a social media user, asking him to explain why contempt proceedings should not be initiated over YouTube videos allegedly containing contemptuous remarks against a sitting judge in connection with the collapse of a multi-storey building in Said-ul-ajab in May.

A Bench of Justices Prathiba M. Singh and Vikas Mahajan also declined to recall its June 8 order directing social media platforms to block the accounts and handles of Kapil Kakar.

The proceedings stem from a petition filed by the Delhi High Court Bar Association (DHCBA), which sought criminal contempt action against Mr. Kakar over videos in which he allegedly held a sitting high court judge responsible for the building collapse that claimed six lives.

According to the DHCBA, Mr. Kakar uploaded several videos on social media platforms containing allegations against the judge, who had allegedly earlier dealt with a case concerning illegal construction in the building.

On June 8, the court directed social media platforms to remove the offending links and block Mr. Kakar’s accounts and handles.

Mr. Kakar subsequently moved an application seeking recall of the direction, contending that the order directing the blocking of his accounts amounted to a “wide relief”.

However, in its August 20 order, the two-judge Bench noted that after the June 8 direction, Mr. Kakar had uploaded another video in which he allegedly stated that new social media accounts would be created to upload further videos.

The court observed that the video was uploaded after the DHCBA’s petition had been served on him and indicated that he was aware of the proceedings and anticipated that his existing accounts could be blocked.

In these circumstances, the Bench held that its earlier direction to block Mr. Kakar’s social media accounts was “fully justified” and did not warrant recall.

The court had earlier directed the removal of the videos, observing on June 8 that the allegations made in them were “absolutely scandalous” and “contumacious”, and amounted to a direct interference with the administration of justice.

World.title: 22 minors molested in ashram shala, accused arrested
World.content:
A helper at Temba ashram school in the Thane district’s Shahapur region was arrested on August 26 for allegedly molesting 22 minor female students, a police official said on Friday (August 28, 2026).

The cook identified as Ganpat Gavli (35) is allegedly a repeat offender. According to Thane police, in 2024, he allegedly sexually molested a girl at another ashram shala. Gavli was on bail in the previous case when he joined Shahapur ashram shala as helper to the cook.

On August 24, a 10th-grade student raised a complaint against Ganpat, saying Gavli cornered her and tried to sexually assault her. “21 other girls came forward, raising the indecent behaviour of the accused during the investigation,” a Thane police official said. He was arrested on Wednesday (Aug 26, 2026).

Police have filed a case under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act and arrested the accused. The Integrated Tribal Development Project (ITDP) officer Tejaswini R. Galande, said, “The accused is a repeated offender and previously worked at an ashram school in Aghai. He was 10 months away from his retirement.”

Before joining the ashram school in Temba, he was working at Moroshi Ashram school in Murbad. Police are investigating as to who appointed him, and why he was appointed despite having a criminal record.

World.title: Ritabrata Banerjee-led TMC faction demands immediate students’ union polls in colleges
World.content:
West Bengal Leader of Opposition Ritabrata Banerjee-led Trinamool Congress group on Friday (August 28, 2026) accused the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government of not taking any initiative to hold student union elections and demanded immediate polls in all colleges and universities in the State.

“Our only demand is elections to students’ bodies in all colleges and universities, as otherwise the students’ movement will be hampered. There should also be an upper age limit for those holding the post of student leaders in the party,” he said while addressing the foundation day programme of the students’ wing of the TMC faction led by him.

Mr. Banerjee demanded that the government make a clear statement on whether it will conduct the students’ union election or not. He said that BJP must work on their promises instead of following former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee.

“Mamata Banerjee herself was a product of students’ union. However, she never conducted the union election. BJP came to the power by capitalising on the mistakes of the previous government. Now they must hold the students union election across the state,” he said.

Mr. Banerjee also alleged that the BJP government had nominated its MPs and MLAs to college governing bodies. He said such acts showed that the ruling party had not been able to shed the “ills” of the previous CPI(M) and Mamata Banerjee-led governments.

Student union elections in West Bengal have been in a limbo for the last five years. A PIL was also filed in the Calcutta High Court last year demanding the resumption of campus polls. While the state government stated it is willing to hold elections, it claimed that individual colleges and universities have failed to take adequate initiative. For the last two years, students of Jadavpur University staged protests demanding holding of elections, which have been withheld in the institution for five years.

Meanwhile, the High Court had directed the State government to lock up union rooms in colleges where there was no recognised student body or where student union elections had not taken place recently. It also observed that the governing bodies of higher education institutions in the State should be freed from political influence and should include renowned academicians.

While several Trinamool leaders have been part of the governing bodies of many public universities during their regime, the new BJP government, has appointed MLAs and MPs belonging to the party as presidents of governing bodies in across 247 government-aided colleges across the State.last week.

A notification issued by the West Bengal Higher Education Department pointed out that president of college governing body have been appointed for 247- state run colleges.

Some of the instances include BJP leaders being appointed as heads of college governing bodies, including Health Minister Sharadwat Mukherjee being appointed as the president of the governing body of East Kolkata Girls College. Minister of State for Fire Services Kaushik Chowdhury has been appointed as the head of college managing committee Raiganj B.Ed College.

Union Minister of State and Balurghat MP Sukanta Majumdar has been made president of the governing body of Balurghat College and Speaker of West Bengal Assembly Rathindra Bose as president of Coochbehar College among others.

State Higher Education Minister Jagannath Chattopadhyay said that there is nothing unusual in these appointments. The Minister said that those who have a bachelor’s degree have been made presidents of college governing bodies.

World.title: Government to launch recreational centres for senior citizens: Delhi CMO
World.content:
The Delhi government will launch the ‘Vayo Anand’ scheme for senior citizens, under which recreational centres will be developed for senior citizens where they can play indoor games, meet and interact with one another and take part in social activities, the Chief Minister’s Office (CMO) said on Friday (August 28, 2026).

The recreational centres will provide senior citizens with facilities such as indoor games, including carrom and ludo, seating arrangements, fans, coolers, televisions and computers. Newspapers, magazines and books will also be kept at the centres and yoga and meditation classes will also be organised for senior citizens, as per the CMO.

The government will provide financial assistance of ₹2.4 lakh to organisations to such recreational centres.

Chief Minister Rekha Gupta said senior citizens of Delhi are an invaluable asset to society and that ensuring their dignity, health, active lifestyle and social engagement is a priority of her government.

“The recreational centres will remain open for at least five days a week and a minimum of seven hours a day. These centres will operate between 7 a.m. and 8 p.m. The centres will have adequate ventilation and toilet facilities,” an official statement said.

Keeping the convenience of senior citizens in mind, preference will also be given to centres located on the ground floor or in buildings equipped with lifts. Priority will also be given to organising programmes for women, persons with disabilities and transgender senior citizens.

In addition, the centres will remain in contact with nearby police stations and hospitals for quick assistance in case of an emergency. Under the scheme, recreational centres must have at least 200 members aged 60 years or above, as per the statement.

World.title: 'Profound consequences': Indus Water Treaty must not be weaponised, FM Dar warns India
World.content:
WASHINGTON: Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Friday warned that any attempt to deprive Pakistan of waters “rightfully allocated to it” under the Indus Waters Treaty would have “profound consequences for regional peace and security”.

The IWT has come under strain since India announced in 2025 that it was placing its treaty obligations in abeyance. The announcement followed an attack on tourists in occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam that killed 26 tourists — an incident New Delhi blamed on Islamabad without evidence. For its part, Pakistan strongly denied the allegations and called for a neutral investigation.

In his virtual address to a Washington seminar on “The Indus Waters Treaty: South Asian Security at the Crossroads”, he declared that Pakistan would strongly safeguard its “legitimate rights and interests” under the treaty and international law.

FM Dar said the 1960 agreement remained “valid, binding and fully operative” despite India’s unilateral decision in April 2025 to place it “in abeyance”.

“The treaty contains no provision permitting either party to unilaterally suspend or place it in abeyance,” he said, adding that neither country could, “through a unilateral political declaration, extinguish obligations solemnly undertaken under international law.”

FM Dar said the issue went beyond the bilateral relationship, arguing that it concerned “the sanctity of treaties” and “confidence in international law”.

“If solemn treaty obligations can simply be set aside whenever political relations deteriorate, the very purpose of concluding the treaties is undermined,” he said.

He also stressed that geography made cooperation unavoidable, noting that “states cannot alter the direction in which rivers flow”.

“That is precisely why rules matter,” FM Dar said, urging the international community to preserve treaty-based water governance in South Asia.

The foreign minister further said the treaty had survived wars, military crises, diplomatic breakdowns and prolonged political tensions for more than six decades because both countries had understood that water on which “hundreds of millions of lives depend” was too fundamental to be subjected to fluctuations in political relations.

“Today, however, that principle faces its gravest challenge,” he said.

FM Dar said Pakistan’s position was clear and consistent and that treaty-based proceedings had continued despite India’s assertion of “abeyance”, reinforcing the principle that “unilateral action cannot displace an agreed legal framework”.

Pakistan has pursued arbitration over disputes concerning Indian hydroelectric projects on the Western Rivers, particularly Kishenganga and Ratle.

The Court of Arbitration at The Hague has continued proceedings, with earlier rulings addressing its jurisdiction and questions concerning the interpretation and application of the treaty.

The treaty allocates the three eastern rivers to India and the three western rivers, including the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab, primarily to Pakistan, subject to specified Indian uses.

FM Dar said resorting to the Permanent Indus Commission, a neutral expert or a Court of Arbitration “is not an act of confrontation” but “the implementation of the very legal framework to which both countries agreed and are bound”.

“Pakistan has consistently sought to resolve differences through dialogue, diplomacy and the mechanisms provided under the Treaty,” he said.

He said the dispute was especially serious because Pakistan’s agriculture, food security, energy production, livelihoods and economic development depended heavily on the Indus River system.

“The Indus Basin is the lifeline of more than 250 million Pakistanis,” Dar said. “Water security for Pakistan is therefore inseparable from economic security, food security and, ultimately, national security.”

Against this backdrop, he warned that unilateral interference with the treaty could affect not only South Asian stability but also create “a dangerous precedent for treaty relations everywhere”.

“International agreements derive their value from certainty and predictability,” FM Dar said. “If solemn treaty obligations can simply be set aside whenever political relations deteriorate, the very purpose of concluding the treaties is undermined.”

He linked the dispute to climate change, saying Pakistan was already among the world’s most water-stressed countries and faced changing precipitation patterns, glacial retreat, floods, droughts and increasing hydrological variability.

“These realities should compel greater and stronger cooperation,” he said, calling for improved data-sharing, sustained technical engagement and greater transparency.

“But,” he added, “adaptation cannot mean abandonment of agreed legal rights and obligations”.

Dar added that the treaty’s dispute-settlement architecture had been designed precisely to withstand disagreements between the two countries.

“The answer to disagreement was therefore built into the Treaty itself: dialogue, technical engagement and lawful dispute resolution,” he said.

The foreign minister also emphasised that treaty implementation “was never made contingent upon political convenience”.

For Pakistan, he said, the preferred approach remained “law over unilateralism, dialogue over confrontation, and cooperation over coercion”.

At the same time, Dar sought to make clear that Islamabad considered its water rights a matter of vital national importance.

“Any attempt to deprive Pakistan of the waters rightfully allocated to it under the Indus Waters Treaty would have profound consequences for regional peace and security,” he said.

“Pakistan will safeguard its legitimate rights and interests under the treaty and international law.”

Dar further stated that the IWT had demonstrated for more than 65 years that Pakistan and India could insulate a vital shared resource from their wider political relationship.

“That achievement should not be dismantled. It should be preserved,” he said.

He proposed three principles for the way forward: that the treaty be “respected and implemented in letter and spirit”; that all questions, differences and disputes be addressed through its mechanisms; and that Pakistan and India restore and strengthen “technical engagement, transparency and data-sharing”.

“These are not unreasonable demands,” Dar said. “They are the requirements of an agreement solemnly concluded by two sovereign states and sustained for more than six decades.”

He also invoked Pakistan’s recent diplomatic role in facilitating dialogue during the US-Iran crisis, saying the effort reflected Islamabad’s belief that difficult disputes should ultimately be addressed through “engagement, diplomacy and peaceful settlement”.

“Pakistan seeks to be a force for peace and stability, in South Asia and beyond,” he said.

Dar concluded by urging that the Indus remains “a source of life, livelihood and civilisation, not a fault line for confrontation”.

“Shared waters must never be weaponised,” he said. “They should remain a bridge between nations, governed by law, sustained through cooperation, and protected for generations to come.”

World.title: Govt cuts petrol price by Rs0.58, HSD by Rs0.17
World.content:
The government on Friday reduced the price of petrol by Rs0.58 per litre and high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs0.17 per litre.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs342.02 per litre while HSD will cost Rs371.44 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

According to a Petroleum Division notification, the new prices will be applicable from Aug 29 to Aug 31.

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Earlier, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

The government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

World.title: Nepal flood death toll rises to 579, nearly 2,000 still missing: disaster authority
World.content:
Nepal’s disaster authority on Friday put the number of people missing after devastating floods at 1,924, two days after the disaster killed at least 579 people in the country.

The number of missing includes 517 foreigners, as well as 933 workers on hydropower projects on the rivers where a wall of water powered down on Wednesday morning, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

Rescue teams used heavy machinery to dig through mud and debris in Nepalese towns devastated by a flash flood two days ago, as hopes of finding survivors faded and officials worked to reduce the risk of further catastrophic flooding.

The flood ripped through villages and valleys, destroying power stations, roads and bridges along a route that links Kathmandu with Lhasa in Tibet and is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.

Authorities in Nepal used helicopters to search for survivors and drop emergency supplies to thousands cut off in towns and valleys while emergency services, some using sniffer dogs, recovered dozens of bodies swept down into the plains.

Around 320 Indian nationals are still missing in the aftermath of the devastating flash flood, a spokesperson for India’s foreign ministry said, adding that at least 400 were stranded but safe on the Chinese side, while another 96 had crossed into Nepal by land.

Rescuer help women to move through a muddy road following flash floods and a mudslide in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal on August 28, 2026. —Reuters

Dibga Tamang was among the last people rescued from the hard-hit town of Rasuwa on Thursday, airlifted along with three others to an army camp in Nuwakot.

“All of our people have gone. They are dead,” Tamang said. “I have no one left waiting for me. Everything and everyone is gone. The end.”

The sheer amount of water and debris stirred up now risks triggering a further disaster.

Nepal’s disaster management authority warned that a lake formed by debris blocking the Bhotekoshi River was rising and at risk of bursting, while on the other side of the border China said that some three million cubic metres of water, the equivalent of about 1,200 Olympic-sized swimming pools, was expected to flow into an already dammed lake over the next three days.

There is a high risk the lake could breach, with peak flow expected around September 1, Chinese state media said, citing the water resources ministry.
