World.title: Georgian minister quits politics shortly after ex-PM’s accusations
World.content:
Georgian minister quits politics

Georgia’s Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze is stepping down from his post and leaving politics. He announced the decision at a briefing at the government administration, saying he wanted to devote more time to his family.

Until April 2026, Mamuka Mdinaradze served as head of the State Security Service. On 21 April, he was appointed deputy prime minister and state minister for the coordination of law enforcement agencies. On 29 July, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that Mdinaradze would take up the post of state minister for regional policy. The new position was due to be created in September, and until then Mdinaradze was appointed regional development minister.

Mdinaradze said his 10 years in politics had been marked by hard work, service to his country and cooperation with the team of the ruling Georgian Dream party. At the briefing, he thanked party members and leaders, including its founder and honorary chairman, Bidzina Ivanishvili.

Mdinaradze said he had been considering leaving politics for the past several weeks and had made the decision on his own initiative before discussing it with Irakli Kobakhidze and Bidzina Ivanishvili. He said they initially disagreed with his decision, but he ultimately managed to convince both that it would be better for him.

Mdinaradze explained his decision to leave politics by saying he wanted to spend more time with his family. According to him, his children, aged nine and 13, had grown up with him largely absent.

The former minister stressed that his decision had not been prompted by any political or personal crisis. He also said there was no need for him to remain involved in regional development, as the ruling team had other leaders capable of overseeing the area.

Mdinaradze did not rule out returning to politics one day, but said he would do so only if necessary.

“I will return only if the team really needs me and there is no other option,” he said.

Mamuka Mdinaradze

As for his future plans, Mdinaradze said he might try his hand in the private sector, including business, although he does not yet have any specific plans.

“Believe it or not, I haven’t thought about it. Perhaps I’ll try my hand in business,” Mdinaradze said.

Reflecting on his 10-year political career, Mdinaradze said its intensity and the level of responsibility had not been easy for him, and that he now wanted to focus on the part of his life that he had put on the back burner for years.

Mamuka Mdinaradze’s announcement that he was leaving politics came after his name was mentioned in connection with serious allegations made by former Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili. Garibashvili, who is currently serving a prison sentence, alleged that he had been pressured “on Bidzina Ivanishvili’s orders”, with Mdinaradze acting as an intermediary, to confess to a corruption offence in order to prevent him from returning to politics in the future.

On 24 August, Garibashvili was charged with a new corruption offence. The charge carries a prison sentence of 11 to 15 years.

According to investigators, key testimony in the case was provided by former Defence Minister Juansher Burchuladze, who has also been convicted of a corruption offence. According to his testimony, of the 1.5m lari (around $555,000)received as a bribe from businessman Zurab Tukvadze, who won a tender for the Gori Military Hospital, Burchuladze personally handed 750,000 lari (around $277,000) in cash to Irakli Garibashvili in several instalments.

Garibashvili denies the allegations. He says the demand that he admit guilt was politically motivated and intended to limit his ability to return to politics in the future. It was in this context that he mentioned Mamuka Mdinaradze as an intermediary and alleged that the demand had been made on Bidzina Ivanishvili’s orders.

Mdinaradze did not address the allegations against him when explaining his decision to step down.

World.title: ‘No to occupation and de facto annexation’: Anti-annexation platform launched in Georgia
World.content:
Anti-annexation platform launched in Georgia

A new public association, the Anti-Annexation Platform, has been established in Georgia.

Its founders say the group will be non-partisan and apolitical, with its main goal being to oppose Russia‘s occupation and de facto annexation of Georgian territories through legal and peaceful means.

At the platform’s launch at the Tbilisi Marriott hotel, a declaration entitled “No to occupation and de facto annexation – yes to justice, peace and Georgia’s territorial integrity” was adopted.

According to the declaration, the platform brings together Georgian citizens who regard the country’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, the principles of international law, freedom and human dignity as core values.

The founders say that Russia’s occupation in any form, the de facto annexation of the Abkhazia and Tskhinvali regions, support for separatism and forced demographic changes in the occupied territories constitute violations of international law and fundamental human rights.

The declaration also states that the organisation is ready to cooperate with members of any political party, regardless of their political affiliation.

Among the platform’s main objectives are supporting Georgia’s territorial integrity and sovereignty and promoting a legal assessment of Russia’s continuing occupation and de facto annexation.

The group plans to work to protect the rights of internally displaced people and refugees from the occupied territories, prepare legal research and analytical papers, and raise public awareness of developments in the occupied regions.

The platform also intends to cooperate with international partners, think tanks and diplomatic missions. Its activities will include organising conferences, discussions and educational events, as well as helping to protect the rights of people affected by the occupation and de facto annexation.

The platform supports targeted international sanctions against the leaders of the de facto regimes in the occupied regions and individuals involved in the annexation process. The declaration also calls for efforts to initiate international criminal proceedings.

The document stresses that the group’s activities will not be limited to the political agenda.

“We believe that the struggle against occupation and de facto annexation by the Russian Federation is not only a political issue. It is a struggle for justice, human dignity, historical truth and the security of future generations,” the declaration says.

According to its founders, the platform is based on the peaceful and legal resolution of conflicts, respect for international law and the protection of human rights.

“Russia’s de facto or de jure annexation will never become a legal reality, and borders changed by force will never acquire moral or legal legitimacy,” the declaration says.

The declaration was signed by the founders of the Anti-Annexation Platform:

World.title: Why China's censors are scrubbing videos of the Nepal-Tibet floods
World.content:
When security camera footage emerged on Wednesday of a wave of ice, mud and water smashing into the Tibet region, people across the world were horrified.

The distressing vision showed the China-controlled Tibet border crossing into Nepal being completely wiped out, along with dozens of people running for their lives.

It was harrowing to watch and gave undeniable proof of the severity of the Himalayan border disaster.

Nepal flash floods updates: Follow this story as it unfolds with our live blog.

But inside China the online video disappeared as quickly as it surfaced. Beijing's censors were at work.

China's censorship in effect

China's control of information is well-documented and common, including inside Tibet, which has been under Beijing's control since the 1950s.

An aerial view shows the damage following flash floods and a mudslide in the Tibet Autonomous Region. (Reuters: PLA Tibet Military District/Handout)

China's media only distributes state-approved messages, content and pictures, while communication channels inside the country, including peoples' social media, are heavily monitored.

Content that does not follow strict government regulations can be restricted or deleted by a team of censors, or by AI algorithms that flag "problematic" content.

Chinese authorities have provided scant detail of the people affected by in the Tibet region, only broadly confirming that 558 people were missing, including 260 foreign nationals. There was no breakdown of nationalities.

Giant glacial avalanche buries Nepal villages Climate scientists have been warning that the Himalayas are warming faster than the rest of the world, increasing the chances of a disaster of this scale.

They have also not provided any specific information about the settlements and villages in the areas that have been affected.

The top news story on Thursday's prime time bulletin of the state-operated CCTV news was a piece on the launch of a new book by President Xi Jinping.

That story also led the front page of the country's most popular newspaper, People's Daily, on Friday.

At the bottom of the front page was an article about 800 metres of roads in the landslide-stricken areas having been reopened, with pictures of rescue teams.

Throughout the disaster, China's main state media coverage has mostly relayed information about the size of the rescue attempt.

The difference between Tibet and Nepal

In Nepal, where a flash flood from the same disaster has killed hundreds and left hundreds more missing, the flow of information could not be more different.

Nepali authorities quickly released a detailed breakdown of suspected missing tourists, including their tour companies and their citizenship.

Families are looking for missing loved ones in the wake of the tragedy. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

They have also provided rolling updates on the situation.

The humans at the heart of this catastrophe have been put at the centre of the story, given the opportunity to share their harrowing accounts and experiences.

But it has been a challenge to hear the same stories from people in Tibet.

Undoubtedly it has been incredibly difficult for authorities to get accurate information from the site after communication channels were affected and road access impacted.

But the ability to hear from real people in Tibet is made near impossible due to China's reporting restrictions that block foreign journalists from independently travelling to the region.

According to Human Rights Watch, Beijing has restricted the free entry of foreign journalists into Tibet since 2007 — and seeking government permission to travel there is rarely granted.

Since the disaster hit I've made multiple formal requests to Chinese authorities for a permit to travel to Tibet to cover the unfolding disaster, either independently or with a state sponsored group.

The response has been a polite but consistent "no", with the foreign ministry telling me there are difficulties accessing the area and the potential for future disasters.

An untold tragedy

Officials from Nepal and China were forced to suspend operations for more than an hour on Friday due to the flooding risk posed by the overflowing barrier lake, but the search and rescue has now resumed.

Other foreign journalists have also made requests to officials to visit the area and have been knocked back.

Houses have been washed away or buried under the mud following the flash flood. (Reuters: Navesh Chitrakar)

The ABC has approached China's foreign ministry for a formal response on why foreign media are not being given access on the ground.

While the high risks and challenges of getting to the disaster zone are true, these are circumstances correspondents regularly experience and navigate around the world.

In Nepal, journalists have entered the country freely and been able to speak with witnesses, survivors and families of those impacted, although many affected areas are inaccessible due to damaged roads.

And China's information controls also extend to people inside Tibet.

Nepal-Tibet flood's destruction Satellite imagery over the Nepal-Tibet areas hit by floods show buildings, bridges, and homes completely wiped from the map.

Residents in the country are unable to communicate freely with foreign journalists because, according to Human Rights Watch, everyone is required to install mandatory phone apps with built-in government surveillance.

Human Rights Watch has documented countless examples of people being harassed, arrested or in trouble with authorities for communication their government does not like.

Activists group the International Campaign for Tibet (ICT) says that means many people are too scared to post on social media or share news about the disaster because they fear punishment from Chinese officials.

The result, according to Ryan Fioresi from ICT, is a situation where "only the Chinese government controls the information flow".

"In a disaster situation that means that local residents, afraid of punishment, are not posting about where people are trapped or where the damage is the worst," he said.

"If people are afraid to share that information, or if their posts are removed, potentially useful information may not reach families, relief workers or the wider public."

Several smaller Chinese media outlets, which are also state media, were able to get to the site and initially published interviews with some witnesses.

But within hours those articles were taken down.

In China there are still some people clearly desperate for information beyond what is presented by state-sanctioned news channels.

The ABC has seen some people in China who have posted on social media asking for help to access information that was blocked on the mainland.

One person had a relative working at a construction site near where the disaster struck in Tibet and wanted to know what had happened there.

They were shocked when people outside China managed to inform them the entire construction site had been flattened.

China's tight control of information is not surprising but it can carry different ramifications in a disaster.

Because in an effort to restrict what is getting out, Beijing runs the risk of scrubbing the very real, and desperate, calls for help from affected communities.

World.title: Street artists turn rusting opal machinery into outback spectacle
World.content:
The vast flat plains of outback NSW are not normally associated with the explosive visuals of street art covering Melbourne's laneways.

But acclaimed artist John Murray's love of both places plans to change that.

He has started turning discarded mining equipment in a remote north-west NSW town into a canvas for street artists from across the country.

The artist behind this agitator was inspired by the iridescent colours of opals that Lightning Ridge is famous for. (Supplied: WorksByNathan)

Known for his own colourful murals across regional New South Wales and Queensland, Murray invited street artists to Lightning Ridge to paint old "agitators" — the mixing drums once used by miners to sift soil in the search for opals.

"It's mainly set up just to promote street art," Murray said.

" I've met all these awesome artists in the street art scene and want to bring them to Lightning Ridge. "

John Murray's iconic emu motif graces one side of a discarded agitator … (Supplied: WorksByNathan)

… while his wife and fellow artist Viki painted the other in a nod to local wildlife. (Supplied: WorksByNathan)

From mines to masterpiece

The agitators-cum-canvases were all donated for the project, Murray said.

The retired drum mixers are scattered around Lightning Ridge, mostly scrapped or left to rust in paddocks.

"The agitators are all old, abandoned mixers from the opal mines," Murray said.

Visiting artists are given a blank canvas to work with as part of John Murray's art agitator project. (Supplied: WorksByNathan)

Unlike most public art projects, the artists were not given a brief, and there was no committee sign-off.

"There are no gatekeepers on the project, so they can paint whatever they want," Murray said.

"It's an opportunity to do free-form street art."

So far, six of a planned 20 agitators have been painted by artists Manda Lane, Joanne Travis (N2O), James Wilson, Lukas Kasper, Oli Ruskid, and John and his wife Viki, a fellow artist.

Murray said a goal was to host a 50/50 split of women and men to support the growing cohort of female street artists.

John Murray wanted to give artists the opportunity to paint whatever they liked. (Supplied: WorksByNathan)

"The women are awesome," he said.

"It used to be such a male-dominated field, and it's great to see more women coming through."

He and Viki have self-funded the effort, with his estimated final cost expected to be around $150,000.

Visiting artists are covered for around four nights' accommodation, meals, and $500 towards fuel costs.

They are also shown around the town and given some materials like the base coat and finish for their agitator.

Yabbies and the bright outback night sky feature on Lukas Kasper's agitator in Lightning Ridge. (Supplied: Lukas Kasper)

Yabbies under a night sky

An artist who had already made the trip was Melbourne-based Lukas Kasper, who met Murray in 2019 and had been inspired by his work.

Lukas Kasper has previously collaborated with John Murray on a water tower in Bourke. (ABC Western Plains: Catherine James)

"[John] came down many years ago now and wanted to paint in the laneways," the 32-year-old said.

"We painted heaps all through the city, all through Melbourne, and he basically became one of my best mates."

The pair have painted together several times, including working on a water tower in the nearby town of Bourke where Kasper assisted Murray with two other artists, Bob Barrett and Brian Smith.

"So when he pitched the idea of coming back, I couldn't get there quick enough," he said.

For his agitator, Kasper drew inspiration from a mural he had just finished in the western NSW town of Coonamble, where he had painted a series of yabbies.

Lukas Kasper painted a toilet block in Coonamble, south of Lightning Ridge, with a team of local artists. (Supplied: Lukas Kasper)

The other side of the toilet block in Coonamble. (Supplied: Lukas Kasper)

Murray told him local kids in Lightning Ridge often went yabbying in local dams and waterways.

"There's that little connection to the local space," Kasper said.

His finished design added a "galactic" flair, with a star-studded sky across the top — a nod to the outback sky he said he rarely got to see from Melbourne.

Lukas Kasper travelled from Melbourne to Lightning Ridge as part of the art agitators project funded by John Murray. (Supplied: WorksByNathan)

An open-air outback gallery

When finished, Murray envisioned the painted drums would be arranged as an open-air gallery in the region's renowned Three Mile opal field alongside the Opal Miners Hall of Fame.

Murray said visitors would be able to scan a QR code on each "agi" to learn about who donated the agitator and the artist who painted it.

"Nowhere else in the world would be able to do something like this," he said.

"There's just not that many agitators anywhere else in the world that could be given to something like this."

Artists are supported to come to Lightning Ridge by local artist John Murray to paint old mining agitators. (Supplied: WorksByNathan)

World.title: Push to declare garden favourite sold at Bunnings a weed
World.content:
These pretty, purple flowers with a deceptively pleasant name are becoming a problem in Australia.

Polygala, sold under innocent-sounding labels as "sweet pea", "Bellerine pea" and "parrot bush", is overtaking large tracts of Australia's coastline.

That has prompted the Invasive Species Council to nominate Polygala myrtifolia (also known as myrtle-leaf milkwort) as one of Australia's most significant weeds, even as potted examples continue to line shelves in retail stores.

Polygala is routinely sold at Bunnings and other retail chains.

Rows of potted milkwort, also known as polygala or "sweet pea", on sale at Bunnings. (ABC News: Gavin McGrath)

Invasive Species Council policy director Carol Booth said the thick shrub, originally from southern Africa, had colonised the south-eastern Australian coastline at the expense of native flora.

"It just takes over," Dr Booth explained.

" It forms a dense shrub layer which excludes native plants, mainly on and near the coast, but it also transforms the habitat and, through that, deprives native wildlife of important resources. "

Dr Carol Booth. (Supplied: Invasive Species Council)

The Invasive Species Council targeted Bunnings last year for stocking gazania seeds.

Gazania, banned in South Australia and recognised as an environmental weed in Victoria, Tasmania, Queensland, and New South Wales, is still permitted to be sold in most states.

ABC News found packets of gazania in a Victorian store when it discovered the rows of potted polygala.

Bunnings has confirmed Polygala myrtifolia and its hybrids are sold through nurseries and plant retailers across Australia but that it focused on selling hybrid polygala, which differs from Polygala myrtifolia.

The hardware and gardening retailer said it would continue to monitor invasive weed regulations, update its products accordingly and customers should read plant label descriptions before buying.

Gazania seeds for sale at Bunnings. (ABC News: Gavin McGrath)

A growing problem

Australia has a government-endorsed list of 32 Weeds of National Significance (WONS), which threaten the nation's agriculture and environment.

Dr Booth said the list needed updating to include milkwort and other plant varieties that threaten Australia's biodiversity.

At the very least, milkwort should be added to a list of plants banned for sale in Australia, he said.

"Unfortunately, this is fairly typical in Australia. Plant regulation in Australia is a complete mess," Dr Booth said.

"It's not aligned with risk, it's not focused on preventing most invasions and it's not in the public interest," he said.

Polygala is native to South Africa. (Supplied: Biosecurity SA)

The Invasive Species Council estimates about 3,000 introduced plant species have naturalised in Australia.

That means about one in nine species growing in the wild is not native to that area.

More than 1,000 are considered invasive, which means they cause harm to native species and ecosystems.

"Australia's got a huge weed problem. It's our most expensive land management problem, our most expensive nature conservation problem," Dr Booth said.

"Most plants that can cause harm out in the wild are still available for sale.

" It's leaving future generations an immense burden because a lot of plants still have a long way to spread. "

We will fight them on the beaches

The characteristics that make polygala popular with suburban gardeners as a ground-covering shrub – hardiness and an ability to survive and thrive in dunes, rocky outcrops, and other marginal environments – also ensure it is especially difficult to remove once established.

Volunteer groups, including Nepean Peninsula Landcare, are on the front line of efforts to control the invasive bush, and say it is an uphill battle.

Removing Polygala along the coastline is labour-intensive prompting calls for a biological solution. (Supplied: Invasive Species Council)

"If you come down to the Mornington Peninsula, you can't miss it. You don't have to look for it, it's everywhere," Nepean Peninsula Landcare volunteer John Dewhurst said.

"It is the most dominant plant through the coastal dune systems and all along the foreshore.

" When it gets an opportunity to thrive, it takes over the whole zone that it occupies. We call it 'the beast.' "

Polygala is found along Australia's southern coastline, from Western Australia through South Australia, Victoria and the New South Wales coast.

There are two ways to remove the weed, but each has its drawbacks.

Herbicides may be effective but are expensive and have the potential to damage native flora.

The most practical way to deal with milkwort is to remove it manually, which is time-consuming and exhausting for the volunteers.

Landcare volunteers manually removing milkwort along the southern Victorian coastline. (Supplied: Nepean Peninsula Landcare)

That's prompted Nepean Peninsula Landcare and the Invasive Species Council to investigate a potential biological control.

"We have engaged some expert scientists, both in Australia and South Africa, to try to find a biocontrol for Polygala," Mr Dewhurst said.

Nepean Peninsula Landcare volunteer John Dewhurst. (Supplied: Nepean Peninsula Landcare)

"It's called 'the Poly Gone project' and that involves locating insects or fungus in South Africa where it comes from that control it naturally.

"Whenever you mention the word 'biocontrol', people think cane toad, but there've been many, many successful biocontrols introduced into Australia, like the prickly pear moth.

"The research is being done in South Africa to ensure it's safe before something happens here."

More weeds of national significance

In 1999, Australia's federal and state governments nominated their original 20 weeds of national significance (WONS) that represented the greatest threat to Australian agriculture and the environment.

A further 12 were added in 2012.

Flowering Gazania (Gazania rigens) plants. (Supplied: Andrew Mitchell, Centre for Invasive Species Solutions)

The National Biosecurity Committee, made up of Australian Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry representatives, plus others from each state and territory government, was in the process of adding new weeds to the WONS list, said Dr Booth.

Those prioritised as potential weeds of national significance include:

African lovegrass (Eragrostis curvula)

European olive (Olea europaea)

Amazon frogbit (Limnobium laevigatum)

Ox-eye daisy (Leucanthemum vulgare)

Arum lily (Zantedeschia aethiopica)

Sea spurge (Euphorbia paralias)

Calotrope (rubber bush) (Calotropis procera)

Siam weed (Chromolaena odorata)

Giant rat's tail grass (Sporobolus pyramidalis)

Spanish heath (Erica lusitanica)

Harrisia (Harrisia martinii)

Tropical soda apple (Solanum viarum)

Neem tree (Azadirachta indica)

Wandering trad (Tradescantia fluminensis)

"The list will grow but it's only a very small proportion of the weeds that really are nationally significant, so it's ultimately the ones which state and territory governments agree to put some money into coordinating control," Dr Booth said.

"Unfortunately, we have got so many more than this small list of species that really warrant substantial control," he said.

World.title: Can frustrated voters today propel One Nation into WA's parliament?
World.content:
One Nation's growing support will be put to the test today, as Pauline Hanson's party goes head to head with Labor in a Western Australian by-election.

The poll in Secret Harbour, a beachside suburb south of Perth, will provide the clearest indication yet of any shift in the political landscape and if One Nation can turn frustration at major parties into seats in Parliament.

Who are the main candidates?

Georgia Tree Labor Read more Read more Secret Harbour has long been considered a safe Labor seat and the by-election was triggered by last month's retirement of high-profile minister Paul Papalia, who represented the electorate for almost two decades. So it is unsurprising the party was first out of the gates with their candidate, a former staffer to federal Resources Minister Madeleine King, and more recently a lobbyist with Woodside. Georgia Tree, 34, has been leaning into her working-class roots, pointing out her dad raised her on a single wage working in the area after her mum died when she was nine. "Labor built Medicare. My Mum's chemo would have bankrupted our family without it, and now Labor's building a brand new hospital in Mandurah," she said. "Dad's apprenticeship helped him turn his life around, and now Labor's made TAFE free." She's been criticised for living in Perth's northern suburbs, rather than her prospective electorate, telling The West Australian she had tried to find a home in the area but was "not prepared to pay in excess of market value". In 2023 she published Old Boy, a biography of her father's life, including his struggles with heroin addiction before turning his life around in WA's mining industry. Ryan Robertson Liberal Read more Read more The Liberals confirmed Ryan Robertson as their candidate on Saturday – a 35-year-old former submariner turned real estate agent and podcast host. The father of three is currently a City of Rockingham councillor, representing its Rockingham/Safety Bay ward since last year. Mr Robertson has a similar career background to Mr Papalia, with his LinkedIn profile stating he served in the navy between 2009 and 2021, during which time he was awarded Submariner of the Year. "I feel as if the people of Secret Harbour are not quite getting heard on issues that we truly believe matter to all of us," he said at his first press conference as a candidate. "Lots of promises, no delivery, and that's not something that sits comfortably with me." He said the three pillars of his campaign would be "listen, work hard, and deliver for the people of Secret Harbour". Pushed on how he would deliver from opposition, both he and leader Basil Zempilas said the opposition could often raise issues and force the government to act. The Nationals have confirmed they won't run in the seat, urging their supporters to back the Liberals instead. Luke Herdegen One Nation Read more Read more Gym owner and former champion weightlifter Luke Herdegen will be One Nation's candidate for the by-election. His LinkedIn profile shows he has been working in the fitness space since at least mid-2019, including as a coach and manager. One Nation likes its chances of winning the by-election and has been active in attacking Labor on social media with AI-generated content that focuses on Labor's "neglect of the seat". "Crime is up in the suburbs with the electorate, as is homelessness. Traffic for morning commuters is getting worse," leader Rod Caddies wrote in one post. "And despite spending billions on Metronet, they have failed to deliver the train station they promised you years and years ago." At the 2025 election, One Nation's candidate received 8.4 per cent of the primary vote, more than double the party's state-wide average. Rhi Davies Greens Read more Read more The Greens have described Rhi Davies as an "active community organiser, defence spouse of many years and a local mum of three teenagers". Concerns about the AUKUS submarine deal tying Australia to "Trump's war machine", the average renter in Secret Harbour spending more than 30 per cent of their income on rent and the "climate crisis" feature in her bio. "We want rents capped to give struggling families immediate relief, and we want housing built for local residents, rather than prioritising American AUKUS workers," she said in a statement. "We want cheap, clean energy delivered by a rapid transition to renewables. We want to stop AUKUS and Westport and protect Cockburn Sound." The Greens polled third in Secret Harbour at the 2025 election, with 8.8 per cent of the primary vote — lower than their state-wide average of 11.1 per cent. Craig Buchanan Legalise Cannabis Read more Read more Craig Buchanan works in the office of the Legalise Cannabis party's only MP, Brian Walker, as a research officer and senior adviser. He recently resigned from Rockingham City Council after six years of service and holds a PhD in literature from the University of Western Australia. Dr Buchanan said he will campaign for "sensible, evidence-based cannabis reform", having credited medicinal cannabis with giving him "freedom of choice" after being diagnosed with bowel cancer two years ago. "It's about the right to heal and function without the fear of outdated stigma or unfair legal repercussions," he said in a statement. His policy positions include repealing driving laws that criminalise patients for driving with trace amounts of cannabis in their system if they are not impaired and protecting medicinal cannabis patients from workplace discrimination.

Why is this important?

Analysis by WA state political reporter Keane Bourke

On paper, this by-election shouldn't be very interesting. It's choosing who will replace a retiring Labor veteran in an area the party has held for decades.

The difference this time is One Nation. Support for the party has been surging in the east, at least according to polling, and to a lesser extent here in the west.

If that's going to translate to a win anywhere in WA, Secret Harbour would be close to the top of the list.

Loading...

It takes in Perth's outer southern suburbs, with a growing population of young families moving into new housing developments.

Cost of living and housing have been key concerns which many voters would be feeling acutely.

Labor, who won the seat with a margin of 11.5 per cent at the last election, is also putting a strong emphasis on fighting One Nation, who are their real opponents here.

People often vote differently in by-elections which won't change the government, compared to general elections.

But this poll is still being watched nationally as a sign of how much of a threat One Nation can pose to Labor, and how both it, and the Liberals, will need to shape their campaigns to account for it.

What do locals think?

The hairdresser has long been a place to shoot the breeze, so it's no surprise that politics was the main topic of conversation at Emma Pender's salon ahead of the by-election.

Both Emma Pender (left) and her client Emma Chellew don't plan on voting Labor today. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

When the ABC visited the Golden Bay hairdressers, many clients voiced their frustration with Labor, which held the seat for almost two decades.

"I did vote for Labor in the past, but I feel really let down by them. I hope they change and start to listen to the community a bit more," Fabian Portese said.

Mr Portese always voted Labor but this time he's undecided. (ABC News: Lucy Murray )

Mr Portese has yet to make up his mind about who to vote for today, but for Ms Pender the choice is clear.

"I put Ryan [Liberal candidate] number one. That was purely because he was local," the hairdresser said.

The Liberal candidate for the Secret Harbour by-election, Ryan Robertson, is a Royal Australian Navy veteran. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

" He is listening to people and he is already aware a lot of the problems. "

Further along the coast, in Port Kennedy, long-time Labor voter Elaine Soltluisch is heading in a different direction.

"I used to be Labor, but I am just tired of it now. This area, down south, we don't get the attention," she told the ABC while watching her grandkids at the skate park.

Elaine Soltluisch says she's voting One Nation. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

"I have been here 30 years and never saw any change … it's too late.

" I'll vote for One Nation. I am tired of watching people go homeless. Labor is not for the general public, I don't think they're helping anyone. "

Labor has held the seat for almost 20 years, but the retirement of veteran MP Paul Papalia and growing frustration with the major parties has given One Nation an opening.

Labor in 'fight for our lives' as by-election opens door to One Nation assault Paul Papalia's resignation for family reasons sparks a by-election in the WA minister and Labor stalwart's southern Perth seat at a time when disgruntled voters are increasingly turning to One Nation.

It remains to be seen whether Pauline Hanson's party can get enough votes to turn this into its first ever lower house seat in Western Australia.

Where does the protest vote go?

Professor John Phillimore, director of the John Curtin Institute for Public Policy, said this by-election was a critical test for One Nation, leading into the state election in Victoria.

Professor John Phillimore says the nation's eyes will be on the by-election. (ABC News: Lucy Murray )

"From a Labor point of view, if the outer suburbs of Perth start falling to One Nation, that might ring some alarm bells in Victoria," he said.

"For the Liberals, it is a big issue for them, these outer suburban areas are traditional swinging seat territory where if a government is going to fall, the opposition picks up those seats."

Luke Herdegen is representing One Nation in the election. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

" In Victoria, is the opposition picking up those seats going to be the Liberal Party or One Nation? "

The Secret Harbour poll is the first time this year Senator Hanson's party has gone up against an incumbent Labor government.

The Australian Labor Party did not run a candidate in the Farrer by-election in New South Wales, which gave One Nation its first lower house seat in federal parliament.

One Nation candidate David Farley (left) and party leader Pauline Hanson celebrate victory in the Farrer by-election. (AAP: Bianca de Marchi)

In South Australia, two of the four seats One Nation won in a March election were taken directly from the Liberals, the others from Independents.

"There does seem to be momentum behind One Nation, so this will be a test of that momentum," Dr Phillimore said.

Whether this momentum can propel the so-called 'orange wave' to claim another seat, this time in Labor heartland, remains to be seen.

Polls close at 6pm WST.

World.title: What makes a 'real' daffodil? Prospective judges learn the ropes
World.content:
Judging daffodils at flower shows is not something Robert and Kerrie Goudsouzian ever thought they would do.

"It never crossed my mind, but now that we've dipped our toe in the water I guess we're learning so much more.

"And it just gives you a different appreciation for nature, for the flowers, the people who are involved in this," Ms Goudsouzian said.

" And it's just lovely. "

The Goudsouzians and about a dozen other daffodil lovers came together in Hobart's northern suburbs last weekend to learn more about how to judge daffodils at flower shows.

Internationally renowned daffodil breeder Rod Barwick took them through the main criteria for judging daffodils — condition, form, substance and texture, pose, colour, size and stem.

Participants were taken through the judging criteria. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

Passing around samples of daffodils cut from his garden nearby, Mr Barwick took the group through the basic form and terminology.

"A real daffodil has six petals," he said.

"Technically they are called perianth segments. Three of the segments have to be at the back, there should be three at the front."

"In front of the petals is what some times, if it's longish, is called a trumpet, if it's medium it's called a cup, if it's small it's called a crown.

"None of those words are terribly important because in daffodil [terms] it doesn't matter what shape it is, it's called a corona."

Some of the parts and features of a daffodil that judges look for. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke/Paul Yeomans)

The exception to the six-petal rule is double daffodils, which either have a doubling of the perianth or doubling of the corona.

'Like going to a Mr World contest'

Then came "the sex part of the evening".

Mr Barwick explained the female part of the flower, the stigma, was in the middle of the corona and around it were six anthers with pollen on them.

"If they are not intact, the flower can't be judged," he said.

" It's like going to a Mr World contest — if you remove the male bits, he's not going to get very far, is he? "

There are more than 26,000 cultivated varieties of daffodil, according to the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

The session was organised by Mr Barwick with his niece Janelle Noble, who is the president of the Claremont Flower Show Group.

In the lead-up to next weekend's Claremont spring flower show, Ms Noble said she and Mr Barwick wanted to make the most of a resurgence they are seeing in interest in flower shows.

Janelle Noble says "the interest is there" for daffodil judging. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

"I am really hoping that more people will get involved [in judging] and have a greater appreciation of daffodils," Ms Noble said.

"The interest is there and people are really keen to get on board and learn and enjoy."

Some of the miniature daffodil entries at last year's Claremont spring flower show. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

Mary Crowe and her husband Kevin have been judging daffodils for about 30 years.

They are among the judges at the Hobart Horticultural Society's early spring show, which continues today.

They started showing daffodils in the late 1980s before becoming judges.

Kevin and Mary Crowe are worried about where the next generation of daffodil judges will come from. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

"Rod Barwick [and fellow Tasmanian daffodil breeder the late] Harold Cross had a judging school which a number of us went to," Ms Crowe said.

She said the course was a mixture of theory and practical lessons and ran over three years.

" There are now fewer judges … we're wondering about how to get the next generation into judging with daffodils because most of us are getting a lot older. "

Getting started as a judge

Ms Crowe said the first thing a prospective judge should be doing is growing exhibition-type daffodils, sourced from specialist growers.

"It's a matter of going to shows, having a look, and if you're interested perhaps contacting some of the people there.

Mary Crowe has been judging for about 30 years. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

"We'll be around the show and we're always willing to chat to people and encourage them."

The Goudsouzians started by "off-siding" one of the judges and judging some of the minor classes at the Claremont shows a few years ago.

"It's a matter of getting out of your comfort zone, doing something different and learning something that you wouldn't ordinarily get exposed to," Mr Goudsouzian said.

As for Mr Barwick's judging session, they both said it had been valuable.

Daffodils are judged according to several criteria. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

"I now feel that, yes, we're getting some skills now.

"It's not just, 'oh that's pretty', 'oh that looks nice'. It's, 'ok does it meet these criteria'," Ms Goudsouzian said.

World.title: Council plans $15-25m bus stop upgrade amid anti-social behaviour concerns
World.content:
Massage shop manager Jim Ji says the sound of rowdy bus passengers is terrible for his business.

He said customers at Tai-Chi Traditional Massage in Launceston often arrived "hoping to fall asleep" and tended not to return if outside noise was too distracting.

Jim Ji is concerned about behaviour in the Launceston CBD. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

He is among many business owners on St John Street who have long been concerned that nearby bus stops are a lightning rod for antisocial behaviour, particularly among young, school-aged people.

Capri Launceston director Heidi Ellen said she shut the doors twice in a week recently because staff felt uncomfortable about behaviour outside.

"We definitely have customers talking about how they're afraid to come into our store, especially from about 2pm onwards," she said.

"It's getting out of hand."

Could new 'Step + Ride' be the solution?

The Launceston City Council recently advertised a design services tender for a "nation-first Step + Ride" to replace the current bus interchange, with an "indicative" construction budget of $15-25 million.

The Launceston City Council is considering a project that could cost $15-$25 million to upgrade these bus stops. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

It is the latest in a long line of plans designed to address issues at the bus stop, which some local business owners said were persisting, even though security guards had been employed to patrol the area since March.

Mayor Matthew Garwood said the aim was to "create a transport hub that works for the way people move around the city now and into the future".

When asked what would make it a "nation-first" project, a council spokesperson said it was "not aware of another facility described as a step and ride interchange facility".

Tender documents show council envisages a hub where commuters can park bikes and scooters or get lifts through ride-share apps, as well as catch buses.

The Launceston City Council is paying security guards to patrol the St John St bus interchange. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

"Stepping as a movement can relate to walking or stepping on and off a bus," it states.

"While 'ride' is a term that can mean riding a bus, riding a bike or ride-sharing."

The chosen designer will be asked to design two potential "Step + Ride" locations — either keeping the bus stops where they are, or moving some of them two blocks north.

The Launceston City Council is currently considering only minor changes to the bus interchange. (Supplied: Launceston City Council)

Council is expected to vote on the exact location in October.

The tender brief states "the project will deliver safer, more attractive, and people-focused bus facilities", which will improve safety through "clear sightlines, passive surveillance and strong day and night presence".

Doubts over plan

Businesses frustrated over the anti-social behaviour doubt whether the planned bus stop redevelopment is the answer.

"I don't think we should spend $15 million or $25 million on that because that's too much," Mr Ji said.

The St John St bus interchange has long been blamed for antisocial behaviour. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Launceston City Councillor Tim Walker also questioned the price tag.

"It was a shock to me when it was pointed out in the tender documents that $15 to $25 million was the price range that we're talking about," he said.

Tim Walker worries antisocial behaviour will persist following the planned bus stop redevelopment. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Asked whether the state government should contribute to the project, a Launceston City Council spokesperson said that was up to them but noted bus interchange funding committed at the 2024 state election never eventuated.

"City of Launceston was disappointed that the state committed $12 million at the state election but then later reneged on this promise," a spokesperson said.

A state government spokesperson said this funding commitment was contingent on the bus stop being relocated to Paterson Street, but that project fell over.

They said it remains committed to working with the council on its revised plan for Launceston interchange.

Cr Walker also questioned whether millions would be spent upgrading the stops, only to have the issues persist.

"Antisocial behaviour, whether it's at bus stops or anywhere else, is an issue that needs to be addressed as a whole of community," he said.

" The bus stops are not going to address that — moving them, changing them, it's not going to make a difference. "

Call for broader strategies

Data from Tasmania Police showed total criminal offences in Launceston were down last financial year, compared to the year before.

It also showed offending among 10 to 17-year-olds had reduced, with 230 total offences last year in that cohort, compared to 337 the year prior.

The age group with the highest level of offending was consistently 25 to 34-year-olds.

The Launceston City Council has commissioned multiple reports which advised leaving the bus stop where it is. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

"Police will continue to work closely with council, local businesses and the broader community to identify appropriate pathways for early intervention and remain proactive in their visibility and interdiction with recidivist offenders," he said.

Vicky Nagy, a senior lecturer in criminology at the University of Tasmania (UTAS), said young people were often blamed for issues because they were highly visible, due to being loud or wearing school uniforms, when they were not doing anything wrong.

But she said if antisocial behaviour was an issue, a broader approach was likely needed.

"Improving sight lines and redesigns of things like bus shelters and where stops are can be beneficial because people feel safer in that sort of area," she said.

" But again, it doesn't actually deal with the issues that underlie it, which are oftentimes social issues. "

Michael Guerzoni, another senior lecturer in criminology at UTAS, agreed focusing on the root causes underlying antisocial behaviour was critical.

Michael Guerzoni says authorities should focus on underlying causes for antisocial behaviour. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

Dr Guerzoni said the focus should be whether there were youth centres where young people could meet friends, if there were enough supports for families or opportunities for young people without "being under constant surveillance".

Mr Ji, meanwhile, suggested there were other ways council could support local businesses, suggesting a program to attract new operators, rebates for customers or a reduction in parking fees.

World.title: Former ASIO agent offers to give evidence to Bondi royal commission
World.content:
A former ASIO agent who claims to have warned the domestic spy agency about the Bondi gunmen years before last December's terror attack says he is willing to give evidence to a royal commission from overseas.

The former agent, known as Marcus, worked with ASIO to infiltrate Islamic State networks in Western Sydney years before the attack.

He told the ABC's Four Corners earlier this year that the agency was warned about both Naveed and Sajid Akram in 2019 and the Bondi terror attack "was a result of a set of errors and a disregard for information".

ASIO has previously said it stood by its assessment at that point in time, and had labelled Marcus "disgruntled and unreliable", which Marcus rejects.

The former agent told the ABC that ASIO had been warned in 2019 about Naveed (right) and Sajid Akram. (Supplied)

The former agent has been living abroad, and has been seeking a visa to return to Australia to give evidence onshore, due to the sensitivity of his evidence and additional legal protections he had gained from being on Australian soil.

But his visa applications have been rejected twice, both times on the grounds that immigration authorities are unconvinced he intends to stay temporarily.

Marcus has previously sought protection and resettlement in Australia.

Earlier this week, Commissioner Virginia Bell SC used the final scheduled day of hearings at the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion to describe the efforts made to hear Marcus's evidence.

She said the royal commission had been in contact with his solicitors, and had been working with the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) on arrangements for him to speak with the commission's lawyers from overseas.

The DFAT officials had worked to find a venue abroad that Marcus could reach, where they could provide a secure line.

Ms Bell says the royal commission has been in contact the former agent's solicitors. (ABC News)

Last week, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Marcus was free to give evidence in public, saying ASIO had no concerns about his evidence, but Ms Bell said the royal commission would not hear his evidence in open hearings due to the risk of prejudicing separate criminal proceedings.

She said that at that point, Marcus had not yet taken up that offer.

The ABC has now been told that Marcus does intend to give evidence from overseas, both to the royal commission and to separate NSW Police investigations into the terror attack, and has reached out through solicitors.

In a statement to the ABC, a spokesperson for the royal commission pointed to Ms Bell's comments earlier in the week, and said it was yet to hear from Marcus.

"The Commissioner noted that the Commission has been in contact with his solicitors and has proposed arrangements for a call with Counsel Assisting. Marcus has not taken up that offer to date," it said.

"The Commissioner noted that regardless of whether Marcus chooses to cooperate further with the Commission, she is satisfied that she is currently in a position to give a full and fair account of the Term of Reference which asks whether in relation to the Bondi Hannukah attack our intelligence and our law enforcement agencies operated or performed to maximum effectiveness."

While the commission has finished its scheduled hearings, it has the capacity to take additional evidence should it decide that is necessary.

Whistleblower advocates call for additional protections

Mr Shipton says the former agent needs a number of reassurances if he decides to give evidence. (ABC News: Nick Haggarty)

Gabriel Shipton from the Information Rights Project, which has been supporting Marcus while he is abroad, said the royal commission needs to put some protections in place if he is to give evidence from abroad.

"If Marcus decides to give his testimony from abroad, the royal commission has to ensure that it's done in a way that is secure, and in a way that ensures his safety from prosecution," he said.

" And it has to ensure that he's not gonna be prosecuted in future, and that he's not breaking the laws of any other country by giving his testimony. So he needs those assurances. "

Mr Shipton said it was disappointing Marcus could not give his evidence in Australia, as he had sought to do.

"The most secure and safest way for Marcus to still give his testimony is in person, in the same circumstances that was afforded to other ASIO agents who gave their testimony in secret to the commission."

World.title: Melbourne council ditches e-bike and e-scooter trial amid complaints
World.content:
An inner-Melbourne council has voted to scrap a trial of shared e-bikes and e-scooters, marking the end of shared e-scooters north of the Yarra River.

Darebin councillors voted to scrap the trial, which had been running for six months in the municipality's southern suburbs of Northcote, Fairfield and Alphington.

Council officers found there had been 14,725 trips over the six months, an average of 98 trips a day, travelling an average 2.15 kilometres.

But Mayor Emily Dimitriadis told a council meeting that 93 per cent of feedback was negative.

"Throughout the trial, residents continued reporting e-scooters and e-bikes blocking footpaths, parked incorrectly and creating accessibility issues, riders with no helmets, e-scooters and e-bikes travelling on footpaths," she said.

Emily Dimitriadis says the community has rejected the scheme. (Instagram: Emily Dimitriadis)

Officers found most people who used the trial used it to connect to public transport, and that usage peaked overnight.

But parking the bikes and scooters was a problem when officers inspected 279 allocated parking bays.

"Untidy parking including non-compliant, toppled or misplaced devices was observed at 30 per cent of all bays," a council report presented at the meeting said.

Cr Dimitriadis said the scheme also went over budget, despite the operator, Lime, paying Darebin $18,000.

"Council not only spent $50,000 to set up the trial, it also spent more money administering and managing the trial," she said.

Residents had raised issues with e-bikes and e-scooters being left in the middle of footpaths. (Supplied: Matthew Zammit)

Environmental and transport benefits argued

Darebin resident Matthew Zammitt organised a petition against the scheme, which attracted 1,227 signatures.

He told the meeting he had had trouble negotiating around abandoned e-bikes with a pram, with bikes blocking footpaths, driveways and entrances to train stations.

"It's the modern-day monorail," he said, referencing an episode of The Simpsons where the city invests in a transport scheme that ultimately fails.

" Councils are being duped into thinking that this solves transport woes. "

In an episode of The Simpsons, the townspeople are convinced to spend millions of dollars on a monorail rather than fixing Main Street. (Supplied: 20th Century Fox)

But former Darebin mayor Suzanne Newton, who brought the initial scheme to Darebin, told the meeting the scheme had many benefits for the climate and getting people out of cars.

"Particularly for the so-called last mile journey, to get people home from the train or tram or bus," she said.

She said there was some "pushback", but the trial also showed benefits, including nearly half of trips started or ended at a public transport stop, and 37 per cent were said to replace a car journey.

Councillor Ruth Jelley called on the council to continue the trial, arguing the climate benefits should not be overlooked — council officers found riders saved approximately 1.16 tonnes of carbon emissions.

"How can we call ourselves climate leaders if we fail to deliver on key actions in our climate emergency plan?" she said.

"We are now falling behind NSW and other cities around the world in supporting micromobility through shared schemes such as this.

"Short-termism is killing our climate leadership ambitions, and it's also killing our planet."

Ninety-three per cent of feedback council received about e-bikes and e-scooters was negative. (Supplied: Matthew Zammit)

In July, Yarra council ended a six-year shared e-bike scheme with Lime, saying the operator refused to take responsibility for dumped bikes.

The City of Melbourne dumped its e-scooter scheme in 2024, although there are 500 shared e-bikes available in the city through Lime.

Across the river, in Port Philip, Lime and Neuron operate shared e-scooter schemes, with more than 1.5 million trips since 2022, according to the council, while bayside Frankston, south of Melbourne, ended its micromobility trial in 2024.

In December 2025, the regional city of Ballarat voted to continue its shared e-bike and e-scooter service.

Lime said in a statement that Darebin's decision to end the trial was "not a failure of the council's judgement, but geography".

"When the City of Yarra ended its e-bike scheme in July, the corridor between Darebin and the city closed, and Darebin was left with a network that couldn't go anywhere," said Lime's head of Asia-Pacific, Will Peters.

"This is the result when a network service is regulated on a municipality-by-municipality basis."

He agreed with council that "shared micromobility is public transport, and public transport is the state's domain."

"Darebin's trial produced real evidence, and council is right to take it into its Integrated Transport Strategy," Mr Peters said.

"It belongs in a state conversation about how shared transport is governed in Victoria.

"We'll keep working with councils and the Victorian government to get there."

World.title: Venomous views, money for jam and a shock guest star: Five things we learnt from week five of ICAC
World.content:
See what we learnt from Operation Rosny week four here. It might be niche programming, but ICAC After Dark delivers. When the Independent Commission Against Corruption sits long past its usual hours of 4pm, they are driving towards a point. On Friday, the commission sat past 5pm when counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, asked Charles Perrottet about one of the key allegations: that branch-stacking among the Liberals in The Hills Shire Council was done to further the interests of property developer Jean Nassif, who is now a wanted man. Charles Perrottet approaches the ICAC on Friday. Sam Mooy Five weeks into the blockbuster inquiry and the revelations keep coming. Here are five things we learnt this week.



Spence had a dim view of Whitelaw Two of the witnesses worked in the office of former planning minister Anthony Roberts, but their evidence was not exactly flattering of each other. Chris Spence, who was chief of staff to Roberts, has denied pushing for David Chandler’s removal from the role of NSW Building Commissioner. Christopher Spence leaves the ICAC during a break on Monday during the Operation Rosny inquiry. Janie Barrett But he had some choice words for Dylan Whitelaw, who was also in Roberts’ office and a member of the Reformers right-wing sub-faction. Whitelaw had told the ICAC Spence wanted then-fair trading minister Eleni Petinos to do something with a supposedly damaging video of David Chandler, but came into his office one day and said words to the effect of “Eleni f---ed it up”. Spence said that evidence was not correct, and pointed out he worked in Parliament House while Whitelaw worked at 52 Martin Place.



“Dylan Whitelaw was not in a position that every time I walked into the office, I would just disclose things like that and rant and rave. He is delusional. It did not happen.” Related Article Operation Rosny Public flock to best show in town, where witness suffers from ICAC-induced amnesia Money for jam Anita Perrottet did a lot of her work verbally, she told the inquiry. She denied lying under oath to cover for her husband Charles, who is a person of interest to the inquiry. The ICAC is investigating whether invoices paid to her company were not for genuine work, but as a way to hide payment made by Jean Nassif to her husband. She denies this.



And there was the curious matter of Charles Perrottet attending a lunch at Jean Nassif’s home, to which he brought the children, but Anita Perrottet said she was not aware of this. The ICAC heard evidence she received significant lump sum payments, which included more than $250,000 in a three-month period for her advice. Perrottet insisted this was for genuine work. Dwyer suggested Perrottet was being paid “money for jam”, referring to the $10,000 a month she invoiced for “starting conversations about greyhounds”. Perrottet replied: “I was working, yes.” Hell on Earth Chandler’s appearance was interesting because he is the alleged victim of Nassif’s plot to remove him from office. He told the inquiry Nassif threatened him while he was investigating one of Nassif’s buildings.



Chandler told the commission about the first time he met developer Nassif in person, at a site inspection of a Toplace development in Botany. Nassif became angry and “really laid it into me well and truly”, Chandler told the corruption inquiry. Loading Chandler also served as a reminder that the victims were those who bought into Nassif’s Toplace developments. “It was hell on Earth and I just felt it was appropriate … to remind everybody that while this is all about people who were on the ascension to heaven and political purpose, at the back end of this there was a whole bunch of their constituents that were hurting, and they were in a world of pain,” he said outside the commission.



You can dial in to give evidence Christian Ellis has so far declined to take up the opportunity to appear at the inquiry, even though the ICAC has said he could appear via video link. Presiding commissioner Fabian Gleeson, SC, has even made a pointed plea to Ellis, “if you’re listening”, to take the opportunity. One man who has apparently seized the invitation is Nassif, who is slated to appear next Friday. Jean Nassif is a person of interest in this inquiry. Instagram The property developer fled Australia in December 2022 to hide in a small village in northern Lebanon. As he is overseas, the ICAC does not have the power to compel him to appear; however, as with all persons of interest, he was invited to give evidence.



Perrottet v Elliott Charles Perrottet has told the ICAC he wanted his brother Dominic to dump David Elliott from cabinet when he became premier. His wife, Anita Perrottet, asked Charles: “Did Dom confirm that he isn’t going to give Elliott a ministry?” In reply, Charles Perrottet wrote: “We execute the prick as soon as the party room is over”. Perrottet told the corruption inquiry he wanted Elliott gone because “I was pretty annoyed at the time of the way David handled himself”.

World.title: These robots can run but can’t stop: Will we ever learn?
World.content:
NationalRobots Opinion These robots can run but can’t stop: Will we ever learn? Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist August 29, 2026 — 9:30am

August 29, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The World Humanoid Robot Games, which have just finished in Beijing, weren’t an event; they were a perfect metaphor. Robots ran the 100 metres faster than Usain Bolt, but kept running until they exploded into a padded wall. We can create technology to do anything. We just can’t make it stop. The robots are a mirror to our moment: no exit plan. Strongmen start wars and their technology can achieve all their aims except finish what they have started. Putin in Ukraine, Netanyahu in Gaza, and Trump in Iran now lie at the base of their padded wall. A humanoid robot crashes into a wall and catches fire at the end of the 100-metre race during the 2nd World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing. Lintao Zhang/Getty Images Humanoids replicate humans in their inability to stop. Five Sydney Swans didn’t know how to stop their big night out. Anthony Albanese didn’t know how to finish the “comic” podcast conversation he had started, and, lacking an exit plan, ended up gibbering about melons. He resembled nobody so much as Lionel Essrog, the character in Jonathan Lethem’s novel Motherless Brooklyn, who can’t help pushing and pushing a joke beyond its use-by moment. His mentor Frank Minna calls it “tugboating”. If only Albo could have stopped tugboating. It would be glib to focus on the trivial side of individuals’ compulsion to tugboat. Humanity tugboats its technology on a grand scale of destructiveness. The artificial intelligence which has been thinking on behalf of some of the robots in Beijing is itself a really big boys’ own adventure without an exit plan. Doomsayers fear that we, humanity, will be the padded wall, just as our planet is the padded wall for the past two centuries of industrial pollution.



What was the aim of the World Humanoid Robot Games? Its thousands of competitors were surely not intending to produce a parable of man’s unlimited limitations. Didn’t it demonstrate something useful, and hopeful? It certainly produced content for social media and contributed more profit to the booming economy of sharable short videos. Human robots have, for now, replaced cats and children in the category of “Look at the funny things they do”. Illustration by Dionne Gain The Beijing games provided a steady stream of robots pratfalling, exploding, air-swinging, misfiring, and generally making poor life choices. Many of the competitors looked like they should have been tested for alcohol or recreational drugs. Their likeness to humans made them that much funnier. Along with the crowds in the Beijing arenas, you could laugh at the victims guilt-free. Being robots, they died painless deaths and suffered unembarrassing embarrassments. Best snuff films ever. In this, the World Humanoid Robot Games offered us a distractingly funny human (or humanoid?) face for Chinese technological development. A global audience of Homer Simpsons, we chuckle at those robots. It’s funny because it’s true. In one hilarious humanoid week, China has achieved more than a decade of soft diplomacy.



But aside from providing laughs, social media content, world records and showing that the fastest way to run is to cradle your arms like you’re stumbling through a crowded bar with a tray of drinks, what have the World Humanoid Robot Games given us? Related Article Climate policy How the Black Summer fires failed to shift Australians’ climate views Thirty of the 50 events in which more than 2000 robots competed were simulations of the Olympics and Paralympics. The other 20 events were modelled on human work, such as shelf stacking, retail service, book sorting, garden management and even fire rescues. You would have seen few videos and memes of humanoid robots performing in the power tool assembly, powder weighing, bricklaying, cap and lid opening, cable connecting, box unpacking and tweezers bean-picking events, but these are some that offer potentially useful and widespread innovations (just as a person who can set up your internet or fix your phone is more useful than Usain Bolt). The “dexterous hand events” in the games, with many more competitors than in the sporting events, reveal “where [the organisers] expect humanoid robots to get deployed commercially first”, according to Forbes magazine. “This is essentially a market map in game form.”



By this reading, the World Humanoid Robotic Games were not a metaphor but a demonstration of a reality coming at us faster than a self-driving taxi. Related Article Analysis

AFL off-field behaviour Nobody knows if any of these five will play for the Swans again The $US8.7 billion ($12 billion) of venture capital plunged into humanoid robotics so far this year is already double 2025’s investment and exceeds that for the entire previous decade, according to the specialist publication dealroom.co. Next year, investment in humanoid robotics is expected to pass the $US13 billion spent annually on addressing world hunger. This is just the beginning. Banks Morgan Stanley and RBC have forecast a $US5-9 trillion robotics economy by 2050, with a billion humanoid robots sharing our planet with us. One robot for every 10 humans, and we’ll never have to assemble a power tool or unpack a box again. The “vast sums of money now being invested means maybe that day is closer than we think”, reported Queensland University of Technology’s Jonathan Roberts in The Conversation. But just like in the human world, while the grunt work takes place in the shadows, the shop window is telling us a very old and enduring fable about ourselves. As futuristic as the Beijing games are, the lessons are ancient. The Greeks told the story of Prometheus, the titan who stole fire from the gods and gave it to humans. With the gift of technology, humans knew how to start but not how to stop. As a cautionary tale, Donald Trump is even older than he looks; he’s as old as classical myth.



Related Article AI Everyone is talking about the AI boom. When it busts, this is who will go down Tech capitalism is programmed for endless growth. The science of enterprise knows no horizons. But the art of restraint? As that original (and still the best) humanoid robot, Robot from Lost in Space, said, “It does not compute.” Zeus punished Prometheus by chaining him to a rock and having an eagle eat his liver, and the liver grew back again overnight so that Prometheus, like the reassembled humanoid robots in Beijing, had to go through it over and over. Prometheus would be re-embodied as Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein, who created a monster of unintended consequences. Will we ever learn? Hold that thought. I have to show you this hilarious clip. Robots compete at the Free Combat event of the World Humanoid Robot Games. AP Photo/Achmad Ibrahim



Malcolm Knox is a journalist, author and columnist for The Sydney Morning Herald. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: ‘Next chapter’: Magpie legend Scott Pendlebury to join Gold Coast
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Next chapter’: Magpie legend Scott Pendlebury to join Gold Coast Jon Pierik Updated August 29, 2026 — 9:28am ,first published 8:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Collingwood great Scott Pendlebury’s transition into coaching will begin next season when he joins the Gold Coast Suns, with the Magpies legend having played his last game for the club. Pendlebury’s manager Anthony Panozzo, of Hemisphere Sports, confirmed to this masthead on Saturday that the sport’s games record holder (442) will take to the field for the Suns next season, while also being a quasi assistant coach. All over: Tim Membrey is consoled by teammate Scott Pendlebury on Friday night. AFL Photos But from 2028 he will fully transition into coaching, although the length of that contract has yet to be determined. Pendlebury’s decision came just hours after the Magpies lost a heartbreaking wildcard clash against the Western Bulldogs when forward Tim Membrey missed a set shot to win after the final siren. Pendlebury, 38, did not play the game because of injury.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Why the wildcard final was lost for the Pies well before Tim Membrey’s kick after the siren “He will be playing on for the Gold Coast, an on-field assistant, that type of role, and then transition into coaching,” Panozzo said. “It’s the next chapter of his journey. Collingwood have been unbelievable and have been super supportive to Scott around Scott’s decision. “But, at the same time, unfortunately things go their way last night, but at the same time he is really excited for him and his family and the kids for what’s next.” Panozzo said Pendlebury’s wife Alex and family would make the move north with the dual premiership great.



Pendlebury is widely regarded as a future senior coach, and knows he needs to experience life outside of Collingwood where he has plied his trade since being drafted in 2005. As reported by this masthead, Pendlebury had been linked to the Suns, while Essendon had also emerged as an option, as the Bombers rebuild under new coach Mark McVeigh. Loading He and his management did not get to the point of asking about a contract with the Magpies next season. Rather, discussions had been more about the next footballing phase for Pendlebury. The Suns finished 13th with nine wins this season and were arguably the competition’s most disappointing side, having made finals for the first time last year.



Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 The behavioural red flags the Swans should have noticed before Melbourne bender Caroline Wilson Football columnist for The Age Pendlebury will initially join a blue-chip midfield comprising Christian Petracca, Matt Rowell and skipper Noah Anderson, imparting his wisdom on how the team led by coach Damien Hardwick can become a major force. “He [Pendlebury] is looking forward to supporting their young and developing list,” Panozzo said. Pendlebury’s departure adds to the winds of change at the Magpies, for fellow veteran premiership star Steele Sidebottom played his 375th – and final – game against the Bulldogs. Coach Craig McRae said on Friday night he expected the Magpies to be aggressive through the trade and free agency period, as the club has considerable room in the salary cap.



Related Article AFL 2026 Bulldogs v Magpies player ratings: The crucial moments and costly errors that decided the first wildcard final “I think those that sit on the outside would judge our list heavily, but we had most of our leaders out tonight. So we’ve got players in our building that make us better already; there’s a level of comfort in that, that we’ve got [Harry] Perryman, [Brayden] Maynard, Darcy Moore, Jamie Elliott to name a few that didn’t even play. Everyone would love your best team, but you don’t get that,” McRae said. “I think we’re just in the business of getting better and at what level? I’m not sure, but we’ll be pushing hard. We put ourselves in a position to have a salary cap for the first time that’s got a healthy bank balance for want of a better term. “We’re in the business of improving ourselves. So now the season’s finished, we’ll probably get a bit deeper into those things.” The Magpies were contacted for comment.
