World.title: NRL recruits face narrowing path to Rugby World Cup
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Opinion NRL recruits face narrowing path to Rugby World Cup Paul Cully Rugby columnist August 29, 2026 — 9:22am

August 29, 2026 — 9:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It would be ironic if rugby’s high-profile NRL recruits found the Wallabies a tough nut to crack under former North Sydney Bear Les Kiss, but that is how it looks a year out from the showpiece event. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii is on the bench against Argentina this weekend and the frequency of the niggles he picks up is a greater concern than the debate over his best position (his versatility could actually be his trump card). Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii in action for the Wallabies. Getty Images Zac Lomax, who was so impressive during Super Rugby Pacific, hasn’t played since May and his deal with the PNG Chiefs from 2028 onwards should count against him in a tight selection race, no matter what is said publicly. But Angus Crichton, out injured, faces the biggest challenge of all – both against the clock and against an evolution under way in the 15-man mode that is elevating his nominated position – the No.12 jersey – into one of the most important on the field.



Crichton is a very good player, but if he cannot run, pass and kick to an elite standard at the line within six months of his cross-code conversion, he will not be in the Wallabies’ 23. The resurgence of Hunter Paisami in the Wallabies No.12 jersey has been one of the early storylines of the Kiss era, but it has been a tale years in the making. Paisami has grown as a player just as the value of the No. 12 has increased. Hunter Paisami runs the ball in Townsville against Japan. Getty Images Ask yourself: Who was the best player in Super Rugby this year? The Chiefs No.12 Quinn Tupaea. And who was the All Blacks’ best player in their win against the Springboks in Johannesburg last weekend? No.12 Jordie Barrett.



These two are talented individuals but attacking trends in the game mean the No.12 role is moving back to a “second five-eighth” rather than an “inside centre”. It was not long ago that behemoths were all the rage – the Wallabies had one themselves in Samu Kerevi, while the French used the 110kg Jonathan Danty. Injured Rooster Angus Crichton is off to rugby next year. Wolter Peeters Their brief was simple: get over the gain line. But as attacking plans have become more sophisticated the No.12 is the player asked to make split-second decisions at the line, complemented by the skill set to execute them. A long and short kicking game is also a non-negotiable – the No. 12 is taking a lot of the playmaking burden off the No.10, who in turn must be a genuine running threat to take advantage of the time and space being created. The sit-in-the-pocket, kicking No.10 is a near-liability today.



So, it would be an extraordinary success for Crichton to quickly absorb these traits and show he is better than Paisami, Len Ikitau or Isaac Henry. It is not a position in the Wallabies that particularly cried out for an NRL recruit. Lomax is in a similar boat. Kiss has welcomed the competition Lomax provides and has been emphatic that he will pick him if he is good enough, but Max Jorgensen has one wing spot nailed down and the race for the other is intense. Mark Nawaqanitawase will have an edge over Lomax because of his rugby background. NRL Images Harry Potter has rediscovered his form and Dylan Pietsch was the best Australian winger in Super Rugby, but the longer-term challenge for Lomax will come from Mark Nawaqanitawase. The Roosters’ winger has the drop on Lomax because of his history in rugby and his pending shift to the Saitama Panasonic Wild Knights – the Queensland Reds will play them twice later this year as well as two games in Italy – won’t harm his Wallabies chances.



Suaalii’s repurposing into a utility back who can cover No.13 and the back three will also put the squeeze on Lomax, whose move back to the NRL is a shame for rugby given the vast promise he showed for the Force. Related Article Wallabies Why this is one of the most daunting venues the Wallabies have played at Suaalii’s return to the Wallabies via the bench is a subtle demotion because there has been too few of the brilliant, rampaging efforts he produced against the Chiefs and Moana Pasifika last year. His extraordinary athleticism, and lack of midfield alternatives, kept him front-and-centre at the Wallabies but the emergence of Paisami and now Henry has changed the picture. Yet, the shift could be the first step in Suaalii becoming indispensable, if not always a starter. Having a player who can cover midfield and the outside backs is pure gold.



Of the big three NRL recruits, Suaalii has the best chance of doing something special at a home Rugby World Cup next year. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Missing Australian makes contact, number of people unaccounted for nears 2000
World.content:
Warning: This story contains graphic content. One of the 41 Australian travellers reported missing after flash floods devastated the Nepal-China border has made contact with her relieved parents, as the total number of missing people nears 2000 and rescue efforts in the area swung back into action after fears of another major flood dissipated. Cara Severino, 26, called her parents on Friday morning to confirm she was alive and well, but was stranded along the Langtang Trek. People gather to look at posters of people missing in the Nepal flood disaster. KATE GERAGHTY Her parents, Debbie and Frank Severino, said their daughter was hiking the trek with a group, and they lost touch with her because of the floods. But she had subsequently made contact, much to their relief.



Cara Severino, hiking in Nepal, has been able to call her parents. Facebook “We praise God that she has been able to make this brief contact with us. Our thoughts and prayers are with all the families awaiting news,” they said. Nepal’s disaster management authority on Friday night (Saturday morning AEST) said the death toll had risen to 579, although that number could rise dramatically. The agency said the number of people reported missing was 1924, as more locals were added to the tally, and included 517 foreign tourists. At least 41 Australians are still missing. Among them is Sumi Adhikari, who went missing near the Kerung border crossing between China and Nepal.



“Upon speaking with her husband, we learnt that Sumi went missing while returning from the Mount Kailash-Mansarovar pilgrimage,” Non-Resident Nepali Association (NRNA) NSW state co-ordinator Usha Kiran Bariya said. “She has not yet made contact.” Earlier, residents in Nepal’s mountainous Rasuwa district, on the border with China’s Tibet, were forced to rush up hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river level as a lake formed by debris from Wednesday’s glacier collapse began to overflow, according to witnesses. Rescue operations continue in the areas of Nepal devastated by the flash floods. AP/Getty The prospect of the lake bursting prompted all Chinese rescue personnel to withdraw to a safe area, state broadcaster CCTV reported. Authorities in Nepal stopped helicopter rescue operations for 90 minutes.



The disruption was short-lived after Chinese state media said the barrier lake had stopped overflowing, according to the BBC. CCTV said rescue operations on the Tibet side were now “continuing as normal” after water levels of the barrier lake “dropped slightly”, the BBC reported. The lake’s reservoir has topped 2.5 million cubic metres of water, up from the estimated 1.5 to 2 million cubic metres that an eight-member Chinese engineering team sent to monitor the site recorded a day ago. Loading The formation ​of the lake had been captured in aerial footage by a Chinese rescue team, showing ⁠masses of brown water accumulating in a basin with no visible outlet.



Nepalese police said on Friday afternoon: “Information has been received that the water dam on the Tibetan side has burst again. Therefore, all security personnel, rescue workers involved in rescue and relief operations, and the general public, are requested to remain immediately alert and move to safe locations or notify others.” The temporary halt came as Foreign Minister Penny Wong confirmed earlier on Friday that at least 39 Australians were believed to be among those missing, up from 35. This changed to 38 after Cara Severino made contact with her family. On Saturday morning, the number went up to 41, according to DFAT. “The extraordinary scale of this disaster and the remoteness of the affected region mean immense challenges lie ahead for the response and recovery,” Wong said in a joint statement with International Development Minister Anne Aly. Wong told ABC radio it was “an unfortunate possibility” that more Australians could be reported missing in the coming days as the true scale of the disaster became clear.



Nepal’s Foreign Ministry said it did not need foreign assistance for search and rescue operations following the devastating avalanche. Offers of help had come from several countries with nationals missing in the disaster. But the country’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle said Nepal would need at least “a few billion dollars” to recover from the devastation caused by the floods, as he called for international funding for a massive reconstruction effort. The Australian government announced it would provide $5 million in humanitarian assistance as Wong prepared to speak to her Nepalese counterpart on Friday afternoon to discuss how Australia could support the recovery effort. Loading Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a post on social media: “Australia is sending crisis and humanitarian response specialists to help after the devastating Nepal-China floods. We’re also providing humanitarian assistance including food, emergency shelter and medical support.”



Greens senator David Shoebridge said the $5 million pledged by Australia would “not come close” to meeting the need for recovery and repair efforts. “I think Australia needs to step up and really commit to helping rebuild. This is a country with minimal spare resources,” he said. Gallery Gallery icon 24 images Floods Photo gallery: Flash flooding devastates Nepal and Tibet Fast-moving waters swept through villages, wiping out bridges, roads and entire settlements in a Nepalese valley near the border with China on Wednesday. There was more good news on Friday, when 883 locals and labourers were rescued in the Rasuwa district in an effort that included an “extremely dangerous and challenging” rescue mission that freed 350 people trapped in the tunnel of a hydropower plant.



“The troops are still gathering to safely evacuate more than 100 people trapped in the same tunnel,” the Nepalese Prime Minister’s Office said. Footage released by the office showed a team of Nepalese soldiers crawling through thick mud up a steep passageway to enter the tunnel and save those trapped inside. United Nations under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs Tom Fletcher said aid teams were experiencing major difficulties trying to reach the areas most affected by the floods due to the extent of damage to roads and bridges in the area. “It’s a very, very challenging terrain for them to be navigating right now,” Fletcher told CNN. “We’re having to use air assets to reach them. The immediate priority is saving as many lives as we can.”



Footage released by the BBC showed a giant boulder being swept along by the flood, underlining the force of the torrent. Fear of further flooding Nepal and China had both warned of the risks of further flooding in the Himalayas as debris from the initial glacier collapse formed a lake straddling their border. “Residents of the lower banks … passengers, rescuers engaged in rescue operations, and all concerned are requested to exercise special caution and stay in safe places away from the river banks and risky areas,” Nepal’s disaster authority said.



One of the engineers, Chen Hanxiao, said the general approach to reducing the lake’s threat was to excavate a drainage channel at a lower point of the dam, but the width and depth of that channel needed calculations based on how fast the water would flow and how quickly the lake would fill. Related Article Updated

Floods The 41 Australians missing in the Nepal-Tibet floods, and what we know about them China on Thursday said 3 million cubic meters of water, the equivalent of about 1200 Olympic swimming pools, was expected to flow into the lake over the next three days. Peak flow was expected around September 1. Chinese President Xi Jinping dispatched his second-in-command, Premier Li Qiang, to visit the devastated areas of Tibet, demonstrating the severity of the disaster, which may be the worst since an earthquake in 2015 killed about 9000 people. Li inspected emergency rescue and relief operations, and visited first responders and displaced people in temporary shelters, according to the official Xinhua News Agency.



Assessments based on seismic and satellite data indicate the initial flood was triggered by the collapse of a glacier and underlying bedrock in the Himalayan region between Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, causing a 5.2-magnitude seismic event that sent water, ice, rock and debris downstream. Images and videos circulated online show the extent of the water’s force. Walls of grey water swept through villages and valleys, pulling down trees, pushing boulders and sweeping over masses of people attempting to flee. The aftermath from a tidal wave of mud, rock and water that devastated towns and villages along the Lhende River. AFP The flood is a major test for Nepal’s fledgling government and its new leader, former rapper Balendra Shah, who rode to power on a wave of Gen Z enthusiasm. He will need to work closely with regional neighbours China and India. China has deployed at least 574 rescuers to the land crossing, and India says it is co-ordinating closely with Kathmandu on rescue and relief efforts. The country’s tourism industry, which supports over 1 million jobs, will take a hit in a peak period, and it will be anxious about the future given Nepal’s frequency of extreme weather events.



Which regions were hit? The Bhote Koshi River flooded about 9am on Wednesday (1pm AEST), destroying several villages as well as roads and hydropower projects, officials said. Warnings were issued in several districts urging people to stay away from the banks of the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers. Loading The flood triggered a mudslide that hit Gyirong Port, a major land crossing with neighbouring Tibet, cutting roads, communications and power links to the area.



Rasuwa, the worst-affected area, witnessed a flash flood similar to those in August last year, when a glacial lake in neighbouring Tibet overflowed due to high temperatures in the mountain region. Nine people died, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting the two countries, was damaged at the time. Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said the Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi River, had experienced its highest recorded flood on Wednesday. Damaged houses stand precariously near the swollen, debris-choked banks of the Trishuli River after flash floods in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha Rescuers use an earthmover to carry a survivor to safety along the Trishuli River in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha “The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in 14 months, this time triggered by an ice rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream,” said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the climate research group.



“In a warming Himalaya, early warning is the first line of adaptation.” The Himalayan region, which spans Nepal and several neighbouring countries, including India, is especially vulnerable to heavy rain, floods and landslides because it is warming faster than much of the rest of the world due to human-caused climate change. Loading Related Article Floods ‘Most of my family is still missing’: The frantic search in Kathmandu for loved ones Research has shown that extreme weather events, including heatwaves, heavy rain and melting glaciers, have become more frequent in the region.



Members of the Kathmandu research group found this year that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region are melting at an accelerating rate. Ice loss rates have doubled since 2000, primarily due to rising global temperatures and climate change. Australians in need of emergency consular assistance should contact the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s 24-hour Consular Emergency Centre on 1300 555 135, or +61 2 6261 3305 (if calling from overseas). World.title: After 15 years of active service, Rockpool Perth is getting a $3 million makeover
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outEat and drink Perth After 15 years of active service, Rockpool Perth is getting a $3 million makeover When the marquee steakhouse reopens, expect a refreshed dining room and bar, a new private dining room plus a stronger seafood focus. Max Veenhuyzen August 29, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Consistency, insist the personal trainers and motivational speakers, is important. At Rockpool Bar & Grill Perth, consistency is a way of life and helps explain why the luxe steakhouse – despite opening its doors in 2011; despite changing fashion and food trends; despite the dedication of new temples of beef across P-Town; and despite the departure of Rockpool’s famous, ponytailed founder – remains a key figure in the city’s dining landscape as well as the casino’s safest bet. (That the restaurant had a reputation for only putting the best ingredients in its shopping trolley and dry-ageing fridges helps too, as does its ability to cook said ingredients very well and very simply, time after time.) Rockpool Bar & Grill Perth executive chef Brendan Owens, general manager Laura Bartolone, chief executive Frank Tucker, and culinary director Santiago Aristizabal. Shot By Thom After 15 years of active duty, Rockpool is taking a three-week sabbatical later this year and getting some work done: three million dollars of work, to be exact. According to Rockpool owners Hunter Street Hospitality, this makeover will mark the biggest change to the space since Neil Perry and designer Grant Cheyne rebooted the former food court into a gilded, classically inspired steakhouse. For management, this refresh is a chance to start writing the restaurant’s new chapter. “This renovation is our opportunity to begin Rockpool 2.0, which is exciting,” says general manager Laura Bartolone.



So what changes are on the cards? A little more colour, for one. While I’ve appreciated the timelessness of the room’s existing taupe, gold and beige palette, those proposed persimmon-hued banquettes do bring a jolt of energy to the room. (These new bench seats also face towards the restaurant proper and open kitchen; a nicer view, I reckon, than the postcard-perfect white big top circus tent currently squatting in the carpark and whose gracious curves are obscured by hessian curtains.) Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Related Article 14 / 20 Review No, Google Maps isn’t playing up: this Perth gym really does house a great Malay cafe The layout of the dining room (260 seats, an increase of 20 seats) will be rejigged to create more fluid, modular areas that can better accommodate large groups. The bar is also getting upsized and will be able to fit 40 revellers in a revamped, more standalone space. A third private dining room is also being built. Considering the fit-out is being handled by SGB Group – also responsible for the recent facelift of Rockpool Bar & Grill Sydney – it’s safe to assume that the new-look Perth will feel a little more like Sydney (and vice-versa). The food offering, meanwhile, is also being streamlined and brought into line with what’s happening nationally. While fellow collectors of restaurant ephemera will be crestfallen to hear that Rockpool will stop printing daily dated lunch and dinner menus (the carte will now be presented in a leather binder) news that the kitchen will reopen with a stronger seafood focus should help soften that blow. Greenham dry-aged F1 Wagyu reserve T-bone. Kristoffer Paulsen



“The goal is to replicate the beef program into the seafood side of things,” says Rockpool Perth executive chef Brendan Owens. (This new seafood focus has already been implemented at Rockpool’s Sydney and Melbourne siblings.) “We’ve always had good raw seafood on but there’ll be more of a focus on cooked seafood. Things like whole marron, squid, fish and lobsters.” Still, the cornerstones of Rockpool’s identity will remain. There will still be a big focus on beef that’s been aged and butchered in-house. There will still be an encyclopaedic thirst trap of a wine list to thumb through. (Christian Baeppler, Rockpool Perth’s sommelier, placed second in the inaugural Sommeliers Australia Top 100 sommeliers list announced this week.) And there will still be a dining room perpetually set for big night – or big day – out celebrations. “Rockpool will always be the same,” says Bartolone. “We don’t want to be a casual restaurant and we aren’t going to start doing gastronomy. This is a premium, fine dining steakhouse and we need to reflect that across everything. Not only on what you have in your plate and the service, but the ambience, lighting and music. Everything.” Did somebody say something about consistency? Rockpool Bar & Grill Perth closes on Monday October 5 and reopens on Wednesday October 28.

World.title: Carroll scraps plan for statue of Daniel Andrews
World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

A controversial $134,000 statue of former premier Daniel Andrews has been scrapped, with Victoria’s new leader Ben Carroll saying the statue policy did not meet taxpayer expectations.

Previously, any politician who served more than 3000 days as Victorian premier would be immortalised in bronze near Parliament House in Melbourne.

Ben Carroll with Daniel Andrews in 2023, when Carroll was public transport minister in Andrews’ government. Justin McManus

Carroll announced on Saturday that the statue policy would be repealed, and that work on the statue of Andrews, who was premier from 2014 to 2023, would stop.

But Carroll said the contract would not be cancelled, and that an independent panel would recommend an alternative subject for a statue, as part of a broader change which includes scaling back spending on state funerals.

World.title: Right-wing agitator Milo Yiannopoulos detained by ICE in Louisiana
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaTrump's America Right-wing agitator Milo Yiannopoulos detained by ICE in Louisiana Michael Koziol Updated August 29, 2026 — 8:25am ,first published 6:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: British far-right agitator Milo Yiannopoulos has been arrested by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Louisiana and is being held in detention. The Department of Homeland Security said Yiannopoulos “chose to overstay his welcome” after arriving in the US legally in 2019. Milo Yiannopoulos at Canberra’s Parliament House in 2017. Alex Ellinghausen “Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an Immigration Judge on July 22, after failing to show up for his immigration hearing,” DHS said. “He will remain in ICE custody pending removal.” DHS posted Yiannopoulos’ mugshot on X and said he was arrested on Thursday (US time) at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport. Online ICE records showed he was being held but did not indicate which facility.



Entertainment website TMZ, which was first to report the arrest, suggested Yiannopoulos may have been in Louisiana with rapper Ye – better known as Kanye West – with whom the British commentator has sometimes worked. Ye is scheduled to perform in New Orleans on Friday night, local time. Yiannopoulos came to prominence as an editor at the far-right US website Breitbart News, where his targets typically included feminism and Islam. View post on X He corresponded and associated with various far-right figures and white nationalists and was banned from numerous social media platforms. Yiannapoulos was sacked from Breitbart and ostracised from mainstream conservative arenas after he defended the idea of sexual relationships between adult men and teenage boys as young as 13 in certain circumstances.





Last year, Yiannpoulos expressed support on social media for ICE and the deportations being ordered by the Trump administration. “California needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections and government buildings, with on-the-spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally,” he posted from his X account in June 2025. Milo Yiannopoulos wearing a “Make America Straight Again” cap. He branded himself as an “ex-gay”. AP He also queried whether one could masturbate in public if they found themselves observing an ICE raid. An American far-right internet personality and activist, Laura Loomer, took credit for Yiannapoulos’ arrest.



Loomer, who has 1.9 million followers on X and enjoys the ear of President Donald Trump, has been posting about the Brit’s immigration status for more than a year. “When Milo called for me to be assassinated, I reported him to ICE and the FBI,” she said on X on Friday. “I told you all that Milo was an illegal alien.” Loomer’s influence and apparent success in having senior personnel sacked from the Trump administration have led to the popularisation of the term “getting Loomer-ed” when someone she dislikes is dismissed from their post. Yiannapoulos briefly worked as an intern for former Republican congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, who fell out with Trump and is now part of talks to found a new right-wing movement with broadcaster Tucker Carlson. World.title: Venomous views, money for jam and a shock guest star: Five things we learnt from week five of ICAC
World.content:
See what we learnt from Operation Rosny week four here. It might be niche programming, but ICAC After Dark delivers. When the Independent Commission Against Corruption sits long past its usual hours of 4pm, they are driving towards a point. On Friday, the commission sat past 5pm when counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, asked Charles Perrottet about one of the key allegations: that branch-stacking among the Liberals in The Hills Shire Council was done to further the interests of property developer Jean Nassif, who is now a wanted man. Charles Perrottet approaches the ICAC on Friday. Sam Mooy Five weeks into the blockbuster inquiry and the revelations keep coming. Here are five things we learnt this week.



Spence had a dim view of Whitelaw Two of the witnesses worked in the office of former planning minister Anthony Roberts, but their evidence was not exactly flattering of each other. Chris Spence, who was chief of staff to Roberts, has denied pushing for David Chandler’s removal from the role of NSW Building Commissioner. Christopher Spence leaves the ICAC during a break on Monday during the Operation Rosny inquiry. Janie Barrett But he had some choice words for Dylan Whitelaw, who was also in Roberts’ office and a member of the Reformers right-wing sub-faction. Whitelaw had told the ICAC Spence wanted then-fair trading minister Eleni Petinos to do something with a supposedly damaging video of David Chandler, but came into his office one day and said words to the effect of “Eleni f---ed it up”. Spence said that evidence was not correct, and pointed out he worked in Parliament House while Whitelaw worked at 52 Martin Place.



“Dylan Whitelaw was not in a position that every time I walked into the office, I would just disclose things like that and rant and rave. He is delusional. It did not happen.” Related Article Operation Rosny Public flock to best show in town, where witness suffers from ICAC-induced amnesia Money for jam Anita Perrottet did a lot of her work verbally, she told the inquiry. She denied lying under oath to cover for her husband Charles, who is a person of interest to the inquiry. The ICAC is investigating whether invoices paid to her company were not for genuine work, but as a way to hide payment made by Jean Nassif to her husband. She denies this.



And there was the curious matter of Charles Perrottet attending a lunch at Jean Nassif’s home, to which he brought the children, but Anita Perrottet said she was not aware of this. The ICAC heard evidence she received significant lump sum payments, which included more than $250,000 in a three-month period for her advice. Perrottet insisted this was for genuine work. Dwyer suggested Perrottet was being paid “money for jam”, referring to the $10,000 a month she invoiced for “starting conversations about greyhounds”. Perrottet replied: “I was working, yes.” Hell on Earth Chandler’s appearance was interesting because he is the alleged victim of Nassif’s plot to remove him from office. He told the inquiry Nassif threatened him while he was investigating one of Nassif’s buildings.



Chandler told the commission about the first time he met developer Nassif in person, at a site inspection of a Toplace development in Botany. Nassif became angry and “really laid it into me well and truly”, Chandler told the corruption inquiry. Loading Chandler also served as a reminder that the victims were those who bought into Nassif’s Toplace developments. “It was hell on Earth and I just felt it was appropriate … to remind everybody that while this is all about people who were on the ascension to heaven and political purpose, at the back end of this there was a whole bunch of their constituents that were hurting, and they were in a world of pain,” he said outside the commission.



You can dial in to give evidence Christian Ellis has so far declined to take up the opportunity to appear at the inquiry, even though the ICAC has said he could appear via video link. Presiding commissioner Fabian Gleeson, SC, has even made a pointed plea to Ellis, “if you’re listening”, to take the opportunity. One man who has apparently seized the invitation is Nassif, who is slated to appear next Friday. Jean Nassif is a person of interest in this inquiry. Instagram The property developer fled Australia in December 2022 to hide in a small village in northern Lebanon. As he is overseas, the ICAC does not have the power to compel him to appear; however, as with all persons of interest, he was invited to give evidence.



Perrottet v Elliott Charles Perrottet has told the ICAC he wanted his brother Dominic to dump David Elliott from cabinet when he became premier. His wife, Anita Perrottet, asked Charles: “Did Dom confirm that he isn’t going to give Elliott a ministry?” In reply, Charles Perrottet wrote: “We execute the prick as soon as the party room is over”. Perrottet told the corruption inquiry he wanted Elliott gone because “I was pretty annoyed at the time of the way David handled himself”.

World.title: These robots can run but can’t stop: Will we ever learn?
World.content:
NationalRobots Opinion These robots can run but can’t stop: Will we ever learn? Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist August 29, 2026 — 9:30am

August 29, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The World Humanoid Robot Games, which have just finished in Beijing, weren’t an event; they were a perfect metaphor. Robots ran the 100 metres faster than Usain Bolt, but kept running until they exploded into a padded wall. We can create technology to do anything. We just can’t make it stop. The robots are a mirror to our moment: no exit plan. Strongmen start wars and their technology can achieve all their aims except finish what they have started. Putin in Ukraine, Netanyahu in Gaza, and Trump in Iran now lie at the base of their padded wall. A humanoid robot crashes into a wall and catches fire at the end of the 100-metre race during the 2nd World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing. Lintao Zhang/Getty Images Humanoids replicate humans in their inability to stop. Five Sydney Swans didn’t know how to stop their big night out. Anthony Albanese didn’t know how to finish the “comic” podcast conversation he had started, and, lacking an exit plan, ended up gibbering about melons. He resembled nobody so much as Lionel Essrog, the character in Jonathan Lethem’s novel Motherless Brooklyn, who can’t help pushing and pushing a joke beyond its use-by moment. His mentor Frank Minna calls it “tugboating”. If only Albo could have stopped tugboating. It would be glib to focus on the trivial side of individuals’ compulsion to tugboat. Humanity tugboats its technology on a grand scale of destructiveness. The artificial intelligence which has been thinking on behalf of some of the robots in Beijing is itself a really big boys’ own adventure without an exit plan. Doomsayers fear that we, humanity, will be the padded wall, just as our planet is the padded wall for the past two centuries of industrial pollution.



What was the aim of the World Humanoid Robot Games? Its thousands of competitors were surely not intending to produce a parable of man’s unlimited limitations. Didn’t it demonstrate something useful, and hopeful? It certainly produced content for social media and contributed more profit to the booming economy of sharable short videos. Human robots have, for now, replaced cats and children in the category of “Look at the funny things they do”. Illustration by Dionne Gain The Beijing games provided a steady stream of robots pratfalling, exploding, air-swinging, misfiring, and generally making poor life choices. Many of the competitors looked like they should have been tested for alcohol or recreational drugs. Their likeness to humans made them that much funnier. Along with the crowds in the Beijing arenas, you could laugh at the victims guilt-free. Being robots, they died painless deaths and suffered unembarrassing embarrassments. Best snuff films ever. In this, the World Humanoid Robot Games offered us a distractingly funny human (or humanoid?) face for Chinese technological development. A global audience of Homer Simpsons, we chuckle at those robots. It’s funny because it’s true. In one hilarious humanoid week, China has achieved more than a decade of soft diplomacy.



But aside from providing laughs, social media content, world records and showing that the fastest way to run is to cradle your arms like you’re stumbling through a crowded bar with a tray of drinks, what have the World Humanoid Robot Games given us? Related Article Climate policy How the Black Summer fires failed to shift Australians’ climate views Thirty of the 50 events in which more than 2000 robots competed were simulations of the Olympics and Paralympics. The other 20 events were modelled on human work, such as shelf stacking, retail service, book sorting, garden management and even fire rescues. You would have seen few videos and memes of humanoid robots performing in the power tool assembly, powder weighing, bricklaying, cap and lid opening, cable connecting, box unpacking and tweezers bean-picking events, but these are some that offer potentially useful and widespread innovations (just as a person who can set up your internet or fix your phone is more useful than Usain Bolt). The “dexterous hand events” in the games, with many more competitors than in the sporting events, reveal “where [the organisers] expect humanoid robots to get deployed commercially first”, according to Forbes magazine. “This is essentially a market map in game form.”



By this reading, the World Humanoid Robotic Games were not a metaphor but a demonstration of a reality coming at us faster than a self-driving taxi. Related Article Analysis

AFL off-field behaviour Nobody knows if any of these five will play for the Swans again The $US8.7 billion ($12 billion) of venture capital plunged into humanoid robotics so far this year is already double 2025’s investment and exceeds that for the entire previous decade, according to the specialist publication dealroom.co. Next year, investment in humanoid robotics is expected to pass the $US13 billion spent annually on addressing world hunger. This is just the beginning. Banks Morgan Stanley and RBC have forecast a $US5-9 trillion robotics economy by 2050, with a billion humanoid robots sharing our planet with us. One robot for every 10 humans, and we’ll never have to assemble a power tool or unpack a box again. The “vast sums of money now being invested means maybe that day is closer than we think”, reported Queensland University of Technology’s Jonathan Roberts in The Conversation. But just like in the human world, while the grunt work takes place in the shadows, the shop window is telling us a very old and enduring fable about ourselves. As futuristic as the Beijing games are, the lessons are ancient. The Greeks told the story of Prometheus, the titan who stole fire from the gods and gave it to humans. With the gift of technology, humans knew how to start but not how to stop. As a cautionary tale, Donald Trump is even older than he looks; he’s as old as classical myth.



Related Article AI Everyone is talking about the AI boom. When it busts, this is who will go down Tech capitalism is programmed for endless growth. The science of enterprise knows no horizons. But the art of restraint? As that original (and still the best) humanoid robot, Robot from Lost in Space, said, “It does not compute.” Zeus punished Prometheus by chaining him to a rock and having an eagle eat his liver, and the liver grew back again overnight so that Prometheus, like the reassembled humanoid robots in Beijing, had to go through it over and over. Prometheus would be re-embodied as Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein, who created a monster of unintended consequences. Will we ever learn? Hold that thought. I have to show you this hilarious clip. Robots compete at the Free Combat event of the World Humanoid Robot Games. AP Photo/Achmad Ibrahim



Malcolm Knox is a journalist, author and columnist for The Sydney Morning Herald. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: ‘Next chapter’: Magpie legend Scott Pendlebury to join Gold Coast
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Next chapter’: Magpie legend Scott Pendlebury to join Gold Coast Jon Pierik Updated August 29, 2026 — 9:28am ,first published 8:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Collingwood great Scott Pendlebury’s transition into coaching will begin next season when he joins the Gold Coast Suns, with the Magpies legend having played his last game for the club. Pendlebury’s manager Anthony Panozzo, of Hemisphere Sports, confirmed to this masthead on Saturday that the sport’s games record holder (442) will take to the field for the Suns next season, while also being a quasi assistant coach. All over: Tim Membrey is consoled by teammate Scott Pendlebury on Friday night. AFL Photos But from 2028 he will fully transition into coaching, although the length of that contract has yet to be determined. Pendlebury’s decision came just hours after the Magpies lost a heartbreaking wildcard clash against the Western Bulldogs when forward Tim Membrey missed a set shot to win after the final siren. Pendlebury, 38, did not play the game because of injury.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Why the wildcard final was lost for the Pies well before Tim Membrey’s kick after the siren “He will be playing on for the Gold Coast, an on-field assistant, that type of role, and then transition into coaching,” Panozzo said. “It’s the next chapter of his journey. Collingwood have been unbelievable and have been super supportive to Scott around Scott’s decision. “But, at the same time, unfortunately things go their way last night, but at the same time he is really excited for him and his family and the kids for what’s next.” Panozzo said Pendlebury’s wife Alex and family would make the move north with the dual premiership great.



Pendlebury is widely regarded as a future senior coach, and knows he needs to experience life outside of Collingwood where he has plied his trade since being drafted in 2005. As reported by this masthead, Pendlebury had been linked to the Suns, while Essendon had also emerged as an option, as the Bombers rebuild under new coach Mark McVeigh. Loading He and his management did not get to the point of asking about a contract with the Magpies next season. Rather, discussions had been more about the next footballing phase for Pendlebury. The Suns finished 13th with nine wins this season and were arguably the competition’s most disappointing side, having made finals for the first time last year.



Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 The behavioural red flags the Swans should have noticed before Melbourne bender Caroline Wilson Football columnist for The Age Pendlebury will initially join a blue-chip midfield comprising Christian Petracca, Matt Rowell and skipper Noah Anderson, imparting his wisdom on how the team led by coach Damien Hardwick can become a major force. “He [Pendlebury] is looking forward to supporting their young and developing list,” Panozzo said. Pendlebury’s departure adds to the winds of change at the Magpies, for fellow veteran premiership star Steele Sidebottom played his 375th – and final – game against the Bulldogs. Coach Craig McRae said on Friday night he expected the Magpies to be aggressive through the trade and free agency period, as the club has considerable room in the salary cap.



Related Article AFL 2026 Bulldogs v Magpies player ratings: The crucial moments and costly errors that decided the first wildcard final “I think those that sit on the outside would judge our list heavily, but we had most of our leaders out tonight. So we’ve got players in our building that make us better already; there’s a level of comfort in that, that we’ve got [Harry] Perryman, [Brayden] Maynard, Darcy Moore, Jamie Elliott to name a few that didn’t even play. Everyone would love your best team, but you don’t get that,” McRae said. “I think we’re just in the business of getting better and at what level? I’m not sure, but we’ll be pushing hard. We put ourselves in a position to have a salary cap for the first time that’s got a healthy bank balance for want of a better term. “We’re in the business of improving ourselves. So now the season’s finished, we’ll probably get a bit deeper into those things.” The Magpies were contacted for comment.



More to come Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: NRL recruits face narrowing path to Rugby World Cup
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Opinion NRL recruits face narrowing path to Rugby World Cup Paul Cully Rugby columnist August 29, 2026 — 9:22am

August 29, 2026 — 9:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It would be ironic if rugby’s high-profile NRL recruits found the Wallabies a tough nut to crack under former North Sydney Bear Les Kiss, but that is how it looks a year out from the showpiece event. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii is on the bench against Argentina this weekend and the frequency of the niggles he picks up is a greater concern than the debate over his best position (his versatility could actually be his trump card). Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii in action for the Wallabies. Getty Images Zac Lomax, who was so impressive during Super Rugby Pacific, hasn’t played since May and his deal with the PNG Chiefs from 2028 onwards should count against him in a tight selection race, no matter what is said publicly. But Angus Crichton, out injured, faces the biggest challenge of all – both against the clock and against an evolution under way in the 15-man mode that is elevating his nominated position – the No.12 jersey – into one of the most important on the field.



Crichton is a very good player, but if he cannot run, pass and kick to an elite standard at the line within six months of his cross-code conversion, he will not be in the Wallabies’ 23. The resurgence of Hunter Paisami in the Wallabies No.12 jersey has been one of the early storylines of the Kiss era, but it has been a tale years in the making. Paisami has grown as a player just as the value of the No. 12 has increased. Hunter Paisami runs the ball in Townsville against Japan. Getty Images Ask yourself: Who was the best player in Super Rugby this year? The Chiefs No.12 Quinn Tupaea. And who was the All Blacks’ best player in their win against the Springboks in Johannesburg last weekend? No.12 Jordie Barrett.



These two are talented individuals but attacking trends in the game mean the No.12 role is moving back to a “second five-eighth” rather than an “inside centre”. It was not long ago that behemoths were all the rage – the Wallabies had one themselves in Samu Kerevi, while the French used the 110kg Jonathan Danty. Injured Rooster Angus Crichton is off to rugby next year. Wolter Peeters Their brief was simple: get over the gain line. But as attacking plans have become more sophisticated the No.12 is the player asked to make split-second decisions at the line, complemented by the skill set to execute them. A long and short kicking game is also a non-negotiable – the No. 12 is taking a lot of the playmaking burden off the No.10, who in turn must be a genuine running threat to take advantage of the time and space being created. The sit-in-the-pocket, kicking No.10 is a near-liability today.



So, it would be an extraordinary success for Crichton to quickly absorb these traits and show he is better than Paisami, Len Ikitau or Isaac Henry. It is not a position in the Wallabies that particularly cried out for an NRL recruit. Lomax is in a similar boat. Kiss has welcomed the competition Lomax provides and has been emphatic that he will pick him if he is good enough, but Max Jorgensen has one wing spot nailed down and the race for the other is intense. Mark Nawaqanitawase will have an edge over Lomax because of his rugby background. NRL Images Harry Potter has rediscovered his form and Dylan Pietsch was the best Australian winger in Super Rugby, but the longer-term challenge for Lomax will come from Mark Nawaqanitawase. The Roosters’ winger has the drop on Lomax because of his history in rugby and his pending shift to the Saitama Panasonic Wild Knights – the Queensland Reds will play them twice later this year as well as two games in Italy – won’t harm his Wallabies chances.



Suaalii’s repurposing into a utility back who can cover No.13 and the back three will also put the squeeze on Lomax, whose move back to the NRL is a shame for rugby given the vast promise he showed for the Force. Related Article Wallabies Why this is one of the most daunting venues the Wallabies have played at Suaalii’s return to the Wallabies via the bench is a subtle demotion because there has been too few of the brilliant, rampaging efforts he produced against the Chiefs and Moana Pasifika last year. His extraordinary athleticism, and lack of midfield alternatives, kept him front-and-centre at the Wallabies but the emergence of Paisami and now Henry has changed the picture. Yet, the shift could be the first step in Suaalii becoming indispensable, if not always a starter. Having a player who can cover midfield and the outside backs is pure gold.



Of the big three NRL recruits, Suaalii has the best chance of doing something special at a home Rugby World Cup next year. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Missing Australian makes contact, number of people unaccounted for nears 2000
World.content:
Warning: This story contains graphic content. One of the 41 Australian travellers reported missing after flash floods devastated the Nepal-China border has made contact with her relieved parents, as the total number of missing people nears 2000 and rescue efforts in the area swung back into action after fears of another major flood dissipated. Cara Severino, 26, called her parents on Friday morning to confirm she was alive and well, but was stranded along the Langtang Trek. People gather to look at posters of people missing in the Nepal flood disaster. KATE GERAGHTY Her parents, Debbie and Frank Severino, said their daughter was hiking the trek with a group, and they lost touch with her because of the floods. But she had subsequently made contact, much to their relief.



Cara Severino, hiking in Nepal, has been able to call her parents. Facebook “We praise God that she has been able to make this brief contact with us. Our thoughts and prayers are with all the families awaiting news,” they said. Nepal’s disaster management authority on Friday night (Saturday morning AEST) said the death toll had risen to 579, although that number could rise dramatically. The agency said the number of people reported missing was 1924, as more locals were added to the tally, and included 517 foreign tourists. At least 41 Australians are still missing. Among them is Sumi Adhikari, who went missing near the Kerung border crossing between China and Nepal.



“Upon speaking with her husband, we learnt that Sumi went missing while returning from the Mount Kailash-Mansarovar pilgrimage,” Non-Resident Nepali Association (NRNA) NSW state co-ordinator Usha Kiran Bariya said. “She has not yet made contact.” Earlier, residents in Nepal’s mountainous Rasuwa district, on the border with China’s Tibet, were forced to rush up hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river level as a lake formed by debris from Wednesday’s glacier collapse began to overflow, according to witnesses. Rescue operations continue in the areas of Nepal devastated by the flash floods. AP/Getty The prospect of the lake bursting prompted all Chinese rescue personnel to withdraw to a safe area, state broadcaster CCTV reported. Authorities in Nepal stopped helicopter rescue operations for 90 minutes.



The disruption was short-lived after Chinese state media said the barrier lake had stopped overflowing, according to the BBC. CCTV said rescue operations on the Tibet side were now “continuing as normal” after water levels of the barrier lake “dropped slightly”, the BBC reported. The lake’s reservoir has topped 2.5 million cubic metres of water, up from the estimated 1.5 to 2 million cubic metres that an eight-member Chinese engineering team sent to monitor the site recorded a day ago. Loading The formation ​of the lake had been captured in aerial footage by a Chinese rescue team, showing ⁠masses of brown water accumulating in a basin with no visible outlet.



Nepalese police said on Friday afternoon: “Information has been received that the water dam on the Tibetan side has burst again. Therefore, all security personnel, rescue workers involved in rescue and relief operations, and the general public, are requested to remain immediately alert and move to safe locations or notify others.” The temporary halt came as Foreign Minister Penny Wong confirmed earlier on Friday that at least 39 Australians were believed to be among those missing, up from 35. This changed to 38 after Cara Severino made contact with her family. On Saturday morning, the number went up to 41, according to DFAT. “The extraordinary scale of this disaster and the remoteness of the affected region mean immense challenges lie ahead for the response and recovery,” Wong said in a joint statement with International Development Minister Anne Aly. Wong told ABC radio it was “an unfortunate possibility” that more Australians could be reported missing in the coming days as the true scale of the disaster became clear.



Nepal’s Foreign Ministry said it did not need foreign assistance for search and rescue operations following the devastating avalanche. Offers of help had come from several countries with nationals missing in the disaster. But the country’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle said Nepal would need at least “a few billion dollars” to recover from the devastation caused by the floods, as he called for international funding for a massive reconstruction effort. The Australian government announced it would provide $5 million in humanitarian assistance as Wong prepared to speak to her Nepalese counterpart on Friday afternoon to discuss how Australia could support the recovery effort. Loading Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a post on social media: “Australia is sending crisis and humanitarian response specialists to help after the devastating Nepal-China floods. We’re also providing humanitarian assistance including food, emergency shelter and medical support.”



Greens senator David Shoebridge said the $5 million pledged by Australia would “not come close” to meeting the need for recovery and repair efforts. “I think Australia needs to step up and really commit to helping rebuild. This is a country with minimal spare resources,” he said. Gallery Gallery icon 24 images Floods Photo gallery: Flash flooding devastates Nepal and Tibet Fast-moving waters swept through villages, wiping out bridges, roads and entire settlements in a Nepalese valley near the border with China on Wednesday. There was more good news on Friday, when 883 locals and labourers were rescued in the Rasuwa district in an effort that included an “extremely dangerous and challenging” rescue mission that freed 350 people trapped in the tunnel of a hydropower plant.



“The troops are still gathering to safely evacuate more than 100 people trapped in the same tunnel,” the Nepalese Prime Minister’s Office said. Footage released by the office showed a team of Nepalese soldiers crawling through thick mud up a steep passageway to enter the tunnel and save those trapped inside. United Nations under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs Tom Fletcher said aid teams were experiencing major difficulties trying to reach the areas most affected by the floods due to the extent of damage to roads and bridges in the area. “It’s a very, very challenging terrain for them to be navigating right now,” Fletcher told CNN. “We’re having to use air assets to reach them. The immediate priority is saving as many lives as we can.”



Footage released by the BBC showed a giant boulder being swept along by the flood, underlining the force of the torrent. Fear of further flooding Nepal and China had both warned of the risks of further flooding in the Himalayas as debris from the initial glacier collapse formed a lake straddling their border. “Residents of the lower banks … passengers, rescuers engaged in rescue operations, and all concerned are requested to exercise special caution and stay in safe places away from the river banks and risky areas,” Nepal’s disaster authority said.



One of the engineers, Chen Hanxiao, said the general approach to reducing the lake’s threat was to excavate a drainage channel at a lower point of the dam, but the width and depth of that channel needed calculations based on how fast the water would flow and how quickly the lake would fill. Related Article Updated

Floods The 41 Australians missing in the Nepal-Tibet floods, and what we know about them China on Thursday said 3 million cubic meters of water, the equivalent of about 1200 Olympic swimming pools, was expected to flow into the lake over the next three days. Peak flow was expected around September 1. Chinese President Xi Jinping dispatched his second-in-command, Premier Li Qiang, to visit the devastated areas of Tibet, demonstrating the severity of the disaster, which may be the worst since an earthquake in 2015 killed about 9000 people. Li inspected emergency rescue and relief operations, and visited first responders and displaced people in temporary shelters, according to the official Xinhua News Agency.



Assessments based on seismic and satellite data indicate the initial flood was triggered by the collapse of a glacier and underlying bedrock in the Himalayan region between Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, causing a 5.2-magnitude seismic event that sent water, ice, rock and debris downstream. Images and videos circulated online show the extent of the water’s force. Walls of grey water swept through villages and valleys, pulling down trees, pushing boulders and sweeping over masses of people attempting to flee. The aftermath from a tidal wave of mud, rock and water that devastated towns and villages along the Lhende River. AFP The flood is a major test for Nepal’s fledgling government and its new leader, former rapper Balendra Shah, who rode to power on a wave of Gen Z enthusiasm. He will need to work closely with regional neighbours China and India. China has deployed at least 574 rescuers to the land crossing, and India says it is co-ordinating closely with Kathmandu on rescue and relief efforts. The country’s tourism industry, which supports over 1 million jobs, will take a hit in a peak period, and it will be anxious about the future given Nepal’s frequency of extreme weather events.



Which regions were hit? The Bhote Koshi River flooded about 9am on Wednesday (1pm AEST), destroying several villages as well as roads and hydropower projects, officials said. Warnings were issued in several districts urging people to stay away from the banks of the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers. Loading The flood triggered a mudslide that hit Gyirong Port, a major land crossing with neighbouring Tibet, cutting roads, communications and power links to the area.



Rasuwa, the worst-affected area, witnessed a flash flood similar to those in August last year, when a glacial lake in neighbouring Tibet overflowed due to high temperatures in the mountain region. Nine people died, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting the two countries, was damaged at the time. Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said the Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi River, had experienced its highest recorded flood on Wednesday. Damaged houses stand precariously near the swollen, debris-choked banks of the Trishuli River after flash floods in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha Rescuers use an earthmover to carry a survivor to safety along the Trishuli River in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha “The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in 14 months, this time triggered by an ice rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream,” said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the climate research group.



“In a warming Himalaya, early warning is the first line of adaptation.” The Himalayan region, which spans Nepal and several neighbouring countries, including India, is especially vulnerable to heavy rain, floods and landslides because it is warming faster than much of the rest of the world due to human-caused climate change. Loading Related Article Floods ‘Most of my family is still missing’: The frantic search in Kathmandu for loved ones Research has shown that extreme weather events, including heatwaves, heavy rain and melting glaciers, have become more frequent in the region.



Members of the Kathmandu research group found this year that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region are melting at an accelerating rate. Ice loss rates have doubled since 2000, primarily due to rising global temperatures and climate change. Australians in need of emergency consular assistance should contact the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s 24-hour Consular Emergency Centre on 1300 555 135, or +61 2 6261 3305 (if calling from overseas). World.title: After 15 years of active service, Rockpool Perth is getting a $3 million makeover
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outEat and drink Perth After 15 years of active service, Rockpool Perth is getting a $3 million makeover When the marquee steakhouse reopens, expect a refreshed dining room and bar, a new private dining room plus a stronger seafood focus. Max Veenhuyzen August 29, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Consistency, insist the personal trainers and motivational speakers, is important. At Rockpool Bar & Grill Perth, consistency is a way of life and helps explain why the luxe steakhouse – despite opening its doors in 2011; despite changing fashion and food trends; despite the dedication of new temples of beef across P-Town; and despite the departure of Rockpool’s famous, ponytailed founder – remains a key figure in the city’s dining landscape as well as the casino’s safest bet. (That the restaurant had a reputation for only putting the best ingredients in its shopping trolley and dry-ageing fridges helps too, as does its ability to cook said ingredients very well and very simply, time after time.) Rockpool Bar & Grill Perth executive chef Brendan Owens, general manager Laura Bartolone, chief executive Frank Tucker, and culinary director Santiago Aristizabal. Shot By Thom After 15 years of active duty, Rockpool is taking a three-week sabbatical later this year and getting some work done: three million dollars of work, to be exact. According to Rockpool owners Hunter Street Hospitality, this makeover will mark the biggest change to the space since Neil Perry and designer Grant Cheyne rebooted the former food court into a gilded, classically inspired steakhouse. For management, this refresh is a chance to start writing the restaurant’s new chapter. “This renovation is our opportunity to begin Rockpool 2.0, which is exciting,” says general manager Laura Bartolone.



So what changes are on the cards? A little more colour, for one. While I’ve appreciated the timelessness of the room’s existing taupe, gold and beige palette, those proposed persimmon-hued banquettes do bring a jolt of energy to the room. (These new bench seats also face towards the restaurant proper and open kitchen; a nicer view, I reckon, than the postcard-perfect white big top circus tent currently squatting in the carpark and whose gracious curves are obscured by hessian curtains.) Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Related Article 14 / 20 Review No, Google Maps isn’t playing up: this Perth gym really does house a great Malay cafe The layout of the dining room (260 seats, an increase of 20 seats) will be rejigged to create more fluid, modular areas that can better accommodate large groups. The bar is also getting upsized and will be able to fit 40 revellers in a revamped, more standalone space. A third private dining room is also being built. Considering the fit-out is being handled by SGB Group – also responsible for the recent facelift of Rockpool Bar & Grill Sydney – it’s safe to assume that the new-look Perth will feel a little more like Sydney (and vice-versa). The food offering, meanwhile, is also being streamlined and brought into line with what’s happening nationally. While fellow collectors of restaurant ephemera will be crestfallen to hear that Rockpool will stop printing daily dated lunch and dinner menus (the carte will now be presented in a leather binder) news that the kitchen will reopen with a stronger seafood focus should help soften that blow. Greenham dry-aged F1 Wagyu reserve T-bone. Kristoffer Paulsen



“The goal is to replicate the beef program into the seafood side of things,” says Rockpool Perth executive chef Brendan Owens. (This new seafood focus has already been implemented at Rockpool’s Sydney and Melbourne siblings.) “We’ve always had good raw seafood on but there’ll be more of a focus on cooked seafood. Things like whole marron, squid, fish and lobsters.” Still, the cornerstones of Rockpool’s identity will remain. There will still be a big focus on beef that’s been aged and butchered in-house. There will still be an encyclopaedic thirst trap of a wine list to thumb through. (Christian Baeppler, Rockpool Perth’s sommelier, placed second in the inaugural Sommeliers Australia Top 100 sommeliers list announced this week.) And there will still be a dining room perpetually set for big night – or big day – out celebrations. “Rockpool will always be the same,” says Bartolone. “We don’t want to be a casual restaurant and we aren’t going to start doing gastronomy. This is a premium, fine dining steakhouse and we need to reflect that across everything. Not only on what you have in your plate and the service, but the ambience, lighting and music. Everything.” Did somebody say something about consistency? Rockpool Bar & Grill Perth closes on Monday October 5 and reopens on Wednesday October 28.
